title: Android November 2026 Update: Wallet Fills Your CVV, Quick Share Previews and Easier Storage Cleanup
desc: No new Android version needed. Every change in Google's November system updates, in plain words, and how to make sure your phone has them.
text: Written on 26 November 2026. This is based on Google's own System Services release notes and on 9to5Google's report of 23 November. The two lists differ in a few places, and we say where. Google rolls these updates out gradually, so a feature listed here may take a few weeks to reach your phone. Your Android phone gets a quiet update from Google every month, even when your phone maker sends nothing. The November 2026 round brings a few things you will notice: Google Wallet can now fill in your card's security code for you, Quick Share shows a preview of a YouTube link before you accept it, a new storage tool helps you clear large files, and your photos can back up to a Windows PC over Quick Share. Here is everything in plain words, and how to make sure you have it. The short version Wallet fills in your CVV. Google Play services v26.46 (23 November) lets Google Wallet autofill a saved card's security code on card checks, after you confirm it with your screen lock. Quick Share previews YouTube links. The person receiving a shared YouTube link sees a preview before accepting it. Easier storage cleanup. v26.45 (16 November) shows cleanup progress and lets you swipe through large files to keep or delete them. Photos to Windows. v26.43 (2 November) adds automatic backup of photos and videos from Android to a Windows PC through Quick Share. Play Store age controls. Play Store v54.2 lets you manage age range sharing per app in Play settings. Play Protect reminder. Play Store v53.9 reminds you if Play Protect has been turned off for a while. What Google System Updates are Android updates come from two places. Your phone maker sends the big Android version updates and the monthly security patch. Google, separately, updates a set of apps and services that sit underneath Android on almost every phone with the Play Store: Google Play services, the Play Store itself, Android WebView (which shows web pages inside apps), and the Google Play system update. Google publishes a list of these changes every month, tagged by device type, such as phone, Wear OS watch, TV, car or PC. That is why a two-year-old phone can still get new Wallet or Quick Share features without a full system update. Google Wallet: security codes filled in for you The most practical change in November is for online shopping. Google's notes say Play services v26.46 adds autofill of saved card security codes (CVV or CVC) on card verification screens in Google Wallet, after you authenticate with your screen lock. In other words, when a checkout asks you to confirm your card, you can confirm with your fingerprint, face or PIN instead of finding the card. Two other Wallet items arrived earlier in the month in v26.44 (9 November): a Traveler QR feature, and support for residential door keys that work with the Matter Aliro standard, through Google Home. Google's notes do not say which countries get these first. A word of caution for this week: an autofilled code is still only as safe as the shop you are on. With thousands of fake Black Friday sites online, check the address before you let your phone fill in anything. Our Black Friday fake domains report shows what to look for. Quick Share: YouTube previews and backup to Windows Two Quick Share changes landed this month: Link previews. In v26.46, when someone sends you a YouTube link over Quick Share, you see a preview before you accept the transfer. That makes it easier to refuse something you did not expect. Backup to Windows. In v26.43, Google lists automatic backup of photos and videos from Android to Windows through Quick Share. Google's note is short and does not give setup steps, so look for the option in Quick Share on your PC and phone over the coming weeks. Storage cleanup and Family Hub Play services v26.45 (16 November) brings storage management updates under your Google account: you can track your cleanup progress, review large files by swiping to keep or delete them, and see which Google account is being managed. If your phone keeps warning you that storage is full, our step by step guide on freeing up space on Android and iPhone walks you through every option. Earlier, v26.43 added access to the Android Family Hub from Android Settings, which gathers family controls in one place. Play Store v54.2 also adds app-level controls for sharing your age range with apps, managed in Play settings, and Play services v26.44 gives developers a way to ask for the age range of the person using the device. These come as more countries and US states require age checks, a topic we covered in age verification and privacy. Security and Play Store changes Play Protect reminder (Play Store v53.9, 2 November): if Play Protect, Google's app scanner, stays switched off for a while, the Play Store reminds you. Keep it on, especially if you install apps from outside the Play Store. Password Manager imports (v26.43): when you import passwords and passkeys that clash with ones already saved, Google Password Manager now lets you choose which to keep. WebView v158 and v159 (9 and 18 November): security and privacy improvements and bug fixes for the component that shows web pages inside apps. Play Store extras: a large watch face preview on app pages (v54.1), Play Achievements for gaming milestones (v54.2), and quicker sign-in state updates for Play Games (v54.0). Two small differences between the sources: 9to5Google lists an outdoor workout feature where a watch uses the phone's GPS to save battery, and an on-screen gamepad on the Pixel Fold, which we did not find on Google's own page. Google's page also lists an Android AICore update dated 25 November for faster AI model loading on phones and PCs, which came after 9to5Google's article. How to make sure you have the update Update Google Play services. Open Settings, Apps, then find Google Play services and open its app details in the Play Store. If an Update button shows, tap it. Update the Play Store. In the Play Store, tap your profile picture, Settings, About, then Update Play Store. Install the Google Play system update. Its date is shown under Settings, About phone, Android version, or under Security and privacy on many phones. Tap it to check for an update and restart if asked. Update apps. In the Play Store, open Manage apps and device and update everything, which includes Android System WebView. Be patient. Google rolls out server-side features over several weeks, so a feature can be missing even when your version number matches. Menu names vary between phone makers, so if you cannot find an option, search for it in the Settings app. Frequently asked questions Do I need a new Android version to get these features? No. These come through Google Play services and the Play Store, which update on most Android phones regardless of the Android version, as long as the phone is supported. Is it safe to let Google Wallet fill in my CVV? Google requires your screen lock before it fills in the code. The bigger risk is the website itself, so only use it on shops you know, reached by typing the address or using their app. Why don't I see the new features yet? Google releases them gradually. Update Play services and the Play Store, then wait a few weeks. Some features are also limited to certain countries or devices. What is Android WebView? It is the part of Android that shows web pages inside apps. It gets security fixes almost every month, so keep it updated in the Play Store. Where does Google list these changes? On its Google System Services release notes page, linked below, updated through each month. title: Black Friday Phone Deals 2026: How to Spot a Real Deal and Avoid Phone Scams
desc: Which? found 92 percent of tracked deals were no cheaper than other times. A checklist for buying a phone this Black Friday without regret.
text: Written on 26 November 2026. The buying advice comes from the consumer group Which? (articles of 19 November 2026 and 20 November 2025) and the scam warnings from Cleveland19's report of 12 November 2026. Which? is a UK group, so its prices are in pounds, but the checks work in any country. We could not read a ConsumerAffairs article on the same topic, so it is not used. A new phone is one of the most popular Black Friday buys, and one of the easiest to get wrong. Some "deals" are the normal price with a crossed-out number above it. Some are phones meant for another country. And some are not shops at all. Black Friday falls on 27 November this year, so here is how to tell a real phone deal from a bad one, and how to spot the scams that copy big retailers. The short version Check the price history, not the "was" price. Which? found that 92 percent of Black Friday deals it tracked were available at the same price or cheaper at other times of the year. Last year's model is usually the best value. Which? says waiting about 12 months after launch can save hundreds. Count the years of updates. Google promises seven years of support on phones since the Pixel 8, Apple five years, and Xiaomi, according to Which?, two years. Avoid grey imports and unknown marketplace sellers. The phone may not work fully on your network or have a local warranty. Never trust a link in a text about a delayed order, and never call a customer service number from a sponsored search result. Is it really a deal? Which? advises using a price tracker before you buy, such as Keepa or CamelCamelCamel for Amazon, or PriceSpy for other shops. Its rule is simple: if the deal price is not a true historical low, it is not a real deal. The same article cites the group's research finding that 92 percent of Black Friday deals were available for the same price or less at other times of the year. Look at where the discount comes from too. Which? notes that Samsung often discounts its own phones directly, while Apple rarely offers cash discounts on its own site, so real iPhone discounts tend to come from large retailers. Which phone gives you the most for your money Buy last year's model Which?'s November 2026 guide says brands regularly discount older models and that waiting about a year after launch can save you hundreds. Its advice is to shop for a phone released in the previous year. Do not overpay for premium The same guide says phones costing £200 to £350 in its tests had the best battery performance, and suggests aiming for a mid-range phone with a top budget of about £500. Mid-range lines such as the Pixel "a" or Galaxy "A" series are often the best Black Friday value, paired with a SIM-only plan. Check how long it gets updates Security updates matter as much as the camera. A phone that stops getting fixes becomes riskier every month. Which? lists Google at seven years from launch on phones since the Pixel 8, Apple at five years, and Xiaomi at two. A cheaper phone that loses support next year is not a bargain. Divide the price by the years of support left to compare fairly. Contracts, trade-ins and hidden costs Contracts. Which? says you will often pay more overall on a contract than buying the phone outright, calling many contracts a high-interest loan in disguise. It also warns about mid-contract price rises. If you can, pay for the handset upfront and pick a cheap SIM-only plan. Trade-ins. Get an independent valuation before accepting a retailer's "enhanced" trade-in. Values vary widely between shops, and Which? notes you usually have about 14 days to send the old phone after the new one arrives. The charger. Apple and Samsung no longer include a plug in the box. Which? says an official fast charger can cost £20 to £40 and warns that cheap unbranded chargers can be a fire risk. Refurbished phones. Which? suggests buying refurbished only with at least a 12-month warranty, from a well-reviewed seller. Before you trade in or sell your old phone, back it up, sign out of your accounts and reset it. That removes your photos, messages and passwords for good. Grey imports and marketplace sellers A grey import is a genuine phone bought for another country and sold in yours. Which? warns these may have no valid local warranty and may not support all of your country's 4G and 5G bands, which means weaker signal or missing features. On marketplaces, check the seller's detailed ratings, and on Amazon check whether the item is sold by Amazon or by a third party. A price far below every major shop is a warning, not a win. The phone scams that peak on Black Friday Cleveland19's report quotes a ConsumerAffairs writer on the tricks that appear every year: Ghost websites. Fake shops promoted through social media ads, with prices that seem too good to be true. Before you click, search the company name with the word "scam". Fake closing-down sales. Ads for "store closing" or "final close-out" sales that lead to fake sites built to collect your details. Fake customer service numbers. Scammers buy sponsored search listings for big shops' support lines, which can appear above the real number. Use the shop's app or official website to find the number. Delivery problem texts. A message saying your order has a problem, with a link to fix it. A real company will not text you to verify a tracking number or address. The scale is real this year. Check Point counted more than 4,000 new Black Friday themed web addresses, almost one in five of them risky, as we reported in our Black Friday fake domains article. Our older guide to spotting fake shops has a full checklist. Your phone deal checklist Type the shop's address yourself or use its official app. Check the price history in a tracker. Prefer last year's model or a mid-range phone. Check how many years of updates are left. Confirm the phone is meant for your country and has a local warranty. Add up the total cost of any contract. Pay by credit card or your phone's wallet, never by gift card or bank transfer. Know the return policy and keep the receipt. Shopping on your phone? A separate browser profile for shopping keeps a rushed click away from your email and bank. Frequently asked questions Are Black Friday phone deals worth it? Some are, many are not. Which? found 92 percent of the deals it tracked were available at the same price or cheaper at other times, so check price history first. Should I buy a phone on contract on Black Friday? Which? says buying outright with a SIM-only plan often costs less overall. Add up the full contract cost and check for mid-contract price rises. What is a grey import phone? A genuine phone made for another country. It may lack a local warranty and may not work on all your network's 4G and 5G bands. How do I know a phone shop is real? Type the address yourself, search the name with the word "scam", check reviews and the payment options, and be wary of prices far below every big retailer. Is a refurbished phone safe to buy? It can be. Which? suggests choosing one with at least a 12-month warranty from a reputable refurbisher. title: Phone Storage Full? How to Free Up Space on Android and iPhone Without Losing Anything
desc: Most phones hold gigabytes you can clear in minutes. The safe, official ways to get space back on Android and iPhone, quickest wins first.
text: Updated 26 November 2026. Steps are taken from Google's and Apple's own help pages. Menu names differ between phone makers and software versions, so if a step does not match your phone, search for the setting by name in the Settings app. "Storage almost full" is one of the most common phone warnings, and it usually appears at the worst moment, just as you try to take a photo or install an update. The good news is that most phones hold gigabytes you can clear in a few minutes without losing anything that matters. This guide covers Android and iPhone, starting with the quickest wins and the safe way to do each one. The short version Find out what is using space first: Settings, Storage on Android, or Settings, General, iPhone Storage on iPhone. Photos and videos are usually the biggest item. Back them up, then remove the copies on the phone. Empty the trash. Deleted photos stay in Recently Deleted or Trash for 30 days and still take up space. Archive or offload apps you do not use. Both keep your data and remove the app itself. Clear junk files with Files by Google on Android. Old message attachments add up. On iPhone you can make Messages delete old conversations automatically. Step one: see what is taking up space Android Open the Settings app and tap Storage, then tap a category to see what is inside. On Android 14 and newer, Google's help page also describes a Free up space option under Storage, which lists photos, videos and apps you have not used recently. iPhone Open Settings, General, then iPhone Storage. You will see recommendations at the top and a list of apps sorted by size. Tap Show All to see every recommendation, then Enable on the ones you want. Apple notes that some space is used by cached files, which the iPhone removes by itself when it needs room. Photos and videos: the biggest win Back up before you delete anything. Once your photos are safely in the cloud, you can remove the copies stored on the phone. Google Photos on Android Make sure backup is on and finished. In Google Photos, tap your profile picture or initial, then Free up space on this device. Google shows how much space you will get back. Tap Free up to delete the backed-up copies from your phone. Google says photos and videos fewer than 30 days old may stay on your device, but they are still in your Google Photos library. Be careful with one thing: deleting a photo inside the Google Photos app deletes it from your device and your backup too. Use Free up space, not delete, if you want to keep it online. Android can also do this automatically. Under Settings, Storage, Free up space, open the menu, Settings, and turn on Smart Storage, which removes backed-up photos and videos when storage is almost full. iCloud Photos on iPhone Turn on iCloud Photos under Settings, your name, iCloud, Photos, and make sure Optimize iPhone Storage is on. Apple keeps the full-quality originals in iCloud and smaller copies on the phone. Apple gives every account 5 GB of free iCloud storage, which fills quickly, so you may need more space or a computer backup. iOS 17 and newer also offer a Recommended for You view to review large files, and you can merge duplicate photos. Empty the trash, or nothing changes This is the step most people miss. On iPhone, deleted photos go to Recently Deleted and stay there for 30 days. To clear them now, open Photos, Collections, Recently Deleted under Utilities, tap Select, choose items and delete them. In Google Photos, deleted items stay in Trash for 30 days. To empty it, open Collections, Trash, then the menu and Empty Trash. On Android, Storage cleanup moves files to the Trash as well, so check it after you clean. Apps you rarely use Archive apps on Android On Android 15 and newer, you can archive an app: open Settings, Apps, choose the app, and tap Archive. Google says archiving removes the app's software, permissions and temporary files and stops notifications, but keeps the icon and your data. Tap the faded icon later to reinstall it. Or uninstall apps you never use. Offload apps on iPhone In Settings, General, iPhone Storage, tap an app and choose Offload App, which frees the space used by the app but keeps its documents and data. To have this happen automatically, go to Settings, Apps, App Store and turn on Offload Unused Apps. The icon stays with a small cloud symbol, and tapping it reinstalls the app. Clear junk files and app caches On Android, open Files by Google, tap Clean, and on the Junk files card tap the Clean button, then Clear. Google says this removes temporary files and does not change app settings, but the deletion is permanent. Files by Google can also find duplicate files, old screenshots and large files. You can also clear one app's cache in Settings, Apps, choose the app, then Storage. Know the difference: Clear cache deletes temporary data, and the app may be slower the next time you open it. Clear storage deletes all of the app's data, including sign-ins and settings, so avoid it unless you mean to reset the app. Downloads, messages and other hidden space Offline video and music. Remove downloads you have finished with in YouTube, YouTube Music, Netflix, Spotify or the Apple TV app. Old messages on iPhone. Go to Settings, Apps, Messages, Keep Messages, and choose a shorter period than Forever. Apple warns that conversations and their attachments older than that period are then removed automatically, so save any photos you want first. WhatsApp and chat apps. Most have their own storage manager in settings that lists large videos and forwarded files. The Downloads folder. PDFs, installers and saved images build up quietly. Delete what you do not need, or copy it to a computer first. Your browser. A browser's cache and offline pages can grow large too. In Rapid+ you can clear browsing data per profile. Google's November 2026 system update also brings a new storage cleanup tool that lets you swipe through large files to keep or delete them, as we explain in our November update guide. What not to do Do not install "cleaner" or "booster" apps from unknown developers. Many show ads or ask for broad permissions, and your phone already has the tools above. Do not delete before you back up. Check that your backup has finished. Do not tap Clear storage on an app unless you are ready to set it up again. Do not ignore the warning for long. A nearly full phone can fail to install security updates. Frequently asked questions Why is my storage still full after deleting photos? Deleted photos stay in Recently Deleted on iPhone or Trash in Google Photos for 30 days. Empty it to get the space back. Is clearing the cache safe? Yes. Clearing an app's cache removes temporary data only, although the app may load more slowly the next time. Clear storage is different and removes all of the app's data. What is the difference between archiving and uninstalling an app? Archiving on Android, or offloading on iPhone, removes the app but keeps your data and the icon, so reinstalling picks up where you left off. Uninstalling removes both. Will Google Photos Free up space delete my photos? No. It removes only the copies on your phone that are already backed up. They stay in your Google Photos library. Do phone cleaner apps help? Usually not. The built-in tools and Files by Google do the same job without ads or extra permissions. title: Android 17 Security and Privacy Features: Scam Call Checks, One-Time Location and More
desc: A plain guide to the new Android scam, theft and location protections announced by Google, and what to switch on today.
text: Written on 24 November 2026. The features below come from Google's Android security and privacy announcement of 12 May 2026, with Android Authority's report of the same day as a cross-check. Rollout phrases such as "in the coming weeks" date from May, and we did not check which features have reached phones since. Availability also depends on your phone maker and country. Android 17 brings a long list of security changes, with new protection against scam calls, a way to share your location just once, limits on what a thief can do with a stolen phone, and a check on APK files before Chrome downloads them. This guide lists what Google announced, in plain words, and what each feature means for you. It also says which ones you have to switch on yourself. The short version Scam calls: "Verified financial calls" flags spoofed calls pretending to be your bank. It starts with Revolut, Itaú and Nubank on Android 11 and newer. Location: a new button shares your precise location only temporarily, and an indicator appears when an app reads your location. Chrome: if Safe Browsing is on, Chrome checks an APK for known malware before you download it. Theft protection: "Mark as lost" can lock a phone with biometrics, and PIN guessing is limited more strictly. One-time codes: Android hides sensitive codes from most apps for three hours. Scam and call protection Verified financial calls Google describes a new phone call spoofing protection feature, built to keep your money and personal information safe. It starts rolling out on Android 11 and newer with Revolut, Itaú and Nubank, with more banks to follow later in the year. The idea is that your phone can tell when a call that claims to be from your bank really comes from it. Live Threat Detection Live Threat Detection gets new warnings about suspicious behaviour, including SMS forwarding and accessibility overlay abuse. Google gave no version or date for these. Scam detection for chat notifications Google lists scam detection for chat notifications as part of Advanced Protection on Android 17. Chrome on Android checks APKs If Safe Browsing is turned on and you try to download an app file from a website, Google says it will evaluate the APK for known malware and stop you before you download it. Google gave no version or date. Android Authority says the feature had been spotted in Chrome Canary. This is the most useful change for people who install apps from outside the Play Store. Our article on Android developer verification explains the other half of that story. Advanced Protection Advanced Protection is a stricter mode for people at higher risk, and it gains several things on Android 17: Apps that are not labelled as accessibility tools lose access to the accessibility service, which scammers abuse to watch your screen. Android Authority says this was already in Android 17 Beta 2. Device-to-device sign-in and Chrome WebGPU support are turned off. Scam detection for chat notifications is added. USB protection is available on all Pixel phones running Android 16 or newer, and is coming to more devices. Intrusion Logging is rolling out to devices on the Android 16 December update and newer. Android Enterprise support for Advanced Protection comes later in the year. If your phone is stolen Mark as lost (in Find Hub) can lock a phone with biometric authentication, disable new Wi-Fi and Bluetooth connections and hide Quick Settings. Default protections: theft features turn on by default on new Android 17 devices, and extend to devices running Android 10 or higher in Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Peru and the UK. PIN guesses: Google says it has significantly reduced the number of tries before a lock-out, with longer waits after failures. IMEI on the lock screen: on Android 12 or higher, a device's IMEI can be read from the lock screen so that police, makers or carriers can verify ownership. It can be turned off in settings. Privacy and location Temporary precise location: a new button lets you share your exact location for just that moment, rather than giving the app permanent access. Location indicator: a marker at the top of the screen shows when your location is being read, and tapping it lists recent apps. Contact picker: apps can ask for specific contacts only, with temporary access and limited fields, in place of your whole address book. OTP hiding: Android hides sensitive security codes from most apps for three hours. Android Authority ties this to Android 17. Under the hood Android 17 introduces AISeal with pKVM, which isolates on-device data used by AI features. Android OS verification arrives on Pixel phones first, with a public record of Google app builds. The disable 2G toggle lets carriers turn 2G off by default. Post-quantum cryptography is introduced. What to switch on today Turn on Safe Browsing in Chrome so that APK checks and warnings can work. Use the one-time location option for apps that do not need constant access, and review which apps have precise location. Check Find Hub and make sure it is on for your phone. Set a longer PIN than four digits, and add biometrics. Consider Advanced Protection if you are a journalist, activist or otherwise at higher risk. Install updates as soon as your phone offers them. New features arrive only with them. The same approach works on any phone: our shopping safety guide and passkey guide cover habits that protect you whichever system you use. Frequently asked questions Is Android 17 out? Google announced the features on 12 May 2026, and some were already in Android 17 beta builds. Whether your phone has received the final release depends on your maker, so check Settings, System, System update. Which phones get these features? It varies. Some, like Verified financial calls, target Android 11 and newer. Others are Android 17 only, and some start on Pixel phones. Does Chrome now block malware apps? If Safe Browsing is on, Chrome will check an APK for known malware before the download finishes and stop it if it is flagged. It checks only for known malware, so it is not a guarantee. How do I share my location just once? Android 17 adds a location button that apps can use to ask for your precise location temporarily. If an app uses it, you choose to share only for that moment. Can apps still read my one-time codes? Android 17 hides sensitive security codes from most apps for three hours. Your messaging app and some system parts still see them. title: Artex: The AI Hacking Tool the FBI Says Breaches Networks in Under Three Hours
desc: ConnectWise, Barracuda and South Korean banks were hit. The FBI warning on an AI tool that finds simple weaknesses faster than people can respond.
text: Written on 24 November 2026. This is based on TechCrunch's report of 16 November on an FBI advisory about an AI hacking tool named Artex. We did not read the FBI advisory itself. TechCrunch does not list the FBI's recommendations, so the advice section is our own reading of the weaknesses described, and we say so. The FBI has warned that criminals and spies are using Artex, an open-source tool that runs penetration tests with AI agents, to break into real networks. In some cases it took under three hours from picking a target to being inside. Victims include the IT software firm ConnectWise, the security company Barracuda and several South Korean financial institutions. The common thread is not clever tricks. It is simple weaknesses that were left open. The short version Artex is one of several open-source platforms that use AI models to probe networks. It can be connected to hosted models, open-source models and non-US models. The first public release was in July. The developer later made it closed-source, but the FBI says the earlier open version still circulates and is widely available. The FBI says attackers have targeted financial services, government, technology, defence, phone and internet companies, and law firms. Artex was used against several South Korean financial institutions, stealing personal data of at least 68,000 people, according to the FBI as reported by TechCrunch. In some cases, Artex-linked attacks went from targeting to active compromise in under three hours. What Artex is A penetration test is a controlled attack that a company pays for, to find its weak spots before a real attacker does. Artex does this with AI agents. It scans a network quickly, finds simple bugs, exposed passwords or stolen passwords, uses them to get a foothold and then spreads to databases and mailboxes. The same thing that makes it useful to defenders makes it useful to criminals. TechCrunch notes that after the attacks the developer made the software closed-source, but the earlier open version is still easy to get. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be noisy. They create a lot of traffic and data that can trigger alerts. But the tool moves so fast that human defenders can find it hard to keep up. The victims named ConnectWise TechCrunch says Microsoft previously reported that hackers, whom it believes are likely Chinese, used Artex to break into ConnectWise and reach the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 of its customers. The FBI confirmed this. A ConnectWise spokesperson told TechCrunch the company cannot confirm the number of affected environments. Barracuda Barracuda disclosed that financially motivated criminals breached it in an Artex-linked attack. The tool found an exposed credential belonging to a third-party service that Barracuda had not revoked after it stopped working with that vendor. Attackers used it to reach credential stores that Barracuda uses to collect data from customers' systems. Barracuda said its logs were not detailed enough to rule out access, so it changed all customer credentials. Its security chief, Arve Kjoelen, wrote that defenders who rely on spotting and responding to malicious activity "will often arrive after the attacker has finished". South Korean financial institutions The FBI says Artex was used against several South Korean financial institutions, with the attacks blamed largely on weak defences and missing protections such as multi-factor authentication. At least 68,000 people had personal data stolen. TechCrunch also links an earlier article of 6 November, which says researchers found hundreds of Artex systems exposed on the internet without a password, including the one used against South Korea. What "under three hours" means TechCrunch says that in some cases Artex-linked attacks went from targeting a system to active compromise in under three hours. It is a speed claim about some cases, not an average, and the article gives no method or sample size. It also does not say whether the clock starts at the first scan or the first contact. The point still stands: an attack can move faster than many companies' response plans, which often measure time in days. What these attacks have in common Old, forgotten access. Barracuda's entry point was a credential for a vendor it no longer used. Nobody had switched it off. Missing second factor. The South Korean cases lacked multi-factor authentication. Thin logs. Barracuda could not tell what had been touched, so it had to assume the worst. Exposed tools. Some of the attackers' own Artex servers were open to anyone on the internet. None of these needs a new technology to fix. They need housekeeping. That echoes our report on supplier breaches, where leftover access and thin logging also played a part. What defenders can do (our reading) TechCrunch does not list the FBI's recommendations. These steps follow from the weaknesses it describes and should be read as our inference. Turn on multi-factor authentication everywhere, and prefer phishing-resistant methods such as passkeys. Our passkey guide explains how they work. Revoke access when a vendor leaves. Keep a list of every outside service that holds a key to your systems. Rotate credentials that may have been exposed, and remove passwords from code and storage. Keep detailed logs so that you can say what was and was not accessed. Fix the simple things first. AI tools find the easy bugs fastest. Plan for speed. Decide in advance who can cut off access in the first hour. What it means for everyone else If you are not running a company network, the practical message is that automated attacks lower the cost of going after small targets too. Use a unique password for each service, a password manager and two-step verification on email. Keep software updated, as in our guide to the latest Chrome update. Frequently asked questions What is Artex? It is an open-source platform that uses AI agents to test the security of networks. The FBI says criminals and spies are using it to attack real organisations. Who has been attacked with it? TechCrunch names ConnectWise, Barracuda and several South Korean financial institutions. The FBI says targets also include government, defence, technology and law firms. Is the tool still available? The developer made the software closed-source after the attacks, but the FBI says the earlier open-source version is still widely accessible. Does AI make hacking much faster? In some cases, yes. TechCrunch reports compromises in under three hours. It is not an average, and the article does not explain how it was measured. How can I reduce my risk? Use multi-factor authentication, unique passwords and prompt updates. Companies should also remove old vendor access and keep detailed logs. title: Black Friday 2026: 4,000 Fake Shopping Domains, 10,000 Fake Stores and How to Avoid Them
desc: Fake shops, fake refund pages and fake parcel alerts are everywhere before 27 November. The numbers, the tricks and what to check before you pay.
text: Written on 24 November 2026. The 2026 figures come from Check Point Research as reported by the Swiss site Netzwoche (17 November) and the German site IT-Daily (18 November), and from NordVPN research reported by Money (6 November). We read translations of the German articles and did not find Check Point's own 2026 post. Some well-known "one in eleven" numbers are from 2025, and we keep them apart. Black Friday is on 27 November 2026, and the fake shops are ready. Check Point Research counted more than 4,000 newly registered web domains that combine sale-event words such as "Black Friday" or "Cyber Monday" with big brand or parcel-company names. Almost one in five was flagged as risky. Separately, NordVPN found more than 10,000 fake fashion stores copying 166 brands. This article gives you the numbers, the tricks and a short checklist you can use at the checkout. The short version Check Point Research found more than 4,000 new domains between October and 8 November 2026 with Black Friday, Cyber Monday or Singles' Day words, often plus names such as Amazon, AliExpress, Walmart, DHL or FedEx. Almost one in five of them was classified as risky by Check Point's ThreatCloud AI. It counted 647 new domains that add two to four letters after "Fedex", registered from September to 8 November. Not all are necessarily fraudulent. NordVPN reported more than 10,000 fraudulent stores impersonating 166 fashion and luxury brands in 26 countries. 1,549 were fully working at the time. NordVPN says Perplexity recommended two fake stores, and ChatGPT and Gemini cited other sites tied to the network. Safest habit: type the shop's address yourself or use its app, and do not rely on search results, social posts or an AI chatbot. What Check Point found The company watches newly registered domains. Its 2026 figures, as reported by IT-Daily and Netzwoche, are: More than 4,000 new domains containing Black Friday, Cyber Monday or Singles' Day terms, alongside brand and parcel-service names, from October to 8 November 2026. Almost one in five of those was classified as risky. 647 new.com domains that add two to four letters after "Fedex", from September to 8 November: 139 in September, 439 in October and 69 in the first eight days of November. An average of 2,458 cyber attacks a week per company in consumer goods and services in September and October 2026, up 28 percent since the start of the year, against 22 percent across all sectors. Netzwoche cautions that not every lookalike domain is fraudulent. Some belong to genuine resellers or to people who simply bought a name. Examples Check Point cited A fake Amazon refund page that asks for phone numbers and email addresses. Fake Best Buy and Walmart shops, and imitations of Oakley and AliExpress offers. A fake Amazon giveaway hosted on a Microsoft Azure subdomain that collected personal data through a form. Fake DHL and USPS pages that claim an address must be corrected or a parcel cannot be delivered, and some ask for the card number, expiry date and security code. What NordVPN found Money reports NordVPN research on a large network of fake fashion shops. More than 10,000 fraudulent online stores copy 166 brands, including names such as Adidas, Ralph Lauren, Dr. Martens, Crocs and Birkenstock, across 26 countries. At the time of writing, 1,549 were fully operational, and thousands more might launch before Black Friday. France and Germany were the most targeted countries, and NordVPN found 91 domains aimed at the US. Three details deserve attention: They are built to be found by search. Money says the stores are tuned to appear in Google results, so you do not have to click an advert to land on one. AI assistants can send you there. According to NordVPN, Perplexity recommended two fraudulent stores next to real retailers, and ChatGPT and Gemini cited other sites connected to the network. These are NordVPN's findings, not independent tests. The payment logos lie. The fake shops show PayPal and Klarna logos but do not accept them. They simply collect card details. Why these scams work A fake shop needs only a good deal, a believable address and a checkout. Most people judge a site by its look, and a copied design costs nothing. The name that Black Friday gives to a domain makes it look current. The urgency also helps: a countdown timer and "only 3 left" push you to pay before you think. The padlock in the address bar does not help either. It shows the connection is encrypted, not that the seller is honest, as the FTC says. Our guide to spotting fake shops covers that point in detail. A 60 second checklist before you pay Type or bookmark the address. Go to the shop you know, instead of following a link from search, social media or a chatbot. NordVPN gives the same advice. Read the whole domain. Watch for extra words, hyphens, doubled letters or odd endings such as.top or.cc. The brand name should be right before the first slash and the dot that follows it. Compare the price with the brand's own site. A big gap on a famous product is a warning sign. Check the payment options. If the page shows PayPal but the checkout only asks for a card, leave. Pay by credit card where you can, since it gives the best chance of a refund, or use your phone's wallet. Be careful with parcel messages. A text saying your parcel is stuck should send you to the carrier's official site or app, not to the link in the message. Use a separate browser profile for shopping so that a rushed click does not touch your email and banking. See our profiles guide. If you already entered card details Call your card issuer straight away, using the number on the card, and say you used a site that may be fake. Ask them to block and replace the card. Watch statements for several weeks. Change the password for any account whose details you typed in. A card that is saved in a shop account is a risk too, as in the Revolve breach. Frequently asked questions How many fake Black Friday sites are there? Check Point counted more than 4,000 new sale-themed domains between October and 8 November 2026, with almost one in five classified as risky. NordVPN found more than 10,000 fake fashion stores. The two studies measure different things, so the numbers do not add up. Is the one in eleven figure from this year? No. The one in eleven figure for risky Black Friday domains is from Check Point's 2025 research. The 2026 figure we found is almost one in five, though it is a different measure. Can an AI assistant send me to a fake shop? NordVPN says Perplexity recommended two fraudulent stores and that ChatGPT and Gemini cited sites connected to the fake network. Treat shop links from chatbots like any search result and check the address yourself. What is the safest way to pay? A credit card, or your phone's wallet, because they allow disputes and keep the real number from the shop. Avoid gift cards, bank transfers and crypto. How do I report a fake shop? Tell your card issuer first. Then report it to your national consumer authority. In the US that is ReportFraud.ftc.gov, and the FBI's IC3 also takes complaints. title: CISA Adds Four Exploited Flaws: Cisco Expressway, VMware vCenter, Apache Roller and SAP NetWeaver
desc: A hardcoded password in Cisco Expressway, a spy group's VMware zero-day and two more. The four flaws attackers are using right now.
text: Written on 24 November 2026. This is based on SecurityWeek's report of 23 November on four flaws that the US cyber agency CISA added to its list of known exploited vulnerabilities on 20 November. We could not read two other reports because they blocked our reader, and we did not read Cisco's advisory, so affected version ranges are not listed here. Check the vendor pages for those. On 20 November 2026 CISA added four flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list, which means attackers are already using them. The most serious is CVE-2026-76466 in Cisco Expressway, a hardcoded password weakness rated 9.8 out of 10 that can give an attacker full control. The others affect VMware vCenter, Apache Roller and SAP NetWeaver. If you run any of these products, today is a patching day. If you do not, there is still a useful lesson about how quickly attackers move. The short version Cisco Expressway, CVE-2026-76466 (9.8): a hardcoded credentials flaw that lets attackers run commands as root. Cisco patched it on 21 October in release X15.5.20. VMware vCenter, CVE-2026-123890 (critical): exploited as a zero-day by a China-linked espionage group called Armory Castle, also tracked as Warp Panda. Apache Roller, CVE-2026-129448 (critical): patched on 17 November and exploited as a zero-day. SAP NetWeaver, CVE-2025-42884 (6.5): a medium flaw fixed in November 2025, now confirmed as exploited. CISA told US federal agencies to patch the Cisco flaw within three days. What the "known exploited" list means CISA keeps a public catalogue of software flaws that have been used in real attacks. Being on it is a stronger signal than a high score, because most flaws with a high score are never exploited. For US federal agencies it comes with a deadline. For everyone else it is a plain message: this one is being used, patch it first. A flaw can reach the list in two ways. Either it was a zero-day, used before a fix existed, or it was an old flaw that attackers found still unpatched in the wild. This batch contains both kinds. Cisco Expressway: a password baked into the software Expressway is Cisco's gateway for video and voice traffic. It comes in two forms: Expressway-C, the core, and Expressway-E, the edge that faces the internet. SecurityWeek says the flaw affects devices running vulnerable versions and set up in a cluster. A "hardcoded credentials" bug means the software contains a fixed password that cannot be changed and that anyone who finds it can use. Here, an attacker can use it to run system commands with root privileges, the highest level on the machine. The Russian security firm F6 warned that attackers began exploiting the flaw shortly after proof-of-concept code was published, and that warning came two days before CISA's alert. SecurityWeek links a related issue in which persistent cookies and weak certificate checks could let an attacker reach the database service and call internal commands. The article does not say how many devices were breached or how far attackers got. Cisco's advisory is named cisco-sa-vcs-static-cred-hr7EWZ8t. What to do Check whether you run Expressway, and which versions. The fix is in release X15.5.20. Update clustered devices first, as they are the exposed configuration. Look for signs of a break-in. A patch closes the door, but it does not remove an attacker who is already inside. Limit who can reach the management interface, and keep it off the open internet. VMware vCenter: a spy group's zero-day vCenter is the control panel for many companies' virtual servers, which makes it a favourite target. CVE-2026-123890 is rated critical and was exploited as a zero-day by Armory Castle, a China-linked espionage group that is also tracked as Warp Panda. SecurityWeek's article does not say what the flaw allows or which versions are affected. Treat any vCenter that can be reached from outside as urgent, and follow VMware's advisory for the fix. Apache Roller: patched and attacked within days Apache Roller is open-source blogging software. CVE-2026-129448 is rated critical and was patched on 17 November. It was exploited as a zero-day, and CISA listed it three days later. No attacker has been named, and the article does not describe what the flaw does. If you run Roller, update to the patched version now. If you do not know whether you run it, check, because blogging tools are often forgotten servers. SAP NetWeaver: an old fix that people skipped CVE-2025-42884 is rated 6.5. It involves access to an unintended JNDI provider and could let an unauthenticated attacker read or change server information. SAP fixed it in its November 2025 updates, and SecurityWeek says there were no reports of exploitation before CISA's alert. A year later it is being used. This is the pattern behind the rise in ransomware that Beazley describes: attackers keep going after older flaws on systems that were never updated. What to take from it Patch by exploitation, not by score. A 6.5 that attackers use beats a 9.8 that nobody does. Internet-facing gateways come first. Video gateways, virtualisation consoles and web apps are reachable by anyone. Patching is not cleaning. If a flaw was open for weeks, check logs for earlier access. Keep an inventory. You cannot patch what you do not know you run. For readers who are not administrators, the same idea applies to your own devices. Our report on the Chrome zero-day covers the habit of updating when a vendor says a flaw is being used. Frequently asked questions What is CVE-2026-76466? It is a critical flaw in Cisco Expressway, rated 9.8, caused by hardcoded credentials. An attacker can use it to run commands with root privileges. Has Cisco fixed it? SecurityWeek reports that the flaw was patched on 21 October in Expressway Series release X15.5.20. Check Cisco's advisory for the versions that apply to you. What does the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list mean for me? It means attackers are already using a flaw. US federal agencies must patch by a deadline, and other organisations should treat it as a top priority. Who is exploiting the VMware flaw? SecurityWeek says a China-linked espionage group called Armory Castle, also known as Warp Panda, used it as a zero-day. I am a home user. Does this affect me? These are business and server products, so probably not directly. The lesson still applies: install updates on your own devices soon after they appear. Sources SecurityWeek: SAP NetWeaver, Cisco Expressway flaws exploited in attacks (23 Nov 2026) Written by the Rapid+ Team. We build Rapid+ Browser for Android and Windows. title: Google Retires the Privacy Sandbox: What It Means for Chrome, Cookies and Your Privacy
desc: Years of work on cookie replacements ended for lack of adoption. What is gone, what stays in Chrome and how to block trackers yourself.
text: Written on 24 November 2026. This is based on Google's own Privacy Sandbox announcement of 17 October 2025 and its status page, last updated on 20 November 2026. A vendor blog also claims Chrome version numbers and dates for the removal. Google's pages give none, so we leave those out. Google has not said third-party cookies will be removed. Google has abandoned most of the Privacy Sandbox, the set of tools it spent years building to replace tracking cookies in Chrome. Topics, Protected Audience and Attribution Reporting are retired, and Google's status page now lists most of them as "Deprecated and removed". The reason Google gives is simple: not enough people used them. For people who browse, the real question is what is left, and what still tracks you. The short version On 17 October 2025 Google announced that it would retire most Privacy Sandbox technologies, after evaluating feedback about their expected value and their low levels of adoption. Its status page, updated on 20 November 2026, lists Topics, Protected Audience, Attribution Reporting, Shared Storage and Related Website Sets as deprecated and removed in Chrome. Some privacy features stay, including CHIPS, FedCM, Private State Tokens and bounce tracking mitigations. Google has said it will keep its current approach of giving users a choice about third-party cookies in Chrome. It has not announced removing them. The status page gives no removal dates or Chrome version numbers. What the Privacy Sandbox was For years, advertisers followed people across sites with third-party cookies. Google planned to remove them from Chrome and offer replacements that kept advertising working without tracking individuals. Topics would label your browser with a few broad interests such as "cooking". Protected Audience would let ads be chosen inside your browser. Attribution Reporting would measure whether an ad led to a purchase, without naming you. In the end few companies adopted them, which is the reason Google gives for ending the project. What is retired Google's October 2025 post lists these as retired: Attribution Reporting API for Chrome and Android, IP Protection, On-Device Personalization, Private Aggregation (including Shared Storage), Protected Audience for Chrome and Android, Protected App Signals, Related Website Sets, SelectURL, SDK Runtime, and Topics for Chrome and Android. Status in Chrome (20 Nov 2026) Examples from Google's page Deprecated and removed Topics, Protected Audience, Attribution Reporting, Private Aggregation, Shared Storage, Related Website Sets, Fenced Frames Discontinued IP Protection, Partitioned Popins, Related Website Partition Not launched Fenced Storage Read, Private Proofs, Probabilistic Reveal Tokens, Script Blocking Continue to support CHIPS, FedCM, Private State Tokens, Storage Access, storage partitioning, bounce tracking mitigations, User-Agent Client Hints, User-Agent reduction On Android, the page lists Attribution Reporting, On-Device Personalization, Protected App Signals, Protected Audience, SDK Runtime and Topics as scheduled for phase-out. Google says documentation will stay on its site for reference. Why Google says it did this The only reason in Google's post is that after evaluating ecosystem feedback about their expected value and in light of their low levels of adoption, it decided to retire them. The same post says CHIPS and FedCM have seen broad adoption. Google also says it wants to support an attribution standard being developed at the W3C. Third parties have offered other explanations, such as regulatory pressure and technical complexity, but those are analysts' opinions, not statements from Google. What about third-party cookies? This is the point most readers want answered. Google's October 2025 post does not say third-party cookies will be removed. It refers back to an earlier statement that Chrome will maintain its current approach to offering users third-party cookie choice. Neither the post nor the status page announces a removal. A vendor blog says cookies stay and that Google will not show a standalone prompt, but that claim comes from that blog and not from Google's pages. In practice, that means a site can still try to set third-party cookies in Chrome unless you block them. Other browsers have blocked them for years. What still tracks you Cookies. Third-party cookies still work in Chrome unless you turn them off. Logins. If you sign in to a service, it knows who you are across its own sites. Fingerprinting. Sites can combine details about your device into a recognisable profile without any cookie. See our guide to browser fingerprinting. Data brokers and apps. Tracking does not stop at the browser. What you can do now Block third-party cookies. In Chrome, open Settings, Privacy and security, then Third-party cookies, and choose to block them. Use tracking protection. A content blocker stops many trackers before they load. Keep sessions separate. A separate browser profile for shopping and banking limits what one site can link. Clear cookies on a schedule, or use private windows for one-off visits. Review what you share when a site asks for consent. Reject optional tracking. What it means for advertisers With the replacement tools gone, advertisers lose one route to measuring ads without cookies. Analysts expect more use of first-party data, meaning information that customers give a company directly, and of measurement done on the company's own servers. That is opinion, not a Google statement. For readers, the practical effect is that more of the tracking industry depends on logins and fingerprints, which are harder to block than cookies. Frequently asked questions Is the Privacy Sandbox over? Most of it is. Google's status page lists Topics, Protected Audience, Attribution Reporting and others as deprecated and removed. Some privacy features, such as CHIPS and FedCM, continue. Is Chrome removing third-party cookies? Google has not announced that. Its October 2025 post says it will maintain its current approach of offering users a choice about third-party cookies. Why did Google retire the tools? Google says it evaluated feedback about their expected value and their low levels of adoption. Does this make me less private? Not directly, because most people never used the replacements. But third-party cookies remain possible in Chrome unless you block them, so check your settings. Which browsers already block third-party cookies? Several other browsers block them by default. Check your browser's privacy settings to see what it does. Sources Google Privacy Sandbox: Update on plans for Privacy Sandbox technologies (17 Oct 2025) Google Privacy Sandbox: Feature status (updated 20 Nov 2026) Segwise: Google Privacy Sandbox shutdown, analysis (third-party opinion) Written by the Rapid+ Team. title: Microsoft Entra Connect Health Breach: Admin Emails Exposed, What It Means and What to Do
desc: A July bug, a November fix and a list of admin addresses in the wrong hands. What was exposed and how administrators should respond.
text: Written on 24 November 2026. This is based on BleepingComputer's report of 21 November, which cites a Microsoft admin notification sent on 20 November. We did not read the notification itself. Microsoft declined to give further details, and it has not named the attackers or said how many organisations were affected. Microsoft has told administrators that attackers exploited a flaw in Entra Connect Health, a monitoring service for company identity systems, and read information about their organisations. The data includes the email addresses of administrators and technical contacts. Microsoft says it found no changes to configurations and that passwords were not exposed. The flaw is fixed on Microsoft's side. The risk that remains is targeted phishing aimed at the people whose addresses were taken. The short version The flaw was in the Entra Connect Health API. It was introduced on 23 July 2026, found by Microsoft on 9 November and fixed on 19 November. Microsoft finished its investigation on 20 November. Attackers had unauthorised read-only access to tenant-level metadata. Microsoft says it found no unauthorised configuration changes. Exposed: administrator and technical contact email addresses, tenant IDs, display names, domain names, country codes, licence tiers and sync status. Not exposed, per Microsoft: passwords, password hashes, authentication tokens, valid cryptographic keys, on-premises server and Active Directory layouts, and Azure subscription information. Microsoft says no software updates or customer action are required to close the hole, and recommends watching for phishing. What Entra Connect Health is BleepingComputer describes Entra Connect Health as a cloud-based service that lets administrators monitor the health, performance and alerts of their on-premises identity systems from the Microsoft Entra admin center. Many companies use Microsoft's cloud for sign-in and also keep their own servers. This service helps them watch the link between the two. Timeline Date (2026) Event 23 July The vulnerable code is introduced 9 November Microsoft discovers the flaw 19 November Server-side fix deployed 20 November Investigation complete; customers notified through Azure Service Health 21 November BleepingComputer reports the notice, shared by admins on Reddit The reporting does not say when attackers first used the flaw, so the exposure window could be anywhere from July to November. What the attackers could read According to Microsoft's list, as reported: Email addresses of tenant technical contacts and administrator accounts. Tenant IDs, display names, initial domain names, country codes and regional information. Entra licence tiers and directory sync status, including whether sync was on and the time of the last sync. Connect Health onboarding status. An expired certificate that had been used to register Connect Health agents with a Microsoft internal service decommissioned in late 2024. It was no longer in use but was still returned by the API. The article says the flaw could have allowed changes to Connect Health monitoring settings, but Microsoft found none. Why metadata matters Names and domains do not sound dangerous, but they are what a convincing scam is made from. An attacker who knows who your administrators are, which licence tier you use and when your directory last synced can write an email that sounds like it comes from Microsoft support. Administrators have powerful accounts, so a single successful phish can lead to a full takeover. That is why Microsoft's main advice is about phishing, not about fixing a hole. Who was affected Microsoft has not said how many organisations were affected or who exploited the flaw. BleepingComputer says more than a dozen administrators posted on Reddit that they had received the notice, and some managed service providers reported notices for several customer tenants. If you administer a Microsoft 365 tenant that uses Connect Health, look in the Azure Service Health notifications for your tenant. What administrators should do Read the notice in Azure Service Health, and tell your security team. Use phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication for privileged accounts, such as passkeys or hardware security keys. See our passkey guide. Review your Connect Health configuration and check for anything you did not set. Check Entra audit and sign-in logs for suspicious activity. Warn the people whose addresses were exposed. Tell technical contacts to expect fake support messages. Use Microsoft's script at aka.ms/ConnectHealth/scripts to see which types of tenant metadata could have been exposed. It shows current values, not what was actually read. What staff and customers should know Do not trust a message just because it knows your company name or domain. Microsoft will not ask for your password or a code by email or phone. Treat any such request as a scam. If an "administrator" asks you to approve a sign-in or install software, check through another channel first. A familiar pattern This follows the same story as the Microsoft 365 outage earlier in the month: a change made in July sat unnoticed until November. It also shows why a flaw in a vendor's service can reach many customers at once, as in the supplier breaches we covered. Microsoft's own November updates also fixed an Outlook flaw under attack. Frequently asked questions What was exposed in the Entra Connect Health breach? Administrator and technical contact email addresses, tenant IDs, display names, domain names, country codes, licence tiers and directory sync status. Microsoft says passwords, hashes, tokens and keys were not exposed. Has it been fixed? Yes. Microsoft says it deployed a server-side fix on 19 November and that no software updates or customer remediation are needed. Who was behind it? Microsoft has not said. It also has not said how many tenants were affected. Were configurations changed? Microsoft says it did not identify any unauthorised configuration changes. The attackers had read-only access. What is the real risk now? Targeted phishing and social engineering aimed at the exposed administrators and contacts. Microsoft recommends alerting security teams and using phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication. Sources BleepingComputer: Microsoft Entra Connect Health flaw exploited to steal tenant data (21 Nov 2026) Written by the Rapid+ Team. We build Rapid+ Browser for Android and Windows. title: Outage Week: Apple, Chase, United, the NSA and the FAA All Failed, and Why It Was Not a Cyberattack
desc: Five outages, five stated causes. The week air traffic, banking, iCloud and a classified network stumbled, and what officials said.
text: Written on 24 November 2026. This draws on 9to5Mac, CNBC, NBC News and Nextgov. A Reuters report quoting a US official on cyberattacks could not be read, so we rely on what each company and agency said itself. Every cause below is the organisation's own statement, not an independent finding. In one week in mid-November 2026, Chase's banking apps, Apple's iCloud and App Store, United Airlines, the NSA's classified network and US air traffic control all had trouble. The timing made people suspect a coordinated attack. Each organisation said otherwise: software updates, a bug and a router. This article lays out what each one said, what is still unclear, and why a run of outages can look like an attack when it is not. The short version 13 November: a nationwide US ground stop halted flights for more than four hours. The Transportation Secretary blamed a router in Arkansas. 16 November: a United Airlines systems outage delayed departures, and Chase online, mobile and branch transactions failed for hours. 17 November: Apple iCloud, App Store and other services went down. Apple blamed an internal update. 17 and 18 November: the NSA's classified network, NSANet, was degraded. The NSA said it was scheduled maintenance. United, Apple, Chase and the NSA each said or were reported to say that it was not a cyberattack. 13 November: the FAA ground stop CNBC reports that a nationwide ground stop stopped departures for more than four hours. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed a router in Arkansas that overwhelmed the systems feeding radar and other air traffic control data. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford called the upgrades routine maintenance to move from copper wires to fibre optic cable. CNBC and Nextgov also link other pieces suggesting the root cause was still unclear, so the explanation is not fully settled. 16 November: United Airlines United had what CNBC calls a widespread system outage that briefly delayed departing flights. The pilots' union described multiple pilot-facing applications being affected. United said it had resolved a technology issue and that there was no indication it was a cyberattack, and that it was not related to the ground stop of the Friday before. Flights in progress and United Express flights were not affected. 16 November: Chase NBC News reports that Chase online and mobile transactions failed along with in-person branch transactions. Customers got error messages and had trouble withdrawing money, and Zelle payments were delayed. Chase said it had a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system, and that it was not cyber-related. By about 6:30 p.m. Eastern the bank said transactions were posting normally. NBC notes Chase has about 94 million customer relationships. How many accounts were hit was unclear. Zelle said it was not down. PNC and Capital One reported no direct effect. 17 November: Apple services 9to5Mac says iCloud, the App Store, Apple Pay, Apple Support, iPhone activation, Apple Music and App Store Connect for developers were affected, and that some people were signed out of iCloud or saw verification errors. Apple's status page still showed services as available while outage reports piled up. Apple said an internal update caused some outages that morning, and ruled out a cyberattack, according to a post by journalist Mark Gurman quoted in the article. Consumer services came back first, while developer services still had issues at the last update. 17 and 18 November: NSANet Nextgov reports, citing six people familiar, that NSANet, the classified network the NSA uses to move top-secret data, slowed analysts' work and forced staff to change arrival times. Employees got a Code Orange message that closed the campus to most staff on Tuesday night, then a Code Gray notice setting staggered arrivals. The NSA said it experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance and that mission-critical capabilities remained fully operational. Four sources said there were no immediate signs of a cyberattack, and that it may be linked to a series of software upgrades. A former NSA technology official said intelligence collection was not interrupted. Date What failed Stated cause 13 Nov US flights (ground stop) Router problem during a fibre upgrade, per officials 16 Nov United departures "Technology issue", no sign of cyberattack 16 Nov Chase banking Software bug in on-premise hardware, not cyber 17 Nov Apple services Internal update, not a cyberattack 17 to 18 Nov NSANet Scheduled maintenance, per the NSA Were they connected? NBC says there is no evidence these incidents are connected. Each organisation gave a different cause, and none of the explanations links to another. That does not prove nothing is shared. It means that, on the public record, they look like separate failures that happened in the same week, along with the Microsoft 365 outage of 12 and 13 November. Why failures cluster and look like attacks Big systems change constantly. Updates, migrations and upgrades are routine, and every change is a chance for a bug. Microsoft's outage came from a change made months earlier. A few providers carry a lot. When a payment, cloud or network system fails, thousands of services fail with it. Outages and attacks look the same from outside. Both show up as error pages and silence. Denials are not proof. A company's statement that it was not an attack is a claim, not an audit, though several companies gave specific causes. A real attack did happen the same week at another US agency, in the USDA payments breach, which shows why it is worth checking each case separately. How to cope with outages Keep a second payment method. Carry another card or keep cash for a day. Have a backup for travel. Download boarding passes and note airline phone numbers. Know where to check. Use official status pages and the company's social posts, not rumours. Watch for scams. Fake "outage compensation" or "account restore" messages appear within hours. Go to the company's site yourself. Do not redo big transactions in the middle of an outage. Wait for confirmation to avoid double charges. Frequently asked questions Were the outages caused by a cyberattack? United, Apple, Chase and the NSA each said or were reported to say it was not. Officials blamed a router for the ground stop. These are the organisations' own explanations. Were the outages related? NBC says there is no evidence they are connected. The stated causes are different for each. What caused the Apple outage? Apple said an internal update caused some outages, according to a post quoted by 9to5Mac. It was not a cyberattack. Did I lose money in the Chase outage? Chase said transactions were posting normally by early evening. If something looks wrong on your account, contact Chase and keep records of what happened. Was the NSA network hacked? The NSA said it had temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance. Sources told Nextgov there were no immediate signs of a cyberattack. title: Revolve Card Breach: What Was Taken, How Many People Are Affected and What to Do
desc: Customers who saved a card lost names, card numbers and expiry dates. What is confirmed, what is not, and the five-minute steps to protect yourself.
text: Written on 24 November 2026. This relies on Malwarebytes' report of 3 November, which draws on Revolve's SEC filing and state attorney general listings. We read Malwarebytes' translated version and did not read the filing itself. Revolve has not confirmed a total number of people affected, and we mark which numbers are estimates. Revolve, the online fashion retailer, says someone took payment card details from customer accounts. The company has not said how many people were hit, but figures found in state filings point to as many as 1.5 million. The people at risk are customers who had saved a card in their Revolve account. If you have shopped there, the steps below take about five minutes. The short version Revolve Group Inc. disclosed that an unauthorised party obtained customer data, including names, contact details, card numbers and expiry dates. Only customers who had saved a payment card to their Revolve account were affected. The count is unconfirmed. Texas lists 127,200 Texas residents. Malwarebytes found a figure of 1,515,073 in data behind the Texas listing, which is not on the public list and which Revolve has not confirmed. Texas records give 11 September as the date of the incident and 29 September as the date it was found, though the year is not shown in the text we read. Revolve's filing says the data was likely obtained by "automated means". It has not said how. What happened Revolve filed a notice with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on 29 October, as Malwarebytes reads it. The filing says an unauthorised party likely obtained customer data by automated means, which can mean software that tries large numbers of logins or requests. It gives no total, and no group has claimed the attack. Revolve says it took additional security measures but does not say which. Malwarebytes also cites a customer notice sent to the Massachusetts Attorney General. It does not say when letters went to customers. What was exposed Data Status Names and contact details Exposed Card numbers Exposed. It is unclear whether they were shown in full or masked. Card expiry dates Exposed CVV security code Not mentioned in the filing, according to Malwarebytes Do not read "no CVV" as "safe". Malwarebytes warns that a card number and expiry date can be enough for some online purchases even without the security code, so the card still needs attention. It is also unclear whether the card data sat on Revolve's own systems or with a payment processor. Malwarebytes says that is unknown. How many people This is the part to be careful with, because several sites repeat a number that is not official. 127,200: the Texas residents listed on the Texas attorney general's site. 1,515,073: a total Malwarebytes found in data behind that site. It is not on the public list. Other sites repeat the larger number but appear to rely on the same Texas data. Revolve has not confirmed any total, and its filing does not give one. The honest answer is that it could be well over a million, and that nobody outside the company can say for sure. What to do if you shop at Revolve Check your statements for small charges you do not recognise. Thieves often test a card with a tiny purchase first. Report anything odd to your card issuer at once, using the number on the back of your card. Ask for a new card if you had one saved. Issuers can cancel and reissue quickly, often within days. Remove saved cards from shopping accounts. A password manager or your phone's wallet is safer than a card stored at every store. Be cautious about messages about the breach. Scammers use breach news to send fake notices. Do not click links, and call the number on your card to check. Change your Revolve password, and any account where you used the same one. Why saved cards are a risk Saving a card is convenient, and in this breach it is exactly what put customers at risk. The more places that hold your number, the more places that can leak it. Your phone's wallet, such as Apple Pay or Google Pay, gives stores a one-time token instead of your real number, so a breach at the store does not expose your card. Our guide to paying safely online explains why a credit card also gives you the strongest dispute rights. Why the timing matters This breach came to light just before Black Friday, when millions of people enter card details online. It is a good moment to tidy what you have saved. Our look at this year's fake shopping domains covers the other risk of the season. Frequently asked questions Was my Revolve account hacked? Only if you had a card saved there, and even then the company has not said how many accounts were touched. If you never saved a card, the filing does not suggest your payment data was taken. How many people are affected? Revolve has not said. Texas lists 127,200 residents, and Malwarebytes found a figure of about 1.5 million in data behind the Texas listing. The larger number is unconfirmed. Was my CVV stolen? The filing does not mention CVV numbers, according to Malwarebytes. Still, card number plus expiry can be enough for some purchases. How did the attackers get in? Revolve has not explained. Its filing says the data was likely obtained by automated means. It does not name a method or a group. Should I cancel my card? If you had a card saved at Revolve, asking your issuer for a new one is a sensible precaution. It is quick and free with most banks.
