title: Scattered Spider Suspected Ringleader Tyler Buchanan Gets Six Years: What the Case Shows
desc: The last of five defendants is sentenced. The numbers, the other four sentences and how phishing like this works on ordinary people.
text: Written on 24 November 2026. This relies on The Record's report of 18 November. Two BBC pages and the US Justice Department's press release could not be read, so we do not repeat claims from them, and we do not cover the other Scattered Spider case that BBC reporting links, because we could not verify it. The restitution hearing date comes from The Record, and the year is not stated there. A British man called Tyler Buchanan has been sentenced to six years in a US federal prison for his part in a phishing campaign that stole more than $11.6 million in cryptocurrency. The 24-year-old from Dundee was described as the suspected ringleader of Scattered Spider, the loose group of young hackers linked to the attack on casino giant MGM Resorts. He is the last of five defendants to be sentenced, which makes this the closing chapter of one of the best-known cybercrime cases of the decade. The short version Tyler Robert Buchanan, 24, of Dundee, Scotland, got six years in federal prison, in a case brought in the Central District of California. He was arrested at Palma Airport in Spain in June 2024, and was named in November 2024 with four others. Prosecutors say he admitted to a phishing campaign to steal millions of dollars' worth of virtual currency. The amount stolen from individuals in the US was more than $11.6 million. The MGM Resorts attack is described as costing an estimated $100 million, a figure The Record takes from earlier reporting, not from the court. A restitution hearing, which decides what he must repay, is set for 11 December. The sentence The Record says Buchanan was sentenced on a Tuesday. The article is dated 18 November, so the date was probably 17 November, though the report does not state it. The US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California said he admitted taking part in a phishing campaign "to steal millions of dollars' worth of virtual currency". Prosecutors told the court in a sentencing memo that the crimes had "severe, life-altering consequences for many victims". The five defendants Defendant Age and place Sentence Tyler Robert Buchanan 24, Dundee, Scotland Six years Noah Michael Urban 22, Palm Coast, Florida 10 years Ahmed Hossam Eldin Elbadawy 25, College Station, Texas 45 months Evans Onyeaka Osiebo 22, Dallas 45 months Joel Martin Evans 27, Jacksonville, North Carolina Two years The five were charged together in November 2024, according to The Record, and Buchanan is the last to be sentenced. The article lists the targets in the case as including Coinbase, Twilio, Mailchimp, LastPass and the MGM Resorts ransomware attack. What Scattered Spider is Scattered Spider is the name researchers gave to a loose network of mostly young, English-speaking attackers. Microsoft called it "one of the most dangerous financial criminal groups", as quoted by The Record. It is known less for advanced code than for talking its way in: pretending to be employees or IT staff, tricking help desks and sending convincing phishing messages. The Record's article does not go into the group's methods beyond the phishing campaign. What the case teaches ordinary users You do not need to run a casino to learn from this. The people hurt directly here were individuals who lost cryptocurrency to phishing. The same tools work on anyone: Phishing messages copy real brands. A fake login page can look identical to the real one. Passwords can be handed over without noticing. You type them into a page you trust. Passkeys resist this. A passkey will not work on a lookalike site, which is why we cover them in our passkey guide. Crypto is hard to get back. There is usually no bank to reverse a transfer. How to protect yourself from phishing Go to the site yourself. Type the address or use a bookmark, and do not follow a link in a message. Check the full address before you log in. Our guide to spotting fake pages lists what to look for. Use two-step verification with an app or security key, instead of a text message where possible. Treat urgency as a warning. "Your account will be closed" is the oldest trick. Keep crypto on a device you control for large amounts, and double-check every address you send to. The Optimizely attack showed that even a correct page can be tampered with. Use a separate browser profile for finance. See our profiles guide. What happens next A restitution hearing is scheduled for 11 December, where the court will decide what Buchanan must repay. Ordering repayment and actually collecting it are different things, so victims may recover little. Our report on the current Transport for London incident mentions the 2024 breach there that was linked to the group. The new incident is separate and no group has been named for it. Frequently asked questions How long was Tyler Buchanan sentenced for? Six years in federal prison, according to The Record. He is 24 and from Dundee, Scotland. What did he do? He admitted taking part in a phishing campaign to steal millions of dollars in virtual currency. The amount taken from individuals in the US was more than $11.6 million. Was he behind the MGM attack? The Record lists the MGM Resorts ransomware attack among the targets in the case. MGM's cost is described as an estimated $100 million, from earlier reporting. The article does not give details of his role in that attack. Who else was sentenced? Four others: Noah Urban got 10 years, Ahmed Elbadawy and Evans Osiebo got 45 months each, and Joel Evans got two years. Buchanan was the last of the five. What is a restitution hearing? It is a hearing where the court decides how much a convicted person must repay to victims. Buchanan's is set for 11 December. title: USDA Breach: Hackers Reach the System That Pays Farmers, and Agency Systems Go Offline
desc: Database passwords reset, apps offline and no answers on who did it. The USDA breach as reported by NBC News and Nextgov, with steps for farmers.
text: Written on 24 November 2026. This is a developing story based on NBC News (20 November) and Nextgov (19 November). Both rely on unnamed sources, and neither names a group behind the breach. A CNN report on a breach of an FBI database could not be read, so we do not cover it. Details may change as the USDA says more. The US Department of Agriculture has taken many of its computer systems offline after hackers got into the system that pays farmers. Staff were told to reset every database password, and for days many of the financial tools farmers rely on stopped working. No one has said who did it or whether data was taken. If you farm in the US, or work with the programme, this is what is known so far. The short version Hackers accessed the USDA system that facilitates payments to farmers, according to NBC News, citing sources. The agency told employees on Thursday, 19 November. Nextgov reports that numerous USDA applications were taken offline over several days, and that outages hit many of the financial tools used for payments between the agency and farmers. An internal email on Monday, 16 November, said the IT team had to "reset all database passwords in all environments", according to Nextgov. It is not clear who carried out the intrusion or whether any data was taken. A bulletin dated 19 November warned that applications might have intermittent outages through the week. What happened According to Nextgov, the USDA's Cybersecurity and Privacy Operations Center found a security incident. A message on Monday from an acting assistant CIO at the Farm Production and Conservation Business Center told staff that the Information Services Division had to reset all database passwords across all environments, which in turn forced a reset of every application, causing outages. By Thursday some staff also had trouble with the department's VPN. NBC News adds that the attack came this week, according to two former USDA officials, and that the department told staff on Thursday that hackers had accessed the system that handles payments to farmers. NBC's reporting is for subscribers and we read only part of it. Who is affected Neither article gives a number of farmers. Nextgov says the payments cover things such as crop insurance and losses from bad weather. Staff reported that they could not reach client-facing apps that farmers use to check notifications and the status of loans and other aid. The department's public statements were not available in the pages we read, and Nextgov says that USDA and CISA were asked for comment without a reported reply. Question What the reporting says What was accessed? The system that facilitates payments to farmers (NBC) Which system exactly? Not named Who did it? Unknown. No group or country is named. Was data stolen? Unclear (Nextgov). NBC reports concern that hackers could reach sensitive information. Are systems back? Intermittent outages were expected through the week of 16 November How many farmers? Not stated Staff were left guessing Nextgov's three sources say department leaders have not kept staff fully informed, and it is unclear whether every employee received the notice. That matters, because staff who do not know what happened may reuse old passwords or fall for messages pretending to be IT. In a breach, clear communication is part of the defence. Why resetting every password is a big step A reset of all database passwords in all environments is a heavy response. It suggests the team feared that an attacker held credentials that could still be used, and wanted to cut off access everywhere at once. The price is that everything that depends on those passwords breaks until it is reconfigured. That is why so many applications went down. It is also why a reset is the kind of step you only take when you think access may be widespread. The reporting does not confirm how far the intruder reached. What farmers and agricultural businesses can do Use official channels. Check the USDA's own website and your local Farm Service Agency office for status. Do not trust messages that arrive by text or email. Expect phishing. A real outage is a perfect cover for fake messages about "payment problems" or "update your bank details". Hang up on calls that ask for banking information. Watch your bank account. If you receive USDA payments, check deposits and look for changes to your payment details. Keep records. Save copies of applications, payment notices and loan paperwork, in case a payment is delayed. Change passwords for any USDA online account, and on any other site where you used the same one. Turn on two-step verification where it is offered. The bigger picture This is the latest in a run of government and infrastructure incidents. A week earlier, a string of big outages had officials assuring the public that they were not cyberattacks. This one is different, because the USDA's own staff and sources describe an outside intrusion. Our report on supplier breaches shows how attackers often reach large organisations through weak links, though nothing in the USDA reporting says how this one happened. Frequently asked questions What did hackers access at the USDA? NBC News reports they accessed the system that facilitates payments to farmers. Nextgov says many financial tools used for those payments were taken offline. Was farmers' personal data stolen? Nextgov says it is not clear whether any data was taken. NBC reports concern that hackers could access sensitive information. No confirmation has been given. Who is behind the attack? Unknown. Neither article names a group, a country or a person. Will farmers still get paid? The articles do not say payments stopped, but they describe outages in the tools used to process and track them. Check with your local USDA service office for your own case. How should I protect myself? Use official USDA channels, ignore unexpected messages about payments, watch your bank account, and change passwords on any USDA account. title: Data Breach Roundup: 9 Incidents From 13 to 19 November 2026 and What to Do
desc: All nine breaches in one table, with what was exposed and what is only a claim, plus a short plan for when a breach letter arrives.
text: Written on 23 November 2026. This is built on Privacy Guides' weekly roundup of 20 November, which summarises reporting by BleepingComputer, TechCrunch and WIRED. We did not read the original company filings. Many numbers below are estimates or claims, and we mark them. Where a number appears only in a headline, we say that too. Nine data breaches were reported between 13 and 19 November 2026. Together they touch drivers, cinema-goers, patients, bank customers and commuters. Some figures are confirmed in official filings, and some are only claims. This roundup lists all nine in one place, shows what was exposed in each, and ends with a short plan for what to do when a breach letter lands in your inbox. The nine incidents at a glance Organisation People or records What was exposed Uber (via Fireworks AI) 149,346 drivers (Maine filing) Names, driver's licence numbers, dates of birth, addresses TSMC Attacker claims 46,000 employee records National ID numbers, addresses, contact details, banking details (claimed) Fandango Not stated Card number, security code, expiry, billing ZIP, email Infoblox Not stated "Company information"; one source says sensitive customer data Cursor Up to 5,000 developers (estimate) Source code archives, support emails, credentials shared with support Wellington IT (Irish credit unions) Not stated Payee names, IBAN, account numbers, addresses CreditNirvana (Perfios) Headline says 6.6 million accounts Credit reports, ID cards, call transcripts, legal documents Transport for London About 265,000 customers Names, contacts, addresses, dates of birth, security questions SBC Medical Group 1.6 million (SEC filing) Names, contacts, dates of birth, patient card numbers, member IDs, passwords We have separate reports on Uber and Cursor, Transport for London and the supplier breaches at Infoblox, TSMC and Wellington IT. The three below are the ones we have not covered in depth. Fandango: card details taken at checkout Fandango Media, the US ticketing platform that sells for about 31,000 cinema screens, including AMC, Regal and Cinemark, says payment card details typed into its official website's checkout pages were exposed between 8 and 11 October. The exposed data includes the card number, security code, expiry date, billing ZIP code and email. Fandango did not say how many people were affected and is notifying customers who bought through its own site. Nothing in the roundup names who did it. This kind of attack, in which code on a checkout page copies what you type, is often called card skimming on the web. The same method appears in our report on the Optimizely attack. If you bought tickets there in that window, ask your bank to watch your card or replace it. SBC Medical Group: 1.6 million people SBC Medical Group manages clinics, mainly in Japan, that receive about 7 million patient visits a year. In an SEC filing, the company said two cyber incidents exposed customer and employee information, with the breach on 16 November. It put the number at 1.6 million people. The data includes full names, contact details, dates of birth, patient card numbers, member IDs, passwords and survey responses. The roundup adds that hundreds of thousands of further records were taken, covering reservation requests, treatment information, customer reviews, employee records and a booking platform. "Hundreds of thousands" is approximate. Patients should change passwords for any related account and watch for messages that mention clinic visits. CreditNirvana: a debt-collection platform CreditNirvana, owned by the Indian fintech Perfios, runs an AI platform for debt collection. According to WIRED, two serious vulnerabilities could have exposed sensitive data, including credit reports, ID cards, case details, legal documents, emails, texts and call transcripts. The flaw is fixed, but the exposure potentially lasted years, and the roundup says three corporate customers were affected. The headline of the WIRED article puts the scale at 6.6 million accounts and 315,000 call recordings. That figure appears only in the headline in the summary we read, and the roundup describes exposure, not confirmed mass theft. What to do when a breach letter arrives Do not click links in it. Open the company's website yourself or use a phone number you looked up. Scammers send fake breach notices. Find out what was taken. A letter should say. Passwords and card numbers need fast action. Names and addresses need caution against phishing. Change the password for that service, and for any other account that shared it. Use a password manager so each one is different. Replace the card if card details were taken. Your bank can do it quickly. Look into a credit freeze if ID numbers were exposed, where your country offers one. Watch your accounts for a few months. Breach data is often sold and used later. Turn on a passkey or two-step verification for email first, because it resets everything else. See our passkey guide. Frequently asked questions Which breach this week is the biggest? SBC Medical Group reports 1.6 million people in an SEC filing. TfL's estimate is about 265,000, and Uber's is 149,346 drivers. CreditNirvana's headline figure is 6.6 million accounts but is not confirmed in the text we read. Are these numbers confirmed? Some are, like Uber's count from a state filing and SBC's from an SEC filing. Others are attacker claims, such as TSMC's 46,000 records, or estimates, such as Cursor's 5,000 developers. I bought Fandango tickets in October. Am I affected? Only if you bought through Fandango's official website between 8 and 11 October. Fandango says it is notifying those customers. Ask your bank to watch the card. How do I know whether my data is in a breach? Companies must usually tell you. You can also check a breach-notification service with your email address, and treat messages about it with care. What is the first thing to do after a notice? Change the password on that service, and on any other account that used the same one. Then watch for phishing. title: Fireworks AI Breach: How One Supplier Exposed Uber Drivers and Cursor Developers
desc: Stolen keys at an AI supplier led to leaked driver data and a poisoned code extension. What happened and how drivers and developers should respond.
text: Written on 23 November 2026. This is based on BleepingComputer's reports on Uber and Cursor (14 and 17 November), which cite Cursor's incident post and a filing with the Maine Attorney General. We did not read those primary documents. Uber has not named Fireworks AI itself, so that link rests on TechCrunch's reporting. A breach at an AI infrastructure company called Fireworks AI is spreading to the companies that use it. Uber has told 149,346 drivers that their driver's licence numbers and other details were taken. Cursor, the AI code editor, says attackers used a stolen key to publish a malicious copy of a popular coding extension, which about 5,000 developers may have installed. Notion has also said that AI chat transcripts were exposed. This article puts the pieces in order. The short version Fireworks AI, which provides AI model hosting for other companies, disclosed several breaches in October 2026, including exposed keys and a compromised cloud provider. Uber says a service provider told it on 9 October that an unauthorised party had compromised the provider, and on 13 October Uber concluded the party used credentials to access Uber data. Uber notified 149,346 drivers, according to a filing in Maine. Exposed: names, driver's licence numbers, dates of birth and addresses. Cursor says attackers used a key stored at Fireworks to copy data from a storage bucket, then used credentials found in it to reach more systems. On 29 October, malicious copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension were placed in the cache that serves Cursor's extension marketplace. They stayed live for about 11 hours. What Fireworks AI is Fireworks AI runs infrastructure for training and running AI models. Companies send it data and requests, so it holds keys and storage that belong to its customers. When a company like that is breached, the harm lands on every customer at once. According to BleepingComputer, Fireworks disclosed several incidents in October 2026. One involved exposed API keys and tokens. Another involved attackers reaching developer machines through a compromised third-party cloud provider. BleepingComputer says Fireworks attributed an attack to a financially motivated group linked to "LLMjacking", the theft of access to AI models. Uber: 149,346 drivers Uber's account is that a service provider notified it on 9 October that an unauthorised third party had compromised that provider. On 13 October Uber determined the party had used credentials to access Uber data. Letters went to affected drivers on 10 November. A filing with the Maine Attorney General puts the number at 149,346 and lists names, driver's licence numbers, dates of birth and addresses. Uber did not name Fireworks. The link comes from TechCrunch, as reported by BleepingComputer, and Uber's spokesperson did not respond to BleepingComputer in time. One date is unclear: BleepingComputer says the breach came in early October but also cites TechCrunch for an incident at Fireworks on 24 October. Cursor: a poisoned extension Cursor is an AI code editor built on the same base as Visual Studio Code. Its incident post, as summarised by BleepingComputer, says attackers took an access key stored at Fireworks and used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket that Cursor shared with Fireworks. The bucket held records of AI coding sessions, mostly from 2025, from users who did not have Privacy Mode on. Some contained plain-text API credentials, which gave access to further Cursor systems. Cursor's figures: fewer than 0.05 percent of users had session records exposed, and fewer than 0.01 percent of customers had API credentials compromised. Data copied from its internal tools included archived non-production source code, limited customer support emails, product usage data and credentials some customers had shared with support. The malicious extension On 29 October the attackers placed malicious copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension, versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, on the cache that serves Cursor's extension marketplace. They were live for about 11 hours before removal. The malware tried to install a persistent SSH backdoor. Researchers found coding errors that likely stopped it from working on many Windows and Mac machines where SSH was not already on. Anthropic's own extension and the Open VSX store were not compromised. Cursor estimates up to 5,000 users who requested the affected versions in that window may have received the bad builds. That is an estimate, not a confirmed count. Cursor says production systems, official app releases, customer code repositories and the code and prompts of Privacy Mode users were not affected. Notion and others BleepingComputer also reports that Notion said its AI chat transcripts were exposed through the Fireworks breach. We did not read Notion's own notice, and the full list of affected companies is not known. What developers should do Check your editor. If you use Cursor, follow its remediation guidance, which it links from its incident post. Look at which version of the Claude Code extension you installed and when. Look for SSH changes. Check for unexpected keys in your SSH authorised keys file and for new background services. Rotate keys that touched AI tools. Anything pasted into an AI chat or coding session may be in a log somewhere. Use Privacy Mode or equivalent where a tool offers it, and keep secrets out of prompts. Ask your vendors where your data goes. Your AI tool may send it to other companies you never chose. What affected drivers should do Watch for fake Uber messages. Scammers use leaked data to sound real. Open the Uber app yourself instead of following links. A driver's licence number can support identity fraud. Consider a credit freeze or fraud alert where you live, and read your breach letter for any monitoring offer. Be wary of calls that quote your address and date of birth, and use only the official Uber support route. The larger lesson None of these companies was breached first. One supplier was, and the damage followed the keys. The same pattern showed up in the Optimizely attack and in the vendor breaches of the same week. Frequently asked questions Was Uber itself hacked? Uber says a service provider was compromised and an unauthorised party used credentials to reach Uber data. It did not name Fireworks, but TechCrunch reported the link. How many people are affected? Uber notified 149,346 drivers, per a Maine filing. Cursor says fewer than 0.05 percent of its users had session records exposed and estimates up to 5,000 developers may have received the bad extension. What was the malicious extension? Two fake builds of the Claude Code extension, versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, served from Cursor's marketplace cache for about 11 hours on 29 October. Anthropic's real extension was not compromised. Did the malware work? It tried to install an SSH backdoor. Researchers found coding errors that likely stopped it on many Windows and Mac systems without SSH already on, but some systems may have been exposed. Should I stop using AI coding tools? Not necessarily, but treat them as suppliers: check where your data goes, use privacy settings, and keep secrets out of prompts. title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): The Critical Java Bug CISA Wants Patched Now
desc: A crash and possible remote code execution in the Java runtime, only on certain processors. What it is, who is exposed and what to do today.
text: Written on 23 November 2026. This is based on the US cyber agency CISA's alert of 17 November, the write-up by the security firm Calif that found the bug, and a forum post relaying data from other researchers. We did not read the OpenJDK or Oracle advisories, so check them for exact fixed versions. Calif's exploit claims are its own and have not been independently confirmed. On 17 November 2026 the US cyber agency CISA urged everyone who runs Java to patch at once. The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and nicknamed "Java4Shell", sits in a small piece of the Java runtime that decodes Base64 text. A remote attacker with no password can crash the program, and in some setups may be able to run their own code. It needs a particular kind of processor, so not every Java installation is at risk. This article explains what the bug is, who is exposed, how to check, and what to do if you cannot patch right away. The short version CVE-2026-114938 is a memory-corruption bug in the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine, according to CISA. It can crash the program and allow remote code execution without logging in. Calif rates it 9.2 out of 10 on the CVSS 4.0 scale. It only affects computers with an x86-64 processor that supports AVX-512 VBMI instructions. ARM processors are not affected. Calif says it affects OpenJDK from version 17.0.6 onwards and every Java build made from it, including Oracle, Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin and Microsoft's build. Oracle released a patch on 17 November. None of the sources we read says the bug is being exploited in attacks yet. If you cannot patch, a startup option can switch off the faulty code path. What the bug is Base64 is a common way to write binary data as plain text. It is used in logins, web tokens, email and many web services, so almost every Java program decodes it somewhere. To go faster, Java uses special processor instructions where they exist. Calif found that the fast path, written for the AVX-512 VBMI instruction set, writes past the end of its memory when the input ends in a malformed pattern. On Calif's account, 64 "A" characters followed by an equals sign trigger it, and 128 in OpenJDK 17. Writing past the end of a buffer corrupts the data next to it, which is the classic starting point for taking over a program. Calif says there is no universal exploit, because every target needs its own work, and its published proof of concept only shows the memory being overwritten. It claims to have turned the bug into full code execution against the default setups of tools including Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Artifactory. Those claims are Calif's own. Who is exposed Two conditions must both be true: The software runs a vulnerable Java. Calif says OpenJDK from 17.0.6 onwards is affected, and so are the builds made from it by Amazon, Eclipse, Microsoft, Azul, BellSoft, SAP, Red Hat and Oracle. The processor supports AVX-512 VBMI. Calif lists Intel Xeon chips from Ice Lake onwards and AMD EPYC and Ryzen chips from Zen 4 onwards. ARM processors, including Apple Silicon and many cloud ARM servers, are not affected. Servers are the main concern, because they accept untrusted input all day. But Calif adds that a Java program that connects to a malicious server over TLS can also be attacked, so desktop and developer tools are in scope if they run on such a processor. CISA does not discuss home users or browsers. Modern web browsers no longer run Java, so browsing the web does not expose you through the browser itself. CISA also warns that Java often hides inside other products. It may be bundled in an application, a container image or a network appliance and not show up in a normal software list. How it was found Calif says one of its researchers found the bug with OpenAI's Codex on 24 October 2026, in about an hour, and that AI agents helped build the exploits. It also says the bug had been reported publicly as a crash on 9 June 2026, and that a proposed fix in September was closed without being merged. That timeline is Calif's own and was not independently verified. Is it being used in attacks? None of the three pages we read says so. CISA's alert does not say it is exploited, and Calif's reference to "in the wild" is about the earlier crash report. A forum post quotes the vulnerability firm VulnCheck as saying it does not expect the bug to be easily or widely exploitable, but we did not read VulnCheck's own post. Treat the lack of attacks as a snapshot and not a promise. Exploit chains are not public yet, which buys time. What to do 1. Patch Update Java through your vendor. The OpenJDK project posted an advisory dated 17 November, and Oracle included the fix in its November 2026 update. Check your vendor's page for the exact build number, as notation differs between sources. CISA says to prioritise systems reachable from the internet. 2. Find every Java you run Look for bundled runtimes in applications, containers and appliances. Check whether the machine has the processor feature. On Linux, Calif suggests searching the processor flags in /proc/cpuinfo for avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi and bmi2. All four need to be present for the bug to apply. 3. If you cannot patch yet Start the Java process with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to turn off the hardware-accelerated Base64 path. This comes from Calif and a relayed forum post, not from CISA or Oracle. Or start it with -XX:UseAVX=2, which turns off AVX-512. Use it only on x86-64, since Calif says it will stop ARM from starting. CISA says to restrict and validate Base64 input at the edge of the application, set input size limits and reduce unauthenticated access. Watch for unexpected Java crashes and unfamiliar Java processes. What it means if you just browse the web For most readers, very little directly. You still benefit from keeping every program updated, including your browser. If you use developer tools, a self-hosted app or an office server that runs Java, ask whoever runs it whether it has been patched. Our article on the latest Chrome zero-day covers the update habit. Frequently asked questions Does Java4Shell affect my web browser? CISA does not mention browsers. Modern browsers do not run Java, and the bug is in the Java runtime, so browsing alone does not expose you through the browser. Am I affected if I use an Apple Silicon Mac or an ARM computer? Calif says ARM processors are not affected, because the faulty code is part of the x86-64 AVX-512 path. Is there a patch? Yes. Oracle released one on 17 November, and OpenJDK published an advisory the same day. Other vendors make their own builds, so check yours. Is it being exploited right now? The sources we read do not say so. Calif says no universal exploit exists and that each target needs its own work, but it also claims working attacks on popular server software. How do I disable the risky code path? Start Java with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, or on x86-64 with -XX:UseAVX=2. These are stop-gaps until you patch. Sources CISA: Critical Java vulnerability requires immediate patching (17 Nov 2026) Calif: Java4Shell write-up IFIN: CVE-2026-114938, pre-auth remote code execution in Java (forum post relaying vendor data) Written by the Rapid+ Team. title: Microsoft 365 Outage: Why Exchange Online Went Down for 24 Hours in November 2026
desc: A hidden bug, a traffic surge and failed safeguards. The hour-by-hour story of the Microsoft email outage, who was hit, and how to cope next time.
text: Written on 23 November 2026. The timeline comes from Microsoft's preliminary post-incident report as described by The Register, and from IBTimes Australia, which summarises Microsoft's statements. We did not read Microsoft's own report, and a final version was due on 20 November. Details may change. For about a day, from 12 to 13 November 2026, millions of people could not reliably use Outlook or the email behind it. Microsoft's Exchange Online went down for users around the world, and many Microsoft 365 services that depend on it were hit with it. Microsoft says it was not an attack. It was a defect in a July software change that sat unnoticed until a surge of traffic set it off. This article sets out what happened hour by hour, what Microsoft says went wrong, who was affected, and what a normal business or person can do so that the next outage costs less. The short version The outage ran from roughly 16:00 UTC on 12 November to 16:10 UTC on 13 November, a little under 24 hours, with Microsoft's final customer update on 14 November. Exchange Online was the main casualty. Many users saw it as Outlook not working, and email delivery was delayed for many. Microsoft's first statement called it "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI". Its report says there was no attack. The cause was a defect in a July 2026 change to the Microsoft 365 network gateway servers, triggered when Teams traffic moved to the same gateways. Rolling back was not possible because the defect was months old. Engineers built an update that reverted the faulty change and applied it to servers in groups. What happened, step by step Time (UTC) Event 12 Nov, 01:07 Teams traffic fails over to the primary gateway that also serves Exchange Online. 12 Nov, 16:03 Microsoft's monitoring flags increased connectivity problems. 12 Nov, 16:33 First customer support case arrives. 13 Nov, 00:30 Engineers identify connection negotiation as the main cause of access failures. 13 Nov, 07:20 Mitigation is applied. 13 Nov, 16:10 Microsoft confirms services are healthy again. 14 Nov Final customer update, according to The Register. The Register notes that engineers spent about 15 hours working on the problem before the cause was pinned down. IBTimes gives the outage as 23 hours and 50 minutes, though it also describes it as lasting "more than a day", so treat the exact length as approximate. What Microsoft says went wrong Microsoft's report, as relayed by The Register and IBTimes, describes three problems that stacked on each other. A hidden defect. A change made in July 2026 to the network gateway servers contained a bug that caused lock contention inside an internal Windows process, which used up the machine's processor and memory. It stayed dormant. Microsoft said its load testing focused on weaker hardware with fewer cores, and the problem is worse on newer machines with more cores. A traffic surge. When Teams failed over to the primary gateway, the load landed on servers already running with about 14 percent of capacity out of service for an unrelated reason. A cascade. The barriers meant to stop one group of servers failing from overloading the rest did not hold. At the worst point, more than 80 percent of the servers were affected. Charles Lamanna, a Microsoft executive, summed it up on X in the same three points, according to IBTimes. How it was fixed A normal rollback would not work, because the defect had been present since July and the code from before it was long gone. Microsoft instead built an update that returned the faulty code path to a known good state. Engineers disconnected servers in batches, applied the update, restarted them and brought them back. This is why recovery took hours even after the cause was known. Who was affected IBTimes reports that the outage touched more than 70 countries, and that Microsoft 365 has about 430 million users. It lists downstream effects including hospitals and clinics in Britain's NHS, a hospital network in Toronto, courts in the Philippines and Singapore, a Japanese government service and staff in the US House of Representatives. Anderson Economic Group estimated losses of about $7 billion. That is an outside estimate, not a figure from Microsoft. The Register and IBTimes do not mention service credits or compensation. Microsoft apologised to users as the outage ended. Why "not an attack" matters When a big service goes down, rumours about hackers start within minutes. This time they were wrong, and Microsoft said so early. Still, an outage and an attack feel the same to the person who cannot read their email. The practical difference is data: nothing in the reports suggests that anyone's messages were stolen. Be careful with emails claiming to be from Microsoft about "restoring your account" after an outage, because scammers use these moments. Our guide to spotting fake pages applies here too. How to cope with the next outage Know the status page. Microsoft publishes service health on its admin centre and on social channels. Bookmark them before you need them. Keep a second way to reach people. A chat group, a phone tree or a different email address for critical contacts costs nothing. Save what you need offline. Recent calendar entries, key contacts and important documents should not live in one place only. Do not retry in a loop. Hammering a failing service adds load. Wait for the status update. Review dependencies. A business that runs email, files and meetings from one provider has one point of failure. Frequently asked questions Was the Microsoft outage a cyberattack? No. Microsoft said it was not related to cyber, and its report describes a software defect from a July change. It says it ruled out an attack quickly. How long did the outage last? About 24 hours of disruption, from around 16:00 UTC on 12 November to 16:10 UTC on 13 November. Microsoft issued a final update on 14 November. Which services were hit? Exchange Online, which many people experience as Outlook, was the main service. Other Microsoft 365 services that depend on it were affected. Teams, OneDrive and SharePoint could fail away from the faulty gateway and were less affected. Did I lose any email? The reports describe delayed delivery and access problems, not lost mail. IBTimes said Microsoft reported the email backlog processed after recovery. If you think a message is missing, ask the sender to resend it. Will I get compensation? The reports we read do not mention credits. Business customers should check their service agreement and ask their account contact. Sources The Register: Microsoft blames monster email outage on software defect introduced in July fix (16 Nov 2026) IBTimes Australia: Microsoft outage explained, hidden bug and Teams traffic surge (22 Nov 2026) Windows Central: Microsoft outage drags on as Outlook, Teams and Microsoft 365 show signs of recovery Written by the Rapid+ Team. title: Optimizely Supply-Chain Attack: Malware Hit Visitors of BBC, CNN, Zoom and 170+ Sites
desc: One vendor script, 178 organisations, about 17 hours. What the malicious code did on the BBC, CNN, Zoom and others, and what to do if you visited.
text: Written on 23 November 2026. This story is still developing. The most detailed account is by Report URI, whose researcher Scott Helme found the attack, and we also drew on Krebs on Security and BleepingComputer. We did not read Optimizely's own incident report. Where sources disagree or nobody knows, we say so. On 16 November 2026, malicious code was delivered to visitors of at least 178 well-known organisations through a single marketing tool, Optimizely. The affected sites include the BBC, CNN, Zoom, Equifax and the hardware wallet maker Ledger. For about 17 hours, pages that loaded Optimizely's script could swap cryptocurrency addresses, skim card numbers and try to attack older iPhones. The attack is over, but it shows how one trusted script can reach a very large audience at once. This article explains what Optimizely is, what the code did, who might have been affected, and what you can do today, whether you only browse the web or run a website. The short version Attackers added malicious JavaScript to customer projects inside Optimizely Web, a tool that websites use for A/B testing and personalisation. Report URI found 188 infected snippets belonging to 178 organisations among the 1,611 it could check. It says the real number is likely higher. The code swapped crypto wallet addresses, tried to capture card details typed into a site's own forms, and sent cookies and screenshots to the attacker. On iPhones and iPads running iOS 18.6 or earlier, it tried to load exploit kits named Coruna and DarkSword. Report URI estimates about $7,000 to $7,500 in cryptocurrency reached the attacker's wallets. The number of stolen cards and cookies is unknown. Optimizely says it has removed the injected code and fixed the vulnerability. How the attacker got in is not fully explained. What Optimizely is and why it matters Many large websites use Optimizely Web to test two versions of a page and see which works better. To do that, each customer loads a small script from Optimizely's servers on every page. That script can include a field called Project JavaScript, where the customer can add its own custom code. The script runs as soon as the page loads, before any cookie banner has been answered, as researcher Zach Edwards told Krebs. That arrangement is the weak point. A site that trusts one vendor's script has handed that vendor the ability to run code on every visitor's browser. If an attacker can write into the vendor's system, they can reach every site at once, with no need to break into any of them. How the attack worked According to Report URI, the attacker wrote malicious code into the Project JavaScript field of customer projects. The rest of each script was unchanged, and it was still served from Optimizely's own domain with Optimizely's own certificate. Report URI stresses this was not a poisoned cache: Optimizely's network served exactly what it was given. The injected code loaded a second script from a domain registered that morning. Report URI describes three loader variants, including one that carried a full copy of the payload so that blocking the domain would not stop it. Timeline (UTC, from Report URI) Time on 16 November What happened 02:21 Last clean capture of the BBC's Optimizely script. 04:21 First infected script seen, on the BBC. 13:43 Card-skimming code added to the payload. 19:24 to 19:59 Report URI's sweep finds 186 of 1,611 snippets infected. About 20:40 to 21:10 Mass clean-up begins; Ledger, Smartsheet and the BBC are cleaned. 23:11 All infected Optimizely files clean and staying clean. The attacker's two domains were put on hold by their registrar on 17 November, which stopped the code from loading even where it remained. What the malicious code did Swapped crypto addresses. It replaced Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tron, Solana and other wallet addresses on the page, in the clipboard and in outgoing requests with the attacker's own. Copy an address from an affected site and you might have pasted the attacker's. Skimmed card details. From 13:43 UTC it watched forms for card numbers, expiry dates and security codes, and sent them to the attacker. Cards typed into hosted payment frames such as Stripe or Adyen were out of reach. Cards typed into a site's own fields were not. Sent cookies and screenshots. It collected the page address, cookies that are not marked HttpOnly, and a screenshot. Report URI says to treat any session tokens kept in such cookies as exposed. Tried to exploit iPhones. On iPhones and iPads it loaded exploit kits in a hidden frame: Coruna for iOS 13 to 17 and DarkSword for iOS 18. A third chain for iOS 26 only fingerprinted the device. Pages on iOS 18.6 or earlier reloaded every 60 seconds to retry. Report URI cannot say how many cards, cookies or iPhones were affected. Krebs calls the iOS kits "zero-click" and says they chain together about six security holes, a description Report URI does not use. Whether any phone was actually compromised is not confirmed. Who was affected Report URI lists the BBC, CNN, Zoom, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock among the 178 organisations. BleepingComputer, which says it confirmed the script on its own, adds Fox News, American Eagle, Smartsheet and UNICEF USA. Banking and finance made up the largest group in Report URI's table, with 32 organisations. At least 12 Dutch websites also warned visitors, according to NL Times. Only people who loaded a page during the window could be affected, and the strongest signs of harm are for people who copied a crypto address, typed a card number or used an old iPhone. Most readers who visited these sites will have been unaffected. What you should do If you visited an affected site on 16 November Update your iPhone or iPad to iOS 18.7.3 or later, or iOS 26.3 or later, which the kit's own code treats as patched. If you sent cryptocurrency that day, check that the address you sent to matches the one you meant to use. If you paid by card on one of these sites, watch your statement and ask your bank about anything you do not recognise. Our advice on paying safely explains why a card gives you the strongest protection. Change passwords on sensitive accounts you used that day and prefer passkeys where offered. If you run a website that used Optimizely Open every project's Project JavaScript and each experiment's custom code, and look for the attacker's domain, atob( and any code you did not write. Review who and what has write access to your Optimizely account, and rotate credentials. Treat card data entered on your own forms that day as potentially exposed, and rotate secrets stored in cookies without HttpOnly. Deploy a Content Security Policy that limits which domains scripts can load from and send data to. In Report URI's data, 24 of the 256 organisations it checked had a policy that blocked the payload, while 68 had none. The lesson about third-party scripts Every extra script on a page is a promise that its owner stays safe. Browsers cannot judge that promise for you, but you can reduce your exposure. A content blocker stops many third-party scripts from running at all, and Krebs notes that modern blockers can block most requests of this kind. Site owners can load fewer vendors, audit what they load and limit what scripts may do. Rapid+ Browser includes content blocking for this reason, though no blocker catches everything. Frequently asked questions Was the BBC or CNN itself hacked? Not directly. The code came from Optimizely, a tool those sites use, and ran in visitors' browsers. Report URI says the vendor's network served exactly what it was given, so the tool's own systems were the point of attack. Is the attack still going? No. Report URI reports that all infected Optimizely files were clean by 23:11 UTC on 16 November and stayed clean. The attacker's domains were also put on hold on 17 November. Could my iPhone have been hacked? Only if it ran iOS 18.6 or earlier (or iOS 13 to 17) and loaded an affected page. Report URI says it cannot tell how many devices were infected. Updating to iOS 18.7.3, iOS 26.3 or later closes the holes the kit relied on. How did the attacker get in? That is not fully known. Report URI says it does not know how write access was obtained. Optimizely told BleepingComputer that the attacker used a vulnerability in its account signup flow and says it has fixed it. How much money was stolen? Report URI counted roughly $7,000 to $7,500 in cryptocurrency across the attacker's wallets. The number of stolen card records and cookies is not known. Sources Report URI: World's largest brands infected with malware via Optimizely (Scott Helme, 16 Nov 2026, updated) Krebs on Security: Attackers used Optimizely to A/B test malware on top websites (17 Nov 2026) BleepingComputer: Optimizely supply-chain attack delivers malware to CNN, Fox News, BBC, Salesforce sites (16 Nov 2026) NL Times: At least 12 Dutch websites warn of malicious code that tried to hack old iPhones Written by the Rapid+ Team. title: Outlook Flaw CVE-2026-124194 Is Being Exploited: How to Update and Stay Safe
desc: November updates fix over 1,000 flaws, including an Outlook bug under attack. What it does and the quick steps to protect your computer.
text: Written on 23 November 2026. This is based on Malwarebytes' report of 11 November on Microsoft's November 2026 updates. The article does not state the release date, though a linked CISA alert is dated 10 November, which fits the usual second Tuesday. We did not read Microsoft's own advisory. Microsoft's November 2026 security updates fix more than 1,000 vulnerabilities. One of them, CVE-2026-124194 in Outlook, is already being used in real attacks, and the US cyber agency CISA has added it to its list of known exploited flaws. It does not need you to click a link. Opening one specially made message file can be enough to leak the secret that proves who you are on a work network. The fix is a normal Office update. The short version CVE-2026-124194 is an Outlook spoofing flaw rated 6.5 out of 10. Microsoft describes it as the interface failing to warn the user about unsafe actions. It is being exploited in the wild, and CISA listed it on 10 November. An attacker has to get you to open a specially crafted message file. Outlook then connects to an attacker-controlled location without the usual warning about external content. That connection can leak your NTLMv2 hash, which can be used to impersonate you on a network. The same release fixes 48 critical code-execution flaws, including CVE-2026-116928, which is rated 9.8 and involves an email attachment processed by Exchange. Malwarebytes says Microsoft has not reported exploitation of that one. Update Office and Windows now. How the Outlook flaw works When you open an email, Outlook normally refuses to load images or other content from the internet until you allow it. That warning protects you, because loading external content tells the sender's server that you opened the message, and sometimes more. The flaw skips that warning. A crafted message file makes Outlook reach out to a location the attacker controls, and it does so quietly. Windows can send a hashed version of your login secret when it connects to a network location. That is the NTLMv2 hash. It is not your password in clear text, but an attacker can try to crack it or relay it to sign in as you somewhere else. On a company network this can be the first step toward taking over accounts. Home users are at lower risk, but the update is still free and quick. The other flaws in the update Malwarebytes reports that the November updates fix more than 1,000 Microsoft vulnerabilities, including 48 critical remote code execution flaws, some of which need no user action. It singles out CVE-2026-116928, a memory flaw in the Windows search component rated 9.8. Microsoft's description says an attacker could send an email attachment that Exchange Server processes for indexing, and the recipient would not need to open it. Code could then run with the permissions of the affected service. Malwarebytes says exploitation of that flaw has not been reported. How to update Office and Outlook Open any Office app, such as Outlook or Word. Go to File, then Account (in Outlook, Office Account). Under Product Information, choose Update Options, then Update Now. If these options are missing on a work computer, your IT team controls updates. Ask them whether the November Office update has been installed. Windows Open Settings, then Windows Update. Choose Check for updates, install what it finds and restart if asked. Malwarebytes mentions Security Update KB5132061 as an example of an update that may already be installed. Because the Outlook flaw is under attack, it recommends doing the Office update first. Habits that help Be careful with message files. Do not open unexpected.msg files or attachments, especially from people you do not know, even if the subject looks routine. Keep external content blocked in your mail program, and do not turn off warnings to save a click. On a company network, ask your IT team about blocking outbound connections that send Windows login hashes to the internet. This is common advice for this type of leak, not a statement from Microsoft. Use a passkey or two-step verification on important accounts, so a leaked hash alone does not open the door. Our passkey guide explains why. What this means for your browser Updates arrive in waves: the browser this week, Office and Windows the next. Our report on the Chrome zero-day patched on 9 November covers the browser side. Treat both as part of the same habit: when a vendor says a flaw is being used in attacks, update the same day. Frequently asked questions Is CVE-2026-124194 being used in attacks? Yes. Malwarebytes says it is exploited in the wild, and it links a CISA alert from 10 November adding it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Do I have to click a link to be affected? You have to open a specially crafted message file in an affected version of Outlook. Outlook then connects to the attacker's location without the usual warning. What is an NTLMv2 hash? It is a scrambled version of your Windows login secret that your computer sends when it connects to a network resource. An attacker who gets it can try to crack it or reuse it to impersonate you. Which is more dangerous, the Outlook flaw or the 9.8 flaw? The Outlook flaw has a lower score, but it is being exploited. CVE-2026-116928 has a higher score and could run code without the recipient opening the attachment, but Malwarebytes says exploitation has not been reported. Patch both. How do I know the update is installed? In Office, open File, Account and check the version under Product Information. In Windows, open Windows Update and look at the update history. Sources Malwarebytes: Microsoft Patch Tuesday fixes Outlook flaw already under attack (11 Nov 2026) Written by the Rapid+ Team. We build Rapid+ Browser for Android and Windows. title: Ransomware Up 38%: What Beazley's Q3 2026 Report Says and How to Protect Yourself
desc: Exploited software flaws doubled and attackers now steal logins that are already open. The report in plain words, with steps for people and small firms.
text: Written on 23 November 2026. The figures come from Security Today's report of 19 November on Beazley Security's quarterly threat report for the third quarter of 2026. We did not read Beazley's report itself, and the article does not give the baseline for the 38 percent rise or an average ransom, so we do not state either. Ransomware is growing again, and the way in has changed. Beazley Security says reported ransomware incidents rose 38 percent in the third quarter of 2026. The share of cases that started with an exploited software flaw doubled to 28 percent. Attackers also increasingly steal a login that is already open instead of guessing a password. Here is what the report says in plain words, and what an ordinary person or small business can do about it. The short version Reported ransomware incidents rose 38 percent in the third quarter, according to Beazley Security's report as covered by Security Today. Cases beginning with an exploited vulnerability doubled to 28 percent, up from 14 percent in the second quarter. Vendors shipped almost 80 percent more software updates, and published CVEs reached nearly 37,000. Healthcare remained the most targeted industry, with 21 percent of investigated cases. Malware accounted for 19 percent of initial breaches, up from 14 percent, driven mainly by a trick called ClickFix. Attackers are stealing active login sessions and even registering their own devices. Flaws are the front door A year ago, stolen passwords were the usual way in. Now more attacks begin with a known software flaw that was not patched in time. Beazley says security teams faced a nearly 80 percent jump in vendor updates, with CVEs reaching close to 37,000. More flaws means more chances to fall behind, and attackers move fast on the ones that matter. The targets are often self-hosted, internet-facing apps such as build servers, analytics tools and collaboration software. Attackers who get in often find cloud access keys on the compromised server and use them to deploy ransomware through the victim's own cloud tools. Beazley's advice, quoted by Security Today, is to prioritise known exploited vulnerabilities and internet-facing applications first. That is the same advice behind our reports on the Chrome zero-day and on the Outlook flaw under attack. ClickFix: you run the attack yourself ClickFix is a trick in which a web page shows a fake error or CAPTCHA and tells you to fix it by pressing a key combination, then pasting something into the Windows Run box or a terminal. What you paste is a command that installs malware. Because you did it yourself, some security checks do not see it as an attack. Beazley says malware was behind 19 percent of initial breaches, up from 14 percent, mostly because of ClickFix. Extortion or ransomware typically followed an infection by two to three weeks, so the damage is not immediate and people forget the earlier odd page. The rule: no real website needs you to paste a command to prove you are human. If a page tells you to, close it. Stealing the login that is already open Beazley says attackers increasingly steal active login sessions instead of passwords. They use tools that sit between you and a real site, device-code phishing, and malware that copies saved sessions from your browser. Josh Carolan of Beazley says attackers are "waiting until users authenticate to hijack active sessions". Some also register their own device, so they keep access after you reset your password. This matters for a browser user. A session is the small piece of data that keeps you signed in. If a script or malware copies it, the attacker is signed in as you, and a strong password does not help. Our report on the Optimizely attack shows how a script on a page can reach cookies. AI agents on the attacking side The report describes an attack run almost entirely by coordinated AI agents. It got past patching and two-step verification, exploited a flaw in a custom application and used a service account credential to move across the network and steal data. Francisco Donoso of Beazley says the agents work "tirelessly to locate unpatched servers and flat networks faster than human attackers", which makes basic network hygiene and segmentation more important. What an ordinary person can do Update everything quickly. Browser, operating system, Office, router and phone. Turn automatic updates on. Never paste commands from a web page. Treat any fake CAPTCHA that asks for it as an attack. Use passkeys where available. Beazley recommends phishing-resistant sign-in such as passkeys. See our passkey guide. Review where you are signed in. On key accounts, look at the list of devices and sessions, remove ones you do not know and sign out of the rest. Keep an offline backup. A copy that is not connected to your computer cannot be encrypted by ransomware. Use a separate browser profile for banking and work, so one infected session cannot reach everything. Our profiles article explains how. What a small business can do List what is reachable from the internet and patch those systems first. Turn off device-code sign-in where you do not need it, and block new sign-in registrations from unmanaged devices, as Beazley recommends. Keep cloud access keys out of servers and rotate them. Split the network, so a break-in on one machine does not give access to everything. Frequently asked questions How much did ransomware grow? Beazley Security says reported incidents rose 38 percent in the third quarter of 2026. The article we read does not say what that is compared with. What is ClickFix? It is a fake error or CAPTCHA page that tells you to paste a command into your computer to fix a problem. The command installs malware. Which industry is hit most? Healthcare, with 21 percent of the cases Beazley investigated. Can two-step verification be bypassed? Some methods can, for example when attackers steal an already authenticated session or trick you into approving a device code. Beazley recommends phishing-resistant sign-in such as passkeys. What is the single best thing to do? Install updates quickly, especially for anything reachable from the internet, and never run commands that a web page tells you to paste. title: TfL Oyster Data Breach: 265,000 Customers May Be Affected, What to Do Now
desc: Names, addresses, dates of birth and security answers may be exposed. What TfL says, and the steps to take if you hold an Oyster photocard.
text: Written on 23 November 2026. This is based on BleepingComputer's report of 19 November, which draws on customer breach notices and TfL's public page. We did not find a direct TfL statement we could quote, so most of this is paraphrased. TfL's investigation is not finished and its numbers may change. Transport for London says details of around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers may have been exposed after attackers got into its email systems. TfL found out on 16 November 2026, when customers reported getting emails that asked them to create an account, sent from TfL's own mail servers. If you hold an Oyster photocard, here is what was exposed, what was not, and what to do now. The short version TfL discovered the incident on 16 November after customers received emails asking them to create an account. The emails came from TfL's own systems because of a compromise. About 265,000 Oyster photocard customers may have had account details exposed, up from an early estimate of about 250,000. The number could still rise. Possibly exposed: full names, phone numbers, email addresses, home addresses, dates of birth, and security questions and answers. TfL says passwords, bank and payment card details and journey information were not compromised, and it has found no evidence of misuse so far. Oyster photocards still work for travel. The photocard website is offline for maintenance. What happened The first sign was not a TfL announcement but customers' inboxes. People who hold Oyster photocards, the discounted cards for students, older people and some other groups, received emails telling them to create an account. They looked genuine because they were sent through TfL's real mail systems, which attackers had compromised. TfL says it has contained the incident, contacted affected customers, begun sending breach notifications and informed the UK Information Commissioner's Office. The Oyster photocard website has been taken offline. What data may have been exposed Possibly exposed Not compromised, per TfL Full name Passwords Phone number Bank and payment card details Email address Journey information Home address Names and dates of birth of children with Zip Oyster cards Date of birth Security questions and answers The security questions are the part people overlook. If you use the same answers on other sites, such as your first school or your mother's maiden name, anyone holding them could try them there. The phishing risk is the real danger A leaked list of names, addresses, birthdays and phone numbers is exactly what scammers need to write convincing messages. Expect emails and texts that claim to be from TfL, your bank or "the police". A caller who knows your address and date of birth sounds trustworthy, and that is the trick. The emails that started this incident are a reminder that even a real sender address does not prove a message is safe. Our guide to spotting fake pages and messages lists checks that work even when a message looks perfect. What to do if you hold an Oyster photocard Ignore the account-creation email that TfL says to disregard. Do not click links in it. Do not reply to calls or texts that ask for personal details, even if they quote your address. Hang up and use a number you looked up yourself. Change your security answers on every other site where you used the same ones. A password manager can store made-up answers. Change passwords on other services that used the same information as your TfL account. Watch for the prompt. When the photocard portal comes back, TfL says all customers will be asked to change their password and security questions. Report anything suspicious to TfL and to your bank. Your card remains valid, and if you need to renew it or check journey history, TfL Customer Services can help in the meantime. What follow-up scams usually look like After a breach, criminals do not always attack the stolen account. They use the details to build messages that feel personal. For an Oyster breach, common patterns would be: A "refund" or "fare adjustment" message that says you were overcharged and asks you to enter card details to receive money. A "your photocard has been suspended" text with a link to renew it. Real renewals go through the official TfL site that you type in yourself. A call from "your bank" or "the police" that quotes your address and date of birth to prove it is real, then pushes you to move money. A "verify your account" email that asks for your security answers. A company that really needs them would not ask by email. These are general patterns that follow breaches of this type. They are not reports of specific messages sent after this incident. The safe habit is the same each time: stop, do not use the link or number in the message, and contact the organisation through an address you found yourself. Why security questions are a weak lock Security questions ask for things that are not secret at all: a school, a first pet, a birth town. Friends, social media and now data leaks can supply the answers. If your answers were in the TfL data, treat them as public. The best fix is to stop answering truthfully. Invent a long random answer for each site and save it in a password manager, so that a leaked answer from one place is useless anywhere else. Where a site offers a passkey or an authenticator app instead, use that. Our passkey guide explains why they resist this kind of leak. Background: TfL was hit before BleepingComputer notes that in 2024 members of the Scattered Spider group breached TfL and stole customer data. It says that attack cost TfL £29 million, and that two hackers pleaded guilty in June 2026. The current incident is separate and no group has been named for it. Frequently asked questions Was my Oyster card balance or payment information stolen? TfL says bank and payment card details were not compromised. The data that may have been exposed is personal details such as name, address, date of birth and security questions. How do I know if I am one of the 265,000? TfL says it is contacting affected customers and sending breach notifications. If you hold an Oyster photocard, watch for that message, and treat any other email about it with care. Can I still use my Oyster photocard? Yes. TfL says photocards remain valid for travel. The photocard website is offline while the problem is fixed. Should I change my password? TfL says passwords were not compromised, but it will ask all photocard customers to change their password and security questions when the portal returns. Changing passwords on other sites that share your answers is sensible. Has the data been misused? TfL says it has found no evidence of misuse so far. The investigation is not complete. title: UK Forced to Reveal Secret Apple Encryption Order: What the Ruling Means
desc: The order is still secret, but its existence is now acknowledged. What the tribunal decided, what Apple says, and what end-to-end encryption means for you.
text: Written on 23 November 2026. This relies on TechCrunch and on the rights group Liberty, which brought the legal challenge. Neither page reveals what the secret order actually says, and several basic facts are still unknown. We list them below instead of guessing. On 19 November 2026 a UK tribunal ruled that the British government can no longer hide the fact that it ordered Apple to weaken the encryption protecting iCloud. The order itself is still secret, and Apple has refused to comply. But for the first time the government has been forced to admit a secret order of this kind exists, and the case that forced it will go on into 2027. This article explains what was ordered, what the ruling changes, what is still unknown, and what encryption on your own phone and cloud backups means in practice. The short version The order is called a Technical Capability Notice under the UK's Investigatory Powers Act. Liberty says such notices can require companies to change products to help surveillance, including by weakening encryption. It targets Apple's Advanced Data Protection (ADP), the setting that puts iCloud backups under end-to-end encryption, so that even Apple cannot read them. The Investigatory Powers Tribunal rejected the Home Office's argument that confirming the notice would harm national security, according to TechCrunch. Liberty and Privacy International brought the case, and Liberty puts the number of UK iCloud users at an estimated 39 to 40 million, based on a Which? estimate. Apple welcomed the decision, and has said it has never built a backdoor or master key and never will. A further hearing is expected in 2027. What was ordered The exact contents of the notice have not been made public. Liberty says plainly that the details have not been revealed. What is known comes from leaks and reporting. TechCrunch says the notice was reportedly a demand that Apple build a way for UK authorities to reach customer data anywhere in the world, as leaked a year earlier. It says the order was later narrowed to cover the data of British nationals stored in Apple's encrypted cloud, and that Apple challenged the second order too. Until this ruling, Apple was legally barred from even saying that a notice existed. That is why the earlier coverage relied on leaks. What Advanced Data Protection is Most cloud backups are encrypted, but the company holds the key, so it can read the data if the law requires it. With end-to-end encryption, only your own devices hold the key. The company stores scrambled data it cannot open, and cannot hand it over in readable form even when ordered to. That is the whole point, and also the reason governments push back: a company that cannot read your data cannot help investigators read it. TechCrunch reports that Apple blocked UK users from switching on ADP rather than comply with the order, and links to its February 2025 coverage of that step. Neither page we read says whether the block is still in place, so we cannot tell you whether ADP is currently available in the UK. What the tribunal decided The Investigatory Powers Tribunal handles complaints about state surveillance. Liberty and Privacy International, acting with two individuals, asked it to reject the government's "neither confirm nor deny" position on the order. According to Liberty, a September 2026 hearing took place and the tribunal has now agreed. Liberty's director Akiko Hart called the judgment "a victory for transparency". The ruling does not decide whether the order is lawful, and it does not release the order's text. A final hearing on the wider power to issue such notices is expected in 2027, and TechCrunch says a hearing on what details can be released is anticipated next year as well. What is still unknown The actual terms and scope of the notice, including the narrowed second order. Whether ADP is blocked for UK users today. The status of Apple's challenge to the second order. The Home Office's position. TechCrunch says it has yet to confirm the notice exists and did not comment. Whether any more detail will ever be published. The exact date of the tribunal's judgment is not given on either page, beyond TechCrunch's reference to a Thursday ruling, which fits 19 November. Why it matters beyond the UK TechCrunch says US officials and lawmakers criticised the order, arguing it puts Americans' privacy at risk. The reasoning is that an encryption weakness built for one country's investigators is a weakness for everybody, because a system cannot tell good access from bad. Security experts have made that argument for years, and it is the main point of the case. What you can do Check your own settings. If you use an iPhone, look for the Advanced Data Protection option in your Apple account settings. Whether you can turn it on may depend on where you live. Use end-to-end encrypted messaging for private conversations, and know which apps offer it by default. Keep a local backup of what matters to you on a drive you control, encrypted with a password you hold. Protect the account itself. Strong encryption does not help if someone can sign in as you. Use a passkey or a long unique password and two-step verification. Know what a VPN does not do. It does not change what a provider can read in your cloud backup. Our proxy and VPN explainer covers the limits. Frequently asked questions Did Apple give the UK a backdoor? Apple says it has never built a backdoor or master key and never will, and TechCrunch says it refused the order. Reports say it stopped offering ADP to UK users instead, but we could not confirm the current position. What is a Technical Capability Notice? It is an order under the UK Investigatory Powers Act that can require a company to change its products or services to help the state gain access to data. Liberty says it can include removing or weakening encryption. Is my iCloud data readable by Apple? It depends on your settings. With Advanced Data Protection on, most iCloud data is end-to-end encrypted and Apple cannot read it. With it off, Apple holds keys for much of the data. Does the ruling make the order illegal? No. It only stops the government from refusing to confirm that the order exists. A later hearing will consider the wider powers. How many people are affected? Liberty says an estimated 39 to 40 million people in the UK use iCloud, citing a Which? estimate. How many of them used ADP is not stated. Sources TechCrunch: U.K. government forced to disclose secret Apple backdoor order (19 Nov 2026) Liberty: Legal challenge forces government to reveal secret encryption order (19 Nov 2026) Written by the Rapid+ Team.
