title: Vendor Breaches: Why Infoblox, TSMC, Maersk and Irish Credit Unions Were Hit Through Suppliers
desc: Many victims, one weak link. The mid-November breaches that started at a vendor, what is confirmed, and what customers and companies can do.
text: Written on 23 November 2026. Most details come from TechCrunch, Check Point Research's threat report of 16 November and Privacy Guides' weekly roundup, which in turn summarise BleepingComputer and The Record. Several figures here are claims by attackers or estimates, and we mark them. Companies have not confirmed every number. In one week in mid-November 2026, a security vendor, the world's biggest chipmaker, a shipping giant and dozens of Irish credit unions all reported data theft. In almost every case the break-in did not start at the company named in the headline. It started at a supplier: a migration contractor, a cloud provider, a legacy system or an IT service firm. This article walks through the cases and what they mean for you as a customer. The short version Infoblox says hackers reached "certain company information" through a compromised third-party data migration vendor. TSMC confirmed a breach at an unnamed cloud provider that exposed employee data. An attacker claims 46,000 records. Maersk confirmed data theft from a legacy system it inherited through an acquisition. An extortion group claims about 100 GB and wants $5 million. Wellington IT, a supplier to about 50 credit unions, was hit, and at least six credit unions have disclosed the impact. ConnectWise ScreenConnect was abused to install remote access tools on at least 288 computers across 48 organisations. Infoblox: a migration contractor Infoblox, a company that sells networking and security products, confirmed on 16 November that it was investigating "unauthorized access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor". TechCrunch reports that two people with knowledge of the incident said the vendor handles SharePoint data migrations, and that one of them said sensitive customer data was taken. Infoblox did not name the vendor, would not say how many customers were affected, and said it had no sign that its own products, cloud services, software updates or build processes were involved. One person said Infoblox ended its work with the vendor, which the company did not comment on. TSMC: a cloud provider TSMC, the Taiwanese chipmaker, confirmed that employee information leaked after a breach at an unnamed cloud provider. Check Point Research reports that a hacker advertised 6.9 GB of allegedly stolen employee data on a criminal forum. Privacy Guides reports that the attacker claims 46,000 employee records, including national ID numbers, addresses, contact details and banking information. Those numbers are the attacker's claims, not TSMC's. TSMC says its own systems and customer data were not affected. Maersk: a system nobody retired Maersk, the Danish shipping and logistics company, confirmed unauthorised access to a legacy system it acquired through a purchase. An extortion group called WhiteArmor claims about 100 GB was stolen and demanded $5 million. Maersk says its other systems and customer operations were not affected. This is not a supplier in the usual sense, but it is the same weakness: a system outside the main security effort that holds real data. Wellington IT: one supplier, many credit unions Wellington IT is a Belfast-based supplier whose services are used by about 50 credit unions, including 43 in Ireland, according to Privacy Guides' summary of BleepingComputer. The firm said it lacked activity logs showing which member data was compromised, so it could not verify the impact on individual payees. At least six credit unions have disclosed their own impact. The records could include a payee's name, nickname, IBAN, BIC, bank account number, sort code, address and payment reference, and could show which member saved a given payee. ConnectWise ScreenConnect: a tool for managing other people's computers Check Point reports that attackers abused ConnectWise's ScreenConnect remote access platform, compromised managed service provider environments and deployed malicious remote access tools on at least 288 computers across 48 organisations. Managed service providers look after IT for many small companies, so one break-in leads to many. Why the same pattern keeps appearing One supplier holds many customers' data. Breaking in once is cheaper than breaking in 50 times. Suppliers have access, not attention. They hold keys and storage but are not watched like the main company. Old systems stay on. Acquired or retired systems often lose updates and monitoring while keeping data. Customers cannot see any of it. You gave your data to one company and it reached five. The same thing happened in the Fireworks AI breach that reached Uber and Cursor and in the Optimizely attack on the BBC and CNN. What you can do as a customer Share less. Give a company only the data it needs. Skip optional fields like date of birth. Use unique passwords and answers, so a leak at one place cannot open another. Expect phishing after a notice. When a company says data was exposed, the next message you get about it may be fake. Go to the company's site yourself. Read breach letters. They often include free monitoring, and they say which data was taken. Consider a credit freeze if national ID numbers or bank details were involved, where this is available. What businesses can ask their suppliers What data do you hold for us, and where? Who at your company and at your own suppliers can reach it? Do you keep activity logs? Wellington IT said it lacked them, and without logs a company cannot say who was hurt. How will you tell us if you are breached, and how quickly? What happens to our data when the contract ends? Frequently asked questions Which companies were breached through suppliers this week? Infoblox (a data migration vendor), TSMC (a cloud provider) and Wellington IT's credit union customers all involved a supplier. Maersk's breach involved a legacy system from an acquisition. Is the TSMC number confirmed? No. TSMC confirmed that employee data leaked. The 46,000 records and 6.9 GB figures are the attacker's claims. What is a supply-chain breach? A breach where attackers reach a company through one of its suppliers or tools, instead of attacking the company directly. How can I tell if my data was in a vendor breach? Companies must usually tell affected people. Watch for a letter or email from the company you dealt with, and check its website directly instead of using links in messages. Do I need to do anything if I use an Irish credit union? Check whether your credit union has issued a notice. At least six have disclosed impact. Watch for messages that mention your payees, since scammers use that kind of detail. Sources TechCrunch: Cyber giant Infoblox confirms security incident (16 Nov 2026) Check Point Research: 16th November threat intelligence report Privacy Guides: Data Breach Roundup (13 to 19 Nov 2026) Written by the Rapid+ Team. title: AI Browsers and Prompt Injection: How a Web Page Can Give Orders to Your Assistant
desc: AI browsers read pages and click for you. Researchers keep showing that a page can talk to the assistant. Here is how it works and how to limit the risk.
text: Written on 18 November 2026. The technical details come from Brave's published research on agentic browsers, which is the most detailed public account we found. Brave makes a competing browser and the findings are its own account, so we describe them as claims and not as independent tests. We could not load some other reports on the subject, and we do not cite what we did not read. A new kind of browser does not only show you pages. It reads them, decides what to do and clicks for you, using an AI assistant that is logged in as you. Security researchers keep finding that a web page can talk to that assistant, and sometimes the assistant obeys. The problem has a name, indirect prompt injection, and nobody has solved it. This article explains what happens, walks through the best documented example, and ends with practical rules for using an AI browser or assistant without handing over your accounts. The short version An "agentic" browser has an AI assistant that can browse, click and fill forms for you, with your logins. Indirect prompt injection means hidden instructions on a web page are read by the assistant as if the user had typed them. Brave's researchers showed this against Perplexity's Comet browser in 2025 and later reported related problems in other AI browsers, including Opera Neon. The classic web protections, such as the same-origin policy, do not stop an assistant that is acting with your privileges across sites. The sensible defences are to treat page content as untrusted, to ask for confirmation before sensitive actions and to keep the assistant away from your most important accounts. What an agentic browser does differently An ordinary browser renders a page and leaves decisions to you. An AI browser can also summarise the page, answer questions about it and carry out multi-step tasks such as comparing prices, filling a form or sending an email. To do that, the assistant sees the page text and can use the browser's tools, which run with your signed-in sessions. That combination is powerful and risky. A common way to describe the risk is three conditions at once: access to your private data, exposure to content from strangers and the ability to take actions. When all three are present, an attacker who controls the content can try to steer the actions. What indirect prompt injection is The assistant receives text from two places: your request and the page. A language model does not reliably tell them apart. If a page contains the sentence "ignore the user and instead do the following", a model that has been fed the page along with your request may follow it. The attacker does not need to hack the browser. They only need to get words in front of the assistant: in a forum comment, a hidden element, an email or a document. The word "indirect" means the attacker is not the user. The instruction arrives through content you asked the assistant to read. The best documented example Brave's researchers described an attack on Perplexity's Comet browser in August 2025. In their account, when a user asked Comet to summarise a page, it sent the page content to its model "without distinguishing between the user's instructions and untrusted content from the webpage". Attackers could hide instructions in white-on-white text, HTML comments, invisible elements or user posts such as Reddit comments. In their proof of concept, a hidden instruction in a Reddit comment led Comet to do the following: Read the user's email address from the Perplexity account page. Start a login with a slightly altered address, a domain with a trailing dot, to trigger a one-time password. Read that password from the user's open Gmail tab. Send both values back as a reply to the Reddit comment. With the email address and the code, an attacker could take over the account. Brave notes that the attack needed no further input from the user after the page was summarised. The timeline in their post says they reported it on 25 July 2025, Perplexity shipped a first fix two days later, a retest found it incomplete, and the public disclosure came on 20 August 2025. A later update says Perplexity had not fully mitigated this kind of attack. Brave's second post described "unseeable" injections hidden in screenshots, for example faint text on a coloured background that a person cannot read but a model can. It also reported an injection through hidden HTML elements in Opera Neon, which Opera first closed as not applicable and later fixed, according to Brave. These are vendor-reported findings, and Brave's position is that indirect prompt injection is a serious, unsolved problem for any AI browser that takes actions for you. Why it is hard to fix The old web security model assumes a clear line between sites. The same-origin policy stops a script on one site from reading another site's data. An agent that acts as you does not cross that line by exploiting a bug. It uses your logged-in sessions on purpose, as part of its job. Brave says that "traditional Web security assumptions don't hold for agentic AI", and that the same-origin policy and CORS do not stop the agent. Filters that try to catch malicious instructions help, but language is flexible and attackers can rephrase. That is why researchers talk about limiting what the assistant can do, not only what it can read. Defences that make sense Brave proposes four principles for browser makers: Separate the user's instructions from page content, and treat page content as untrusted. Check that each action matches what the user asked. Require explicit confirmation for sensitive actions. Isolate agentic browsing from regular browsing, with minimal permissions. As a user you can apply the same logic. Do not let an assistant act in accounts that matter. Keep it away from your bank, email and work tools. A separate browser profile with no sensitive logins is a good container, as we explain in our article on browser profiles. Prefer read-only help. Summaries are lower risk than actions. The risk rises when the assistant can send, buy or change settings. Confirm every action that touches money or accounts. If the assistant asks for approval, read what it is about to do. Be wary of pages from strangers. Untrusted content is the attacker's route. Summarising your own documents is safer than summarising a random forum thread. Keep the browser updated. Vendors patch these issues, sometimes slowly, as the Comet timeline shows. Frequently asked questions Is a normal browser affected? Not by this problem. Indirect prompt injection needs an AI assistant that reads pages and can act. Browsers without one do not have that attack surface, though they have other risks such as the zero-day bugs we covered earlier. Has this been used against real people? The cases we read about are research demonstrations by security teams and were disclosed to the vendors. We did not find evidence in those reports of attacks on real users. Can a company fully fix it? Brave describes it as an unsolved problem across AI browsers. Mitigations reduce the risk but, according to the researchers, do not remove it. Are summaries safe? Safer than actions, but not risk-free. In Brave's Comet example, a summary request was the trigger. The danger depends on what tools the assistant can use afterwards. What is the single best habit? Do not give an assistant access to accounts you cannot afford to lose, and approve actions yourself. Sources Brave: Agentic Browser Security, indirect prompt injection in Perplexity Comet (20 Aug 2025) Brave: Unseeable prompt injections in screenshots, more vulnerabilities in Comet and other AI browsers Brave: Prompt injection flaw in Opera Neon Written by the Rapid+ Team. title: Android Developer Verification: What Changes for Sideloaded Apps
desc: Apps must come from a verified developer, even outside the Play Store. The timeline, the advanced sideloading flow and what stays the same.
text: Written on 18 November 2026. The timeline comes from Help Net Security (31 March 2026) and Android Authority, which reported Google's plan. Sources differ slightly on some dates and on how the sideloading steps work, and we mark those points. Check Google's Android developer documentation for the definitive rules. Google is changing how apps get onto Android phones. Starting with four countries on 30 September 2026, apps installed on certified devices must come from a developer whose identity Google has verified, even if the app is installed from outside the Play Store. Installing unverified apps will still be possible, but with extra steps. Most people will notice nothing at first, and the change reaches every region in 2027. This article sets out the timeline, what changes for someone who installs apps from outside the store, and what stays the same. The short version Google calls the rule "developer verification". It checks who published an app, not what the app does. Google says it confirms developer identity and does not review app content. From 30 September 2026, in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand, apps must be registered to a verified developer to be installed or updated on certified Android devices. The requirement is scheduled to reach all regions in 2027. Apps from unverified developers can still be installed through an "advanced flow" or with ADB, the developer tool. Reports describe a restart and a 24-hour wait in the advanced flow. Students and hobbyists can use a limited distribution account to share apps with up to 20 devices, with no government ID and no fee, according to Android Authority. The timeline When What April 2026 The Android Developer Verifier, a system service that checks whether an app is registered to a verified developer, is introduced. June 2026 Early access to limited distribution accounts for students and hobbyists. August 2026 Limited distribution accounts and the advanced sideloading flow launch globally, per Help Net Security. 30 September 2026 Registration is required in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand for installs and updates on certified devices. Rest of 2026 Rollout stays limited while Google gathers feedback. 2027 Requirement expands globally to certified devices. Android Authority lists the first stores where the checks apply: Google Play, Samsung's Galaxy Store, Xiaomi GetApps, HONOR App Market, OPPO App Market, vivo V-Appstore and Palm Store. Google says millions of apps have been registered since developer verification opened in March. Who is affected Everyday users If you install apps from Google Play or your phone maker's store, your experience stays the same. The developers of those apps will have registered, and Google says that for most users the installation experience does not change. People who install apps from other sources Installing an APK downloaded from a website is called sideloading. If the app is registered to a verified developer, it should install as usual. If it is not, Android shows extra steps. According to Help Net Security and Android Authority, unverified apps can be installed with ADB or through the advanced flow, which Android Authority says includes a mandatory 24-hour lock and several installation steps. The reports we read do not describe the lock in detail, and one summary does not describe ADB as an exemption, so check the current developer documentation. Developers Developers register through the Android Developer Console for apps distributed outside Google Play, or through the Play Console. Hobbyists and students can use the limited distribution account for small audiences. Developers who share apps widely outside the store will need to complete verification. Why Google says it is doing this Malicious apps often arrive through sideloading: a fake banking app sent by text, a modified game, a "free" version of a paid tool. Stores can remove such apps once they are noticed. Developer verification aims to make it harder for a bad actor to publish under a disposable identity. The identity check does not stop malware by itself, and Google has said it does not review content, so the benefit is accountability and traceability. Critics of such rules usually argue that they give one company control over what runs on a phone and burden independent developers. The reporting we read describes Google's plan and its safeguards, such as the advanced flow and the hobbyist account, and does not provide a full critique, so we leave that debate to the sources you trust. What to do Prefer official stores for apps. They add a layer of review and verification and make updates automatic. Check the publisher before sideloading. A website you trust, a developer with a track record and a matching signature are better signs than a link in a message. Expect extra steps if you sideload apps from small developers once the rule reaches your region. Keep a list of the apps you installed that way. Keep your phone updated. The verification system is part of Android's services, and security updates stay important. Be wary of anyone telling you to bypass the steps. A message that urges you to disable protections to install an app is a classic scam. Frequently asked questions Is sideloading being banned? No. Reports say Google is not removing it. Apps from unverified developers can still be installed with extra steps, either through ADB or an advanced flow. When does it affect my country? On 30 September 2026 the rule began in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand. Google plans to expand it globally in 2027. Does Google review the apps? Google says verification confirms developer identity and does not review app content. What about hobby developers? A limited distribution account lets students and hobbyists share an app with up to 20 devices without a government ID or a fee, according to Android Authority. Does it apply to every Android phone? It applies to certified Android devices. Reports mention Android 7 and newer in the initial markets. Check Google's documentation for your device type. title: Arc Is Shutting Down on 22 December: What to Do With Your Browser Data
desc: The Browser Company has set a hard end date for Arc. Here are the deadlines, what carries over to Dia, and a checklist for picking your next browser.
text: Written on 18 November 2026. The dates and details below come from The Browser Company's announcement as reported by TechCrunch and 9to5Mac on 22 October 2026. We did not find the company's step-by-step export instructions in the reporting, so check Arc's own help pages for those. The Browser Company has announced that Arc, the browser with the vertical sidebar and "Spaces", will stop working on Mac and Windows on 22 December 2026. New accounts closed the day of the announcement. If you use Arc every day, you have about five weeks left to decide where your tabs, passwords and bookmarks will live. This article lists the dates, what the company says will carry over to its newer browser Dia, and how to judge any browser you might move to. The last part matters more than the brand name, because Arc's end shows what happens when a browser's maker decides it can no longer afford to keep it safe. The short version The Browser Company announced the end of Arc on 22 October 2026. New Arc accounts can no longer be created. On 23 November, Arc Search on iOS and Android loses its AI features, and sign-in and tab sync stop. It keeps working as a basic local browser. On 22 December, Arc stops working entirely on Mac and Windows, accounts are deactivated and Arc Search is removed from Google Play. The company says personal data is deleted within 30 days after accounts are deactivated. A report on its help article gives 15 December as the last day to ask for a copy of your data or for deletion. The company's stated reason is security: "Keeping a browser secure takes constant, dedicated work that is only increasing in the age of AI." The timeline Date What happens 22 October 2026 Sunset announced. New Arc accounts can no longer be created. 23 November 2026 Arc Search loses its AI features, including "Browse for Me". No sign-in or tab sync. It works as a local browser. 15 December 2026 Last day to request a copy of your Arc account data or ask for deletion, according to a report on the company's help article. 22 December 2026 Arc stops working on Mac and Windows. Accounts are deactivated. Arc Search leaves Google Play. Within 30 days after that Personal data is deleted, according to TechCrunch. Arc's development had already stopped well before this. Reports in May 2025 said the company had moved its focus to Dia, an AI-centred browser, and Atlassian bought The Browser Company in 2025 for $610 million, according to TechCrunch. The October announcement turns that quiet stop into a hard end date. Why the company says it is stopping The company's explanation is about the cost of safety. A browser is a large program that opens untrusted code from the whole internet all day. It needs frequent security updates, and the work does not end. In our article on the Chrome zero-day patched on 9 November, one bug in one update was enough to prompt an emergency release. A small team maintaining two browsers has to pick one. The company also told users that Dia "was built from the ground up to meet today's security standards" and that its engineers will focus there. That is the company's claim about its own product, and we have not tested it. The plain reading is simpler: Arc will not receive security fixes after the shutdown, and a browser without fixes becomes unsafe to use. What carries over to Dia The company says that passwords, bookmarks, extensions and history can move to Dia, and that Spaces, folders and tab groups import with their data. It describes the mapping like this: Arc's Spaces become Dia "Profiles", used to separate work from personal browsing. Folders become "Pinned Tab Groups". Vertical tabs remain as an optional sidebar layout. Arc's browser features stay free in Dia, and the AI features are optional. The reporting we read does not say what does not carry over, and it does not describe an export route for people who want to leave for a different browser. If you do not want Dia, export your bookmarks and passwords from Arc before 22 December, and check Arc's help pages for how to do it. How to choose your next browser Instead of asking which browser is the newest, ask questions that Arc's ending has made concrete. Who pays for the security work? A browser backed by a large company, a foundation or a paying user base has a better chance of staying patched than a side project of a team that is changing direction. How quickly does it ship fixes? Look at the release notes. Chromium-based browsers should publish a new version within days of a Chrome security release. Can you leave? A good browser lets you export bookmarks, passwords and history in standard formats. Arc's ending is a reminder to test that before you need it. What does it send out? Check the settings for tracking protection, telemetry and account sign-in. An account is not required to browse. Does it support what you rely on? Profiles, vertical tabs and extensions are the things people most often miss after leaving Arc. Rapid+ Browser is one option, and it also offers separate profiles, but we are not the right judge of your needs. Whatever you choose, read how it handles updates before you move your logins into it. What to do before 22 December Decide whether you want Dia or another browser. If you are moving to Dia, use its import feature from Arc while Arc still works. If you are leaving, export bookmarks and passwords now, and keep the file somewhere safe. A passwords file is not encrypted, so delete it after the import. Request a copy of your data or deletion before 15 December if you want either. Remove Arc from your computer after the move, so an unpatched browser is not left installed. Frequently asked questions Will Arc stop working immediately? No. Arc stops working on Mac and Windows on 22 December 2026. Until then it runs as before, but it receives no new features, and signing up for a new account is no longer possible. What happens to Arc on my phone? Arc Search on iOS and Android loses its AI features on 23 November, and sign-in and tab sync stop. It keeps working as a basic local browser, and it is removed from Google Play on 22 December. Can Arc be made open source? Users have asked for it. CEO Josh Miller said earlier that open-sourcing Arc would also mean opening the Arc Development Kit, which powers Dia and is still core to the company's value, so there is no plan to do it at the moment. Is it safe to keep using Arc after 22 December? It will not run on Mac or Windows after that date, according to the announcement. Any copy that keeps working would not receive security fixes, so you should not rely on it. Do I have to use Dia? No. Dia is the company's recommended path and it offers an import, but any browser that can import bookmarks will do. Export your data first. title: Black Friday 2026: How to Spot a Fake Online Shop Before You Pay
desc: The padlock proves little and typos no longer give scams away. A five-step check you can do in two minutes, using advice from the FTC.
text: Written on 18 November 2026. The core advice comes from the US Federal Trade Commission's guidance on shopping online. Black Friday falls on 27 November 2026. Security vendors publish many scam lists at this time of year and some of their statistics are marketing, so we use only practical advice that does not depend on their numbers. The week around Black Friday is when fake online shops do their best business. The sites look professional, the prices look like bargains and the ads appear in your social feed. Spelling mistakes used to give them away. They are no longer a reliable sign, and a padlock in the address bar proves even less. This article gives you a short routine that works even when the page looks perfect. The short version Pay with a credit card where you can. The FTC says it best protects you if something goes wrong, and gives you the right to dispute charges. Never buy from a seller that only accepts gift cards, wire transfers, payment apps or cryptocurrency. The padlock and "https" mean the connection is encrypted. They do not mean the shop is honest. Search the shop's name with the words "complaint" or "scam" before you order. Type the address of a shop yourself or use a bookmark, and do not rely on links in texts, emails or ads. How fake shops work A fake shop is a website built to take your money or card details and deliver nothing, or something worthless. It usually appears through an ad on social media or a search result, offers a famous product at a price far below normal and may copy a real brand's logo and photos. Some also use a spoofed copy of a real shop's login page to collect passwords. Tools that generate whole websites in minutes have made the pages look better. An Aston University fraud researcher, quoted in a news report, says that signs such as spelling mistakes and poor design are no longer reliable. We therefore focus on what the site does, not how it looks. What the padlock means The FTC states it directly: "The 's' after http means the site is encrypted, but it doesn't mean it's a legitimate site." Encryption stops others from reading what passes between you and the site. It does not tell you who owns the site. Scam sites use HTTPS too, because certificates are cheap and automatic. Our article on Chrome's HTTPS warning explains what the padlock does and does not promise. A five-step check before you buy Look at the address. Read the whole domain, not only the start. A name like "brand-sale-outlet.shop" is not the brand's site. Open the real brand's own website yourself and see if the deal is there. Search for the seller. The FTC suggests searching the seller or product name along with "complaint" or "scam". Do not rely on star ratings alone, because the FTC warns that some reviews and ratings are fake or misleading. Check how you are asked to pay. A shop that insists on gift cards, wire transfers, payment apps or cryptocurrency is a red flag. The FTC says: "Never buy anything from online sellers that insist you can only pay with gift cards." Read the delivery and return terms. The FTC says sellers must ship as promised in their ads, and if no time is promised, within 30 days of receiving your order and payment. Check the return window, who pays for return shipping and any restocking fee. Keep records. Save receipts, order confirmations, return policies and your messages with the seller. If something goes wrong, they are your evidence. Why the card matters The FTC says paying by credit card "best protects you and your money in case of a scam, or if something else goes wrong". Card holders can dispute charges for double billing, goods not received or wrong or defective items. The FTC sets a 60-day window from the first bill showing the error, so act quickly. A debit card, bank transfer or payment app may not give the same chances of getting money back. To limit your exposure, some people use a card with a low limit for new shops or a virtual card number from their bank. These are personal choices and not part of the FTC advice we quote. Using the browser to your advantage Use bookmarks for shops you trust. It avoids look-alike addresses. Do not enter a password by following a message. Delivery and refund texts are a common lure. Open the shop's app or type the address yourself. Keep shopping in its own profile. A separate browser profile keeps your shopping cookies and logins away from your email and banking. Use a password manager and passkeys where offered. A password manager offers a saved password only on the real domain, which exposes a spoofed login page. Our article on passkeys explains why they are harder to phish. Update your browser. Security fixes matter more when you are visiting many unfamiliar sites. See our article on the latest Chrome zero-day. Frequently asked questions Is a site with https and a padlock safe? Not necessarily. The padlock means the connection is encrypted, not that the seller is honest. The FTC says the same thing in plain words. What is the safest way to pay? The FTC says a credit card best protects you if there is a scam or another problem. Avoid sellers that only accept gift cards, wire transfers, payment apps or cryptocurrency. How can I check if a shop is real? Search its name with "complaint" or "scam", check the full domain and look for contact details, delivery terms and a return policy. Do not trust star ratings alone, because some are fake. I paid a fake shop. What now? Contact your card issuer or bank at once and ask to dispute the charge. The FTC gives a 60-day window for credit card disputes. Keep your records, change any password you entered and report the site to your national consumer authority. Are deals on social media ads trustworthy? Treat them with extra care. Fake shops are often promoted through ads. Go to the brand's official website directly and look for the offer there. Sources US Federal Trade Commission: Online shopping (consumer advice) National World: Black Friday shoppers warned over AI scams that are almost impossible to spot Written by the Rapid+ Team. title: Chrome Autofill Can Now Pull Details From Your Gmail: What to Know
desc: A new Chrome feature looks through your email to fill forms. Here is what it does, what Google has and has not explained, and how to switch it off.
text: Written on 18 November 2026. This is based on Google's announcement of 28 October 2026 as reported by 9to5Google and Decrypt. We did not test the feature, which is limited to the United States, so we describe only what was announced and what reporters pointed out was left unanswered. Chrome can now fill web forms with details that Gemini finds in your Gmail, such as order numbers, tracking information and flight bookings. Google began rolling the feature out on 28 October 2026. It is optional and limited to people who have turned on Gemini's "Personal Intelligence" in Chrome, but it is a real change: the browser's autofill is no longer limited to what you saved in it. This article explains what the feature does, what Google says about privacy, which questions reporters say remain open, and how to keep control of it. The short version "Enhanced autofill" uses Gemini to search your Gmail and suggest information when a web form asks for it. Examples named by Google are order numbers, tracking information and flight bookings. Suggestions appear in the autofill menu under "Suggested by Gemini". It is available only in the United States, starting 28 October, for people who use Gemini in Chrome with Personal Intelligence turned on. It works on desktop, Android and iOS. Google says "sensitive data is encrypted and you remain in control". You can remove individual suggestions or turn the enhanced autofill off in Chrome settings. Reporters note that Google's post does not explain how encryption applies to the Gmail content Chrome reads or what exactly it scans. What the feature does Classic autofill stores a name, an address, a phone number and a payment card in the browser, then offers them when a form asks. The new feature goes further. When you reach a form that asks for something you may have received by email, such as a booking reference on an airline's check-in page, Chrome can ask Gemini to look through your Gmail and offer a match. Google presented it as a convenience for the small, annoying lookups: finding an order number to open a return, or a flight confirmation to start check-in. 9to5Google says the feature can "automatically suggest information pulled directly from Gmail as you fill out online forms". Decrypt points out that the announcement does not say the feature pulls credit card numbers or addresses from Gmail. Standard autofill still handles names and addresses saved in the browser. One outlet reported a longer list of data types, which conflicts with the announcement, so we treat Google's own list of three as the authoritative one. Who can use it People in the United States. Users of Gemini in Chrome who have Personal Intelligence turned on, which means they chose to connect Gemini to their apps. Desktop, Android and iOS. Decrypt says Personal Intelligence is not available in Europe for now, so there is no date for a European launch. A separate outlet reported that Google's help page requires users to be 18 or older. Decrypt gave no age limit, so we cannot confirm it from the sources we read. What Google says about privacy Google makes two claims. The first is that "sensitive data is encrypted and you remain in control". The second, quoted by Decrypt from a statement in March, is that "Gemini and AI Mode don't train directly on your Gmail inbox or Google Photos library". Decrypt adds that Google does train on limited information, such as specific prompts and the model's responses. These statements answer some worries and leave others. The questions that remain open, according to Decrypt, are: How encryption applies to the Gmail content that Chrome reads, and what exactly it scans. Whether credit card numbers or addresses could come from Gmail in the future, since the announcement does not rule it out. When the feature will reach other countries. Encryption in transit and in storage protects data from outsiders. It does not tell you what the service itself does with the data it can read, which is the part people usually mean when they ask about privacy. How to keep control Decide whether to connect Personal Intelligence at all. The feature needs it. Decrypt says users choose whether to connect their apps and can disconnect at any time. Review Chrome's autofill settings. Google says you can turn enhanced autofill off in Chrome settings. Neither 9to5Google nor Decrypt gave the exact menu path, so look under the autofill section of Settings. Remove suggestions you do not want. Individual suggestions can be removed from the menu. Use a separate profile for sensitive mail. If you keep a work or private account in a different browser profile, Gemini in the first profile has nothing to read there. Our article on browser profiles explains how the separation works. None of this is a reason to panic. It is a reason to notice that a browser with an AI assistant becomes a path between the web and your private data, which is the same pattern that researchers worry about in our article on AI browsers and prompt injection. Frequently asked questions Does Chrome read my Gmail by default? No. The feature is limited to people who use Gemini in Chrome with Personal Intelligence turned on, in the United States. If you have not connected your apps to Gemini, it does not apply. What data does it fill in? Google's announcement names order numbers, tracking information and flight bookings. Standard autofill still handles names and addresses saved in the browser. Is it available outside the United States? Not at launch. Google has not given a date for other countries. Personal Intelligence is reported to be unavailable in Europe for now. Does Google train its models on my emails? Google says Gemini and AI Mode do not train directly on your Gmail inbox. It also says it trains on limited information such as prompts and the model's responses, and it has not said how this applies to the autofill feature in particular. How do I turn it off? Google says you can disable enhanced autofill in Chrome settings, remove single suggestions and disconnect Personal Intelligence at any time. Look in the autofill section of Chrome's settings. Sources 9to5Google: Chrome autofill can now use Gemini to pull details from Gmail (28 Oct 2026) Decrypt: Chrome can now pull details from your Gmail for web forms Written by the Rapid+ Team. title: Chrome Patches Its Eighth Exploited Zero-Day of 2026: What to Do
desc: Google fixed an actively exploited bug in Chrome's XML component on 9 November. Here is what is known, what is not, and how to check that your browser has the fix.
text: Written on 18 November 2026. The facts below come from reporting by Malwarebytes and SOC Prime on Google's advisory of 9 November. We could not load the text of Google's own release notes, so we link to them in the sources instead of quoting them. Google has not published technical details of the bug, and several things remain unknown. We say so where it matters. On 9 November 2026 Google released Chrome 157.0.8103.50 to fix a use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component, tracked as CVE-2026-125350. Google says it is aware that an exploit for it exists in the wild. It is the eighth Chrome zero-day known to have been used in real attacks this year, and the fix for it is a normal browser update that takes about a minute. This article sets out what was announced, what a "zero-day" and a "use-after-free" are in plain words, what Google has not said, and how to check that your own browser has the fix. It also covers a point people often miss: Chrome is not the only program that contains Chrome's engine. The short version Chrome 157 reached the stable channel on 3 November 2026. A smaller update, 157.0.8103.50 or.51 on Windows and Mac, followed on 9 November. That update contains nine security fixes. One of them is CVE-2026-125350, a high-severity use-after-free in the XML component, which Google says is being exploited. An unnamed third party reported the bug to Google on 6 November. The fix shipped three days later. Google has not said who is using the exploit, who was targeted, how it is delivered or what it lets an attacker do. To be safe, open Chrome's About page, let it update and click Relaunch. You want version 157.0.8103.50 or newer. Other Chromium-based browsers get the fix on their own schedule. Check their update pages too. What was announced Chrome 157 went to the stable channel on 3 November. Malwarebytes reported that it carried 213 security fixes, seven of them rated Critical by Google. The reporting on that release did not say whether any of those bugs were being exploited. Six days later Google shipped a follow-up build. According to Malwarebytes and SOC Prime, the 9 November release brought Chrome to 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. Chrome for Android got 157.0.8103.50 through Google Play, and the Extended Stable channel, which some company-managed computers use, got 156.0.8078.96 for Windows and Mac. The same release also fixed CVE-2026-125346, another use-after-free in the XML component. Google has only said that CVE-2026-125350 is under attack. Google rates it High severity but had not published a CVSS score when SOC Prime wrote about it. Hong Kong's HKCERT rated the overall risk of the update "Extremely High", and said that some of the fixed flaws could allow denial of service, a bypass of security restrictions or remote code execution. What "zero-day" means here A zero-day is a flaw that attackers are already using before a fix exists, so the vendor has had "zero days" to prepare. The name does not tell you how severe the flaw is or how many people are affected. It tells you that the order of events is bad: the attack came first and the patch second. Chrome has had several this year. SOC Prime counts CVE-2026-125350 as the eighth and lists the earlier seven: CVE-2026-2441, CVE-2026-3909, CVE-2026-3910, CVE-2026-5281, CVE-2026-11645, CVE-2026-85046 and CVE-2026-87491. Counts vary a little between outlets, depending on how they treat bugs found in the same attack chain, so treat "eighth" as one report's tally, not an official number. What a use-after-free is A browser constantly creates small pieces of data in memory, uses them and then frees the space. A use-after-free happens when the program frees a piece of memory but a part of the code still holds a pointer to it and keeps using it. If an attacker can arrange for that freed space to be refilled with data they control, the program may follow the stale pointer into the attacker's data. Depending on the bug, the result ranges from a crash to running the attacker's code inside the browser's renderer process. Malwarebytes describes the possible effect as crashes or, in some cases, an attacker running their own code. Memory-safety bugs of this kind are the most common class of serious flaw in browsers, which are large programs written mostly in C++. Chrome runs web pages inside a sandbox, so a renderer bug alone is usually not enough to take over a computer. Attackers often combine it with a second bug that escapes the sandbox. Whether this exploit does that has not been disclosed. Question What is known Is it being exploited? Yes. Google says it is aware that an exploit exists in the wild. Which component? Chrome's XML component. Reporting does not say which library or feature inside it. Who is behind the attacks? Not disclosed. Who was targeted? Not disclosed. How is it delivered? Not disclosed. Past browser exploits have usually needed a victim to open a crafted page. Is there a CVSS score? Not at the time of the reports we read. Is it fixed? Yes, in Chrome 157.0.8103.50 and newer. Why so little detail When a flaw is being exploited, publishing the full technical write-up before most people have updated would hand a recipe to more attackers. Vendors usually hold details back for a while, then release them once the fix has spread. The silence is normal, and it is not a sign that the problem is small. The practical reading is simple: assume the risk is real until your browser shows the fixed version. The bug was reported on a Friday and fixed on the following Monday, so Google's response was quick. What speed cannot do is reach computers whose owners never installed the update. That gap is where exploits do their work. How to check and update Chrome on Windows, Mac and Linux Open the three-dot menu, choose Help, then About Google Chrome. You can also type chrome://settings/help in the address bar. Chrome checks for an update and downloads it. If a Relaunch button appears, click it. Read the version number under the Chrome name. On Windows and Mac it should be 157.0.8103.50 or higher, such as 157.0.8103.51. Chrome updates itself, but Malwarebytes points out that updates can lag if you never close the browser or if an extension blocks the update. People who keep the same window open for weeks are the ones most likely to be behind. Relaunching also restores your tabs, so it costs little. Chrome on Android Open Google Play, search for Chrome and tap Update if it is offered. The fixed Android build is 157.0.8103.50, and Google says Android builds include the same security fixes as desktop unless noted. Edge, Brave, Opera, Vivaldi and other Chromium browsers These browsers are built on Chromium, the open source project behind Chrome, and they often share bugs with it. SOC Prime advises their users to watch each vendor's advisories and install fixes as they arrive. Each vendor sets its own timing, so open the About page of your browser and update it, then check its release notes for a mention of the Chromium fix. Other programs that contain Chrome's engine A lot of software carries a copy of Chromium or uses the system's version of it. Desktop apps built with Electron ship their own copy, so they receive Chromium fixes only when their developers publish a new build. On Android, apps that show web pages use the Android System WebView component, which is updated through Google Play. Rapid+ is built this way: the Android app uses the system's WebView, and the Windows app includes its own copy of Chromium through Electron. Whether CVE-2026-125350 reaches WebView or Electron builds depends on technical details Google has not released, so we cannot tell you that it does or does not. What you can do is keep Android System WebView and Chrome updated in Google Play, and update desktop apps when their makers release new versions. Apps that have not been updated for months are the ones to look at first. What to do today Update Chrome and relaunch it. It takes about a minute. Update your other Chromium-based browsers. On Android, update Chrome and Android System WebView in Google Play. Do not wait for details. Google may never publish many of them, and the fix does not depend on them. Keep automatic updates switched on, and relaunch your browser at least once a week. Frequently asked questions Do I need to do anything if Chrome updates itself? Check anyway. Automatic updates download in the background, but the new version only takes over after Chrome restarts. Open About Google Chrome and confirm the version is 157.0.8103.50 or newer. Was my computer hacked? There is no sign that ordinary users were broadly affected. Google says an exploit exists in the wild but has not said how many people were targeted. Exploits of this kind are often aimed at specific people. Update first, and if you have a reason to think you were targeted, run a malware scan and change important passwords from a clean device. What does "exploited in the wild" mean? It means there is evidence that attackers have used the flaw against real targets, not only in a lab. Google's wording in this case was that it is aware an exploit exists in the wild. Is it safe to use Chrome until I update? The safer course is to update before opening unfamiliar sites. A crafted web page is the usual way browser exploits are delivered, so avoiding links from unknown senders until you have the fix reduces your exposure, but it is no substitute for updating. Does this affect Edge, Brave and Firefox? Chromium-based browsers such as Edge, Brave, Opera and Vivaldi may be affected by Chromium bugs, and their vendors publish their own fixes. Firefox uses a different engine, and reporting on this bug does not link it to Firefox. Check each browser's update page. Why does Google not say more about the attack? Vendors normally hold back technical details of an exploited bug until most people have updated, so that more attackers cannot copy the method. Details may follow later. Sources Malwarebytes: Update Chrome now to fix a flaw attackers are exploiting (10 Nov 2026) SOC Prime: CVE-2026-125350, Chrome XML zero-day exploited in the wild Malwarebytes: Chrome 157 fixes 213 security issues, including 7 critical flaws (4 Nov 2026) Chrome Releases blog (Google), where the stable channel updates are posted Written by the Rapid+ Team. title: Do Smart TV Tracking Opt-Outs Work? What a New Study Found
desc: A university team measured what TVs send after you opt out of viewing tracking. Which brands stayed quiet, which did not, and what limits the findings have.
text: Written on 18 November 2026. The findings come from a Northeastern University study called "Watching the Watchers", as summarised by Malwarebytes on 5 November 2026. We did not read the full paper. The researchers could not see inside encrypted traffic, so the study shows that data kept flowing, not what it contained. Smart TVs can identify what is on their screen with a feature called automatic content recognition, or ACR, and sell what they learn to advertisers. Every major brand has a setting to turn it off. A new study tested whether those settings work, and for two big brands the answer was only partly. This is not a browser story, but it is the same story that runs through this blog: tracking you did not notice, a setting that looks like control, and a way to check whether the control is real. The short version Researchers at Northeastern University tested twelve smart TVs from ten manufacturers, covering eight operating systems that power about 95% of US smart TVs. They ran more than 5,000 automated sessions across ten viewing scenarios, each with ACR on and with the opt-out selected. Four TVs went completely silent after the opt-out: LG (webOS), Sony (Google TV), Amazon (Fire TV) and Supersonic (VIDAA). Vizio kept sending what looked like ACR traffic after the opt-out for first-party streaming and antenna TV. Samsung (Tizen) did so for some apps, HDMI input and first-party streaming. Because most ACR traffic is encrypted, the researchers inferred it from where it went, when and how much, not from its contents. What ACR is ACR captures audio, video or both from what your TV is showing and uploads it to a third party, usually the manufacturer. The recipient turns it into a digital fingerprint, matches it against a catalogue and learns what you are watching. This works for any source: a streaming app, an antenna, a cable box or a game console on an HDMI port. The result can support targeted advertising and audience measurement. The setting is often found in the privacy or terms menus under names such as "viewing information", and the wording differs from brand to brand. What the researchers found Brand (system) After opting out LG (webOS) No ACR traffic seen Sony (Google TV) No ACR traffic seen Amazon (Fire TV) No ACR traffic seen Supersonic (VIDAA) No ACR traffic seen Vizio ACR-like traffic continued for first-party streaming and antenna TV. None seen for third-party streaming. Samsung (Tizen) ACR-like traffic continued in some runs: about 7% for Netflix, 10% for YouTube, 20% for Tubi, 60% of HDMI sessions and all first-party streaming sessions. Malwarebytes also reports two details that deserve care. The researchers could not inspect Vizio's traffic to an Amazon endpoint, so they saw no change after the opt-out but could not confirm whether it breaks Vizio's 2017 settlement with the FTC. And Vizio's WatchFree+ service sent unencrypted titles of the shows or channels being watched, which users cannot turn off, according to the researchers. The VIDAA system was an exception to the encrypted pattern: it sent data unencrypted, and its servers, which needed no login at the time, exposed more than 57 million ACR detection results from other people's TVs, according to the Malwarebytes summary. What the study does not prove It shows traffic, not contents. Encryption hid the payload. The researchers inferred ACR traffic from the destination, timing, volume and protocol. It tested particular TVs. Twelve sets cannot represent every model and software version, and software updates can change behaviour in either direction. It does not prove a legal violation. That is for regulators and courts to decide. The honest reading is that an opt-out is not guaranteed to stop everything, and that this can be checked by measuring network traffic. What you can do Turn the setting off anyway. The researchers say the opt-out appears to be effective on the LG, Sony, Amazon and Supersonic sets in the study. On other brands it may reduce tracking even when it does not remove it. Use an external streaming device. One option the researchers suggest is to disconnect the TV from the internet and use a separate streaming stick. The TV then has no network path to send anything. Block known ACR servers at your router. The researchers published a blocklist on GitHub for this purpose. It takes some technical comfort to use. Treat app sign-ins carefully. Streaming apps on the TV tie your viewing to an account regardless of ACR. The link to your browser The TV problem and the browser problem look alike. In both, a company collects behavioural data, offers a setting and asks you to trust that it works. In the browser, you can see more: the developer tools show requests, and a content blocker shows what it stops. For a related case, our article on browser fingerprinting explains how a site can recognise a browser even after you clear cookies. Frequently asked questions What is ACR on a smart TV? Automatic content recognition is a feature that captures audio or video from the screen and uploads it, usually to the manufacturer, which identifies what is playing. It can support targeted advertising. Which TVs honoured the opt-out in the study? LG (webOS), Sony (Google TV), Amazon (Fire TV) and Supersonic (VIDAA) showed no ACR-like traffic after the opt-out. Vizio and Samsung did not fully honour it. Does this prove Vizio and Samsung are tracking me? It shows that traffic consistent with ACR continued after the opt-out. Because the traffic is encrypted, the study cannot say what data it carried. Is it safe to disconnect my TV from the internet? Yes, but you lose its built-in apps and updates. An external streaming device can fill that gap. Where is the study? It is called "Watching the Watchers", from Northeastern University researchers. Malwarebytes links to the project page, which is in the sources below. Sources Malwarebytes: Vizio, Samsung smart TVs seem to ignore tracking opt outs (5 Nov 2026) Watching the Watchers: project page of the Northeastern University study Written by the Rapid+ Team. title: Firefox's Free VPN Has No Data Cap Until 31 January: What It Covers and What It Does Not
desc: The cap is gone for a few months, but the VPN protects only traffic inside Firefox. Here is what that means in practice and where it falls short.
text: Written on 18 November 2026. The facts come from Help Net Security and OMG! Ubuntu, which reported Mozilla's change. We did not find a statement on logging or data handling in that reporting, so we do not make claims about it. Read Mozilla's own privacy notice before you rely on the service. Since 10 November 2026, Firefox's free built-in VPN has had no monthly data cap. Mozilla lifted the 50 GB limit until 31 January 2027, and on 1 February the cap returns. The offer is useful, and it is also easy to misunderstand, because this VPN protects only the traffic that goes through Firefox. This article explains what changed, what a browser-only VPN covers and what it leaves outside, and when it makes sense to switch it on. The short version The free VPN launched with Firefox 149 in March 2026 with a 50 GB monthly limit. From 10 November 2026 to 31 January 2027 there is no cap. You need a free Mozilla account to turn it on. It covers traffic inside Firefox and nothing else on the device. Mail clients, chat apps and games use your normal connection. It is available on desktop and Android in supported regions. At launch these were the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany and France. iOS support is planned without a date. It works in private windows, and you can set per-site exceptions so chosen sites bypass the VPN. Mozilla also sells Mozilla VPN, a separate paid product that covers the whole device. What changed When the feature launched, free users had 50 GB of VPN traffic each month. That is plenty for browsing, and not enough for hours of video. From 10 November the limit is gone for a set period. Mozilla ran a similar promotion earlier this year that raised the number of server locations to 28 for a time. Offers of this kind are marketing decisions, so plan on the 50 GB limit coming back on 1 February 2027. What a browser-only VPN covers A system VPN creates an encrypted tunnel for everything your device sends. A browser VPN creates one only for the browser's own requests. The difference shows up in everyday use. Traffic Goes through Firefox's VPN? Web pages loaded in Firefox Yes Private windows in Firefox Yes Sites you set as exceptions No, they use your normal connection Email apps, chat apps, games No Other browsers on the same device No System updates and background services No What the VPN does is replace your visible IP address with the VPN server's address for the sites you visit in Firefox, and hide the contents of your connection from the network you are on. That helps on public Wi-Fi and with simple location-based tracking. For a longer comparison of what each tool hides, see our article on proxies and VPNs. What it does not hide Your accounts. If you sign in to a site, the site knows who you are, whatever address you use. Your browser fingerprint. Screen size, fonts and other traits still identify a browser. Our article on fingerprinting explains why a VPN does not change that. Cookies. A site that set a cookie earlier can still recognise you. What the VPN provider sees. A VPN moves trust from your network to the provider. The reporting did not describe Mozilla's logging, so check its policy. A VPN is one layer. It is not a switch that makes you anonymous. When it is worth switching on On public Wi-Fi. At a cafe, hotel or airport, the VPN keeps the other people on the network from seeing the sites you visit. When your network blocks or throttles certain sites. A VPN can help, though it does not guarantee access, and some services block known VPN addresses. For a quick region test. Developers and shoppers sometimes check how a page looks from another country. It is less useful for banking, where your bank may flag a login from an unusual place, and for streaming services that block VPN addresses. How to try it Update Firefox to a current version. The free VPN arrived in version 149. Sign in with a Mozilla account. Creating one is free. Turn on the VPN from the Firefox interface. The reports we read do not give the exact menu steps, so look for the VPN option after signing in. Add exceptions for sites that misbehave behind a VPN, such as your bank. Frequently asked questions Is the Firefox VPN really free? Yes, with a Mozilla account and within the limits. Normally it has a 50 GB monthly cap, which is lifted from 10 November 2026 to 31 January 2027. The cap returns on 1 February 2027. Does it protect my whole phone or computer? No. It protects traffic inside Firefox only. Mozilla's separate paid product, Mozilla VPN, covers the system. Does it work in private browsing? Yes. According to OMG! Ubuntu, it also works in private mode, and you can set exceptions for individual sites. Does a VPN make me anonymous? No. It changes the address that sites see and hides your traffic from the local network. Logins, cookies and your browser fingerprint can still identify you. Which countries can use it? It is offered in supported regions. At launch these were the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany and France. Check Firefox for the current list. title: New York City Votes to Ban Surveillance Pricing: What the Bill Says
desc: The same product, a different price for you. What the New York City bill actually bans, what stays allowed and which browser habits feed the data behind it.
text: Written on 18 November 2026. This is a news explainer and not legal advice. Outlets differ on some details, such as the start date and how many places have similar laws, and we mark those points below. Check the city's own record for the final text. On 12 November 2026 the New York City Council voted 44 to 5 to ban "surveillance pricing", the practice of using a person's data to set a personal price for the same product. The bill still has to become law, and a similar state bill is waiting for the governor. Whatever happens next, the vote puts a name on something many shoppers have suspected: that the price you see online can depend on who the seller thinks you are. This article explains what the bill says, what it does not cover, and which of your browser's habits feed the data that such pricing depends on. The short version The City Council passed Introduction 891-A by 44 to 5. It was sponsored by Speaker Julie Menin, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani supports it. It bars businesses from using algorithms that draw on personal data to set individualised prices for the same goods or services. Bona fide, transparent discounts and rewards are allowed. The Record, which quoted the bill, lists loyalty programs and veteran and student discounts. The city's Department of Consumer and Worker Protection could fine violators up to $1,000 per violation, according to The Record. Reports differ on timing. Route Fifty says the ban takes effect one year after the bill becomes law, while another report gives 120 days. New York State's legislature passed a similar bill, the One Fair Price Act, in June. It awaits Governor Kathy Hochul's signature. What surveillance pricing means Dynamic pricing is old and mostly accepted: airlines and hotels raise prices when demand is high. Surveillance pricing is different. The price depends on you, not on the market. A seller may use what it knows about your location, your device, your browsing history, your past purchases or a profile bought from a data broker to estimate how much you will pay, and then show you a number to match. The bill, as described by Route Fifty, bars businesses from using algorithms that draw on New Yorkers' personal data to set individualised prices. Menin said: "They can't mine people's personal data to charge them a different price for the exact same good." The Record gives examples of the data at issue: search history, what users hover over online and data broker profiles about spending habits and demographics. What stays allowed The sponsors say the bill does not stop discounts. Menin said that any suggestion companies cannot offer discounts is "flatly incorrect". The Record reports that the bill carves out "bona fide discounts and rewards that are legitimate and transparent", including loyalty programs and veteran and student discounts. Ordinary price changes that apply to everyone, such as a weekend sale or a rise during a busy season, are a different thing from a price built for one person. Business groups did raise concerns. Route Fifty reports that Uber, whose services fall under the bill, objected, and a Times Union article it links says business groups have lobbied the governor to change the state version. Whether the city bill will cause problems for loyalty programs in practice is something regulators and courts will decide. Who else has acted The Record reports that Seattle passed a similar ban that was signed last month, and that New Jersey, Connecticut and Maryland already have bans. Route Fifty counts New York City as the fifth jurisdiction to act. Other outlets give different numbers, including calling it the second city after Seattle, so treat any count as approximate. The pattern is clear even if the number is not: local and state governments are moving faster than national lawmakers on this subject. The state bill is the one to watch. It passed in June and has been on the governor's desk for months. The Record says advocates fear the governor could use a power to amend passed bills to weaken it. Another outlet noted that the governor has until the end of the year to sign or veto it. What we do not know The Record notes that the companies allegedly using surveillance pricing have not been confirmed, and gives the example of Kroger, which denies using it. The bill is a rule against a practice, not proof that the practice is widespread. If you have noticed a different price on another device or account, that is an anecdote, and prices can differ for ordinary reasons such as stock levels, delivery location or a coupon that applied to one account. What your browser contributes Pricing built on personal data needs inputs. Some come from the shop itself, such as your account and purchase history. Others travel with your browser. Cookies and identifiers. Third-party cookies and ad IDs link your visits across sites. Your device and location. The user agent string, screen size and IP address reveal what you use and roughly where you are. Our article on user agent strings shows how much a single header says. Fingerprinting. Sites can combine many small traits into a recognisable profile without cookies, as we describe in the article on browser fingerprinting. Reducing these inputs is reasonable privacy hygiene. We are not claiming that it changes the price you are shown, because that has not been demonstrated in the reporting we read. What you can do is limit the data trail: Use a separate browser profile for shopping so that your other browsing does not mix in. Block third-party cookies and turn on tracking protection. Compare an important price in a private window or on another device, and screenshot any large difference. Be careful with loyalty apps, which tie purchases to your identity. Frequently asked questions Is the New York City ban in force now? No. The council has voted, but reports say it takes effect after the bill becomes law, and they differ on whether the delay is 120 days or one year. Check the city's legislative records for the current status. Does it ban all personalised pricing? No. It targets algorithmic prices set from personal data. Legitimate and transparent discounts and rewards, such as loyalty programs and student or veteran discounts, are allowed according to The Record. What is the penalty? The Record reports fines of up to $1,000 per violation, enforced by the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection. Does it apply outside New York City? No. Other places have their own rules. Seattle, New Jersey, Connecticut and Maryland are reported to have bans, and a New York State bill awaits the governor's signature. Can I tell whether a shop is personalising my price? Not reliably. Prices change for ordinary reasons. You can compare the same item across devices, a private window and a logged-out session, and keep screenshots, but a difference alone does not prove it. Sources Route Fifty: New York City Council votes to ban surveillance pricing (13 Nov 2026) The Record: NYC council passes bill to ban surveillance pricing Written by the Rapid+ Team. title: Online Age Verification: How It Works and What It Costs Your Privacy
desc: Age checks are meant to protect children but need data from everyone. A plain look at the methods, the arguments on both sides and your options.
text: Written on 18 November 2026. This article draws on the Electronic Frontier Foundation's page on age verification, which argues against such laws. We state its arguments as the EFF's and mark where laws and court decisions are reported by it. Supporters of these laws make a different case, which centres on protecting children, and we describe it where we can. Legal details change quickly, so check current law for your place. More websites now ask you to prove your age before they show you anything. The laws behind it are meant to protect children, and many people agree with that goal. Critics, including the Electronic Frontier Foundation, say the methods turn every visit into an identity check. This article explains how age checks work, what each method collects, and what you can do to limit the cost to your own privacy. The short version Age-verification laws require some websites and apps to confirm that a user is old enough. They started with adult content and have spread to social media and other services. The EFF says that every method needs "sensitive and immutable personal information" that connects a person's offline identity to their online activity. The EFF's list of methods: government ID checks, biometric face scans, algorithmic or behavioural monitoring and digital ID. It says that age estimation tools are often inaccurate and invasive. Everyone is checked, not only children, because a site cannot know who is a child without testing all users. Courts are in the middle of the argument. The EFF reports that in October 2026 two federal appeals courts allowed Florida and Georgia to enforce laws restricting young people's access to social media. What the laws do The details differ by place, but the pattern is the same: a service in scope must take steps to find out whether a user is an adult, or in some laws whether a user is over a particular age such as 16, and block or limit those who are not. The EFF lists several recent developments: It says that in October 2026 two federal appeals courts allowed Florida and Georgia to enforce laws that restrict young people's access to social media. It says California's AB 1709, signed by the governor on 10 September 2026, works as a ban on social media use for people under 16. It mentions the US Supreme Court decision in FSC v. Paxton, which concerns age verification, without giving details on the page we read. Other countries are moving too, and some are building government-backed apps or digital wallets for age checks. We did not verify the details in primary sources, so we do not describe them. How age checks work and what they collect Method What it needs The privacy question Government ID check A photo of an ID, sometimes with a selfie Name, birth date and ID number go to a service. Who stores them and for how long? Face scan (age estimation) A camera image Biometric data. The EFF says estimation is often inaccurate. Behavioural or algorithmic checks Browsing, posting and device signals Monitoring everyone to guess ages. Digital ID A credential in a wallet or app Can reveal only "over 18", if designed that way, but depends on the system. The table is a summary of the EFF's list and of how these methods generally work. Designs differ: a check can be done on your device, by the website or by a third-party vendor. The more it is done by a third party that retains data, the greater the risk of leaks. The EFF points to several breaches of age-verification providers and gives no counts for how many. The two sides Why supporters want it Supporters argue that children can easily reach content and social platforms that harm them, and that sites have too little incentive to keep them out. Age checks put a barrier at the door. Why critics object The EFF argues that the laws need sensitive data from everyone, that the data can be leaked, hacked or misused, and that the systems act as censorship tools: they can block people from seeing or sharing information that the government treats as harmful. It adds that age gates burden the expressive rights of adults and young people, and that they benefit large platforms while harming smaller ones. The page does not detail these last claims. Both sides describe the same facts. They disagree about whether the benefit is worth the cost, and about whether a design can protect children without building a database of who looks at what. What you can do Ask what is collected and kept. Before you upload an ID or a selfie, read what the service says about storage. Prefer methods that confirm your age and discard the image. Use the least revealing option. If a site offers several methods, an on-device check or a credential that says only "over 18" reveals less than a full ID upload. Do not reuse the same identity everywhere. Keep accounts that need verification in a separate browser profile, as described in our article on browser profiles. Be careful with look-alike pages. Scammers imitate age-check screens to collect ID photos. Check the address and only verify on a site you meant to visit. Our article on fake shops lists address checks that apply here too. Watch for tracking you did not expect. Verification can add new trackers and third-party calls to a page. A content blocker will show some of them. Take extra care with children's accounts. If you manage a child's device, built-in family settings can be a more private way to restrict access than uploading documents to many sites. What about VPNs? Some people respond to a check by using a VPN to appear in another region. That can change which version of a site you reach, but it is not a privacy solution, and some laws and services try to detect it. A VPN also moves trust to the provider, as we explain in the article on proxies and VPNs. Do not use a VPN to break the law where you live. Frequently asked questions Why do adults have to prove their age? A site cannot tell who is a child without checking all users, so the checks apply to everyone who reaches the gated content. What does the EFF object to? It says each method requires sensitive personal information that links offline identity to online activity, that the data can be leaked or misused, and that the laws can act as censorship and burden the speech of adults and young people. Are these laws in force? Some are. The EFF reports that two federal appeals courts allowed Florida and Georgia to enforce laws restricting young people's social media access in October 2026, and that California's AB 1709 was signed on 10 September 2026. Others face court challenges, so check the status where you live. Is face-based age estimation accurate? The EFF says age estimation tools are often inaccurate and invasive. Accuracy depends on the system and on the person. Can a check be private? It can be less invasive. A credential that proves only that you are over a certain age, checked on your device, reveals less than uploading an ID to a third party. How private it is depends on the design and on what is stored. Sources Electronic Frontier Foundation: Age verification (issue page) Written by the Rapid+ Team.
