title: Passkeys in 2026: What They Are, Who Uses Them and How to Start
desc: Passkeys replace passwords with a key pair that cannot be typed into a fake site. What the 2026 survey says and how to start safely.
text: Written on 18 November 2026. The adoption figures come from the FIDO Alliance's "State of Passkeys 2026" report, published on 7 May 2026. The FIDO Alliance promotes passkeys, so read the numbers as its own survey results. We used only figures stated on the report page. The FIDO Alliance says 5 billion passkeys are now in use and that 75% of surveyed consumers have turned them on for at least one account. Yet most people still type passwords every day. This article explains what a passkey is, why it resists phishing, what the surveys show, and how to start using them without locking yourself out. The short version A passkey replaces a password with a pair of cryptographic keys. The private key stays on your device and the website holds only the public key. A passkey cannot be typed into a fake site, so it blocks the most common kind of phishing. The FIDO Alliance's May 2026 report claims 5 billion passkeys in active use, 90% consumer familiarity and 75% of consumers having enabled them on at least some accounts. In the same report, 68% of surveyed organisations said they are deploying, piloting or rolling out passkeys for employees. Passkeys still have rough edges: moving them between password managers and handling lost devices. How a passkey works When you create a passkey for a website, your device generates two linked keys. The public key goes to the site, and the private key stays with you, protected by your fingerprint, face scan or device PIN. When you log in, the site sends a challenge, your device signs it with the private key after you approve it, and the site checks the signature with the public key. Three things follow from this design. Nothing secret is on the server. A site that is breached leaks public keys, which are useless to attackers. Nothing can be reused. Each site gets its own key pair, so one leak cannot open other accounts. Phishing fails. The browser ties a passkey to the real site's domain. A look-alike site gets no signature to steal, because the passkey will not be offered there. That last point is the main security gain. Passwords can be typed anywhere, including into a page made by a scammer. Our article on fake shops shows why that matters at this time of year. What the surveys show Measure (FIDO Alliance, May 2026) Result Passkeys in active use 5 billion Consumers familiar with passkeys 90% Consumers who enabled them on at least some accounts 75% Organisations deploying, piloting or rolling out passkeys for employees 68% The consumer survey asked 11,000 adults who regularly sign in to services, in ten countries including the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Japan and India. Sapio Research ran it online in April 2026, with a margin of error of 0.9 percentage points. The workforce survey asked 1,400 decision-makers at organisations with 500 or more employees, with a margin of error of 2.6 points. Two cautions apply. First, "enabled on at least some accounts" is a low bar: one passkey on one account counts. The report page does not give a separate figure for how often people use them. Second, a body that exists to promote passkeys published the survey. The numbers are plausible and useful, but they are not independent. The figures also do not tell you how many of your everyday logins use a passkey, because many sites still keep the password as a fallback. The rough edges Moving passkeys between systems A passkey lives in a credential manager such as the one built into your phone, your browser or a third-party password app. Moving it from one to another has been difficult. The FIDO Alliance has been working on standards for secure transfer, but support depends on each vendor, and you should check what yours offers. Losing a device If your passkeys are synced through your phone maker's cloud account or a password manager, a lost phone does not mean lost access. If they are tied to one device, it can. Always keep a second way in, such as a recovery code. Passwords stay as a fallback Many sites let you add a passkey but do not remove the password. An attacker can then try the password route. The security gain is greatest where a site lets you turn the password off, and smaller where it does not. How to start Pick where your passkeys will live. A password manager that you trust and use on all your devices is the simplest answer. Browsers and phones also store passkeys. Start with the accounts that matter most. Your email, your bank and any account that can reset others. A passkey on your email protects everything that relies on it for recovery. Look for "Create a passkey" in the account's security settings. Many services also offer it right after you sign in. Keep recovery options current. Store recovery codes offline, and make sure a phone number or backup email is up to date. Do not delete the password yet. Wait until you have used the passkey on all the devices you need. Major browsers support passkeys on the main platforms, though support varies by operating system and version, so check that the browser and credential manager you use can create and use them. Frequently asked questions Is a passkey the same as a password? No. A password is a secret you type and share with the site. A passkey is a key pair: the private key never leaves your device, and the site stores only the public key. Can phishing sites steal a passkey? Not in the usual way. The browser ties a passkey to the genuine site's domain, so a look-alike site gets no valid response. Attackers have to find other ways in, such as tricking you into approving a login or taking over your device. What if I lose my phone? If your passkeys sync through a cloud account or a password manager, you can restore them on a new device. If they are stored only on the lost device, use your recovery options. Set those up before you need them. Do passkeys work in every browser? Major browsers support them on the main platforms, though support varies by operating system and version. Check that the browser and credential manager you use can create and use passkeys. Should I delete my passwords? Not yet. Keep the password until the passkey works on every device you use and you have a recovery route. Where a site allows it, turning the password off later increases your safety. Sources FIDO Alliance: The State of Passkeys 2026, global consumer and workforce report (7 May 2026) FIDO Alliance: home page and specifications Written by the Rapid+ Team. title: Chrome Now Asks Before Opening Plain HTTP Sites: What Changed and What to Do
desc: Since Chrome 154, a public website without HTTPS triggers a warning before it loads. Here is what the new default covers, what it leaves out, and how it ties in with shorter certificate lifetimes.
text: Written on 8 November 2026. The facts below come from Google's own announcement, the Chrome 154 release notes and news coverage that we opened and read. Browser behaviour can change between builds, so the settings page of your own browser is the final word. Since the Chrome 154 stable release on 22 September 2026, Chrome asks before it opens a public website that does not support HTTPS. The setting is called "Always Use Secure Connections". Google first offered it in 2022 as an option that few people switched on. It is now the default for everyone. For most people nothing will look different, because the large majority of the web already uses HTTPS. The change matters in the places where it does show up: an old forum, a small shop's website, a link in an old email. This article explains what Chrome does now, why Google decided that the time had come, what the warning means, and how it connects to a second, quieter change in how long HTTPS certificates are allowed to last. The short version Chrome 154 reached the stable channel on 22 September 2026. Its release notes list the item "Ask before HTTP on by default". Chrome now tries to open every address over HTTPS. If a public site cannot be reached that way, Chrome shows a warning with an option to continue, and you decide. Chrome does not keep warning you about the same site. It warns on a new site, or one you have not visited recently. Private addresses are excluded. That covers local IP addresses such as 192.168.0.1, single-word hostnames and internal shortlinks. You can switch the behaviour off at chrome://settings/security. Administrators can manage it with the HttpsOnlyMode policy. Separately, the maximum life of a publicly trusted HTTPS certificate has been 200 days since 15 March 2026. It falls to 100 days in March 2027 and to 47 days in March 2029. What Chrome does now Before this change, typing or following a plain http:// address simply loaded the page, usually with a small "Not secure" label in the address bar. Many sites quietly sent the visitor on to the HTTPS version, so the label often never mattered. Under the new default, Chrome tries HTTPS first for every navigation. If the site answers over HTTPS, you arrive as usual and see nothing. If it does not, you get a full-page warning before anything loads. One how-to guide published on 6 November 2026 describes it as a screen headed "Connection is not secure" with a "Continue to site" button. If you press that button, the page opens over plain HTTP, as it always did. Google's announcement says the warning is meant to be rare. Chrome does not repeat it for sites you visit regularly. It appears for a site that is new to you or that you have not opened for a while. The setting itself is not new. It was added in 2022, and an experiment in Chrome 141 turned it on for a small group of users first. In April 2026, Chrome 147 enabled it for people who use Enhanced Safe Browsing, a group Google puts at over one billion users. Chrome 154 extends it to everyone. Why Google did it Google's reasoning, published in October 2025 under the title "HTTPS by default", rests on a simple observation. HTTPS is already normal, so the exceptions are now the dangerous part. The company's HTTPS transparency data shows that the share of page loads over HTTPS rose from roughly 30 to 45 percent in 2015 to about 95 to 99 percent around 2020, and has barely moved since. Google says the remaining plain-HTTP traffic is mostly invisible to users, because the site redirects to HTTPS straight away. That invisibility is the problem. The announcement points out that a single insecure navigation is enough for an attacker who can see or change traffic on the network, because the first request in a redirect chain travels unprotected. In Google's words, an attacker can hijack that navigation and send the visitor to malicious content. The post's conclusion is brief: "Now is the time." The company also had evidence that the change would be tolerable. In the Chrome 141 experiment, the median user saw fewer than one warning a week, and the user at the 95th percentile saw fewer than three. Google says warnings would appear on well under 3 percent of navigations, and expects that figure to fall as more sites move over. SecurityWeek reported that Google had already contacted organisations still running insecure connections. Why a redirect is not enough Many site owners reasoned that plain HTTP was harmless as long as their server redirected to HTTPS. That redirect has a weak point. When you type example.com without a scheme, or follow an old http:// link, the first request leaves your device unencrypted. It asks the server where to go next, and the answer is the redirect. Someone sitting between you and the server, for instance on a shared Wi-Fi network, can answer that first request themselves and send you somewhere else. Everything after that point can look normal. The new default shrinks this window. Chrome sends the first request over HTTPS itself, so there is no unprotected hop for a site that supports it. A site that does not support HTTPS is the one that now triggers the warning, which is the correct place for it. What is not covered Google drew a line between public and private sites. A public site is one such as example.com, which can get a certificate that browsers trust. Private sites cannot, because nobody can prove ownership of them in the same way. The announcement lists three kinds: Local IP addresses, such as the 192.168.0.1 address many home routers use. Single-label hostnames, which have no dot in them. Shortlinks used inside a company, such as intranet/. This is why developers and IT teams were not the main target. Your router's admin page, a test server on your own network and an internal company tool should open as before. The announcement adds one related detail. Once a user grants the new local network access permission, an HTTPS page can talk to devices on the local network without mixed-content blocking, which gives those sites a way to move to HTTPS. Address you open What Chrome 154 does by default A public site that supports HTTPS Opens normally over HTTPS. No warning. A public site with only HTTP Shows a warning first. You can continue. The same HTTP-only site, visited often Does not repeat the warning. A local address such as 192.168.0.1 Excluded from the default. A single-word internal hostname Excluded from the default. A site with an expired or invalid certificate Not this feature. It already gets Chrome's separate certificate error page. What to do when you see the warning The warning is not a verdict that the site is malicious. It says the connection to it cannot be protected. What you do next depends on what you were about to do there. Read the address. If you followed a link, check that the domain is the one you expected. A warning on an address you did not intend to visit is worth taking seriously. Try the secure version yourself. Type https:// in front of the domain. If the site supports it, it opens. Sites with a setup problem sometimes only work with or without www. Decide by what you will do on the page. Reading a public article over HTTP exposes less than logging in. Do not enter a password, card number or personal details on a page that is not protected. Anyone on the same network can read or change what you send. Tell the owner if you can. A shop or club whose site triggers the warning has probably never noticed. A short message often gets it fixed. Leave if unsure. If the page is not important, closing it costs nothing. To switch the feature off, open chrome://settings/security and turn off "Always use secure connections". On Android, one guide gives the route as the three-dot menu, then Settings, then Privacy and security, then Security. We would leave it on. The warning is rare, and the cases where it appears are the ones where the protection matters. The second change: shorter certificates HTTPS depends on certificates, which are small files issued by certificate authorities that prove a site controls its domain. A second change, agreed in 2025, makes those certificates expire much sooner. It matters because it makes HTTPS something sites must automate, and a site that fails to renew simply stops working over HTTPS. In April 2025 the CA/Browser Forum, the body where certificate authorities and browser makers agree shared rules, approved ballot SC-081v3. It sets a schedule that starts in March 2026 and ends in March 2029. Under it, the maximum validity of a publicly trusted certificate drops from 398 days to 47 days. The steps, as set out by a certificate vendor's summary of the ballot, are: From Maximum certificate life How long proof of domain control can be reused 15 March 2026 200 days 200 days 15 March 2027 100 days 100 days 15 March 2029 47 days 10 days Certificates issued before 15 March 2026 keep their original validity. The limits apply to certificates issued on or after each date, and only to publicly trusted authorities that follow the Forum's rules. Private certificate authorities that sit outside the public trust stores are not covered. Let's Encrypt, which already issues 90-day certificates, sits under the 200-day cap and is not directly affected. The people who feel the change are those who bought a one-year or multi-year certificate and renewed it by hand once a year. The two changes point the same way. Chrome now treats a site without HTTPS as the exception that needs your approval, and certificate rules push site owners toward renewing certificates automatically. A small website with a manually installed certificate has more to lose than before. If you run a website Serve everything over HTTPS and redirect http:// to https:// on the same host. Fix mixed content. Images, scripts or styles still loaded from http:// addresses cause trouble even on an HTTPS page. Automate renewal. With certificates lasting 200 days now and 47 days in 2029, a calendar reminder is not a plan. Use your host's built-in renewal or an ACME client, and have something alert you if it fails. Check old links. Search your own pages, newsletters and profiles for http:// links to your site. Test from outside. Open the site on a phone using mobile data, not only on your office network. Habits for everyone else Look at the address, not only the page. A padlock tells you the connection is encrypted. It does not tell you the site is honest, as the search hijack article and the Binance hack write-up both show. Be more careful on public Wi-Fi. The warning helps, but a proxy or VPN changes who can see your traffic, and each has limits. The proxy and VPN comparison covers them. Remember that HTTPS hides the content of a page, not the fact that you visited the site. The fingerprinting guide explains what else sites learn about you. Where Rapid+ fits We build Rapid+ Browser, so here is what we can state about our own app. On Android, when you type a bare domain such as example.com, Rapid+ opens the https:// version. When a site's certificate is invalid, Rapid+ shows a full-page warning and never continues silently. If you choose "Proceed anyway", the choice applies to that site in that tab for the current session only and is not saved. The site information panel says "Connection is not secure" for pages that are not protected. What Rapid+ does not do today is show a warning before it opens a plain http:// link. If you follow an old HTTP link, the page loads and the site information panel is where you see the status. Until that changes, check it before you type anything private. Rapid+ is built on the system's web engine, and this article describes Chrome, so do not assume the two behave the same. Frequently asked questions When did Chrome start asking before opening HTTP sites? Chrome 154 reached the stable channel on 22 September 2026. Its release notes list "Ask before HTTP on by default". Updates reach users gradually, so some people received it later than others. An earlier step in Chrome 147, in April 2026, covered users of Enhanced Safe Browsing. Does the warning mean the website is dangerous? No. It means the connection to the site cannot be protected, so anyone able to watch or change your traffic could read or alter what is sent. A harmless old site can trigger it. What matters is what you do on the page, and logging in or paying on an unprotected page is the real risk. Will I see this warning all the time? Unlikely. Google's experiment found that the median user saw fewer than one warning a week. Chrome also avoids repeating the warning for sites you visit regularly. Does this apply to my home router or a company intranet? No. Local IP addresses, single-word hostnames and internal shortlinks are excluded, because they cannot get certificates that browsers trust. Public websites are the target of the default. Can I turn it off? Yes. Open chrome://settings/security and switch off "Always use secure connections". Managed devices can be configured by an administrator with the HttpsOnlyMode policy. Does this affect Edge, Brave or other browsers? The announcement and the release notes we read describe Chrome. Other browsers set their own defaults, so check the security settings of the browser you use rather than assuming it behaves the same. title: Chrome Extensions Hijacked Search for 13.4 Million Users: What Happened and How to Check Your Browser
desc: Security researchers found 319 extensions that quietly changed the default search engine and sent every query through the operator's servers. What is confirmed, what is not, and a two-minute check.
text: Written on 5 November 2026. The campaign is still being tracked, and researchers keep finding new extensions. Most of the facts below come from the security firm Socket and from reports by BleepingComputer and Malwarebytes. We did not retrieve Socket's own report, so the list of affected extensions is not reproduced here. Use the link in the sources to check it. Socket researcher John Tuckner has documented 319 Chrome extensions that changed the default search engine in users' browsers and sent every search through servers run by the extension's operator before the results appeared. The extensions report a combined 13.4 million installs. Their operators were paid referral fees by Yahoo or Bing for the traffic. It is a search hijack, not a ransomware attack or a stolen password database, and so far there is no public evidence of stolen files or installed malware. It still matters, because a search box is where people type health questions, money worries and workplace problems. This article sets out what was found, what the extensions could and could not do, and how to check your own browser in about two minutes. The short version Socket found 319 extensions with about 13.4 million reported installs. BleepingComputer reported the findings on 29 October 2026. The new report builds on Tuckner's April 2025 finding of 57 extensions with 6 million users. It adds 264 extensions and about 8.7 million users. The extensions replaced the default search engine and routed queries through the operator's proxy before sending them to Bing or Yahoo. The operators earned referral payments. They were disguised as PDF converters, manual finders, "safe search" tools and "AI search" tools, and were promoted through ads. Socket did not find evidence that searches were redirected to phishing or malware pages. It warns that the destination could change at any time. The 13.4 million figure is a cumulative total over roughly a decade, not the number of people affected this week. Check chrome://extensions and the default search engine setting. Instructions are below. What the researchers found In April 2025 Tuckner described 57 extensions with about 6 million users that behaved this way. The October 2026 report widens the picture. It adds 264 extensions with about 8.7 million users, for a total of 319 and 13.4 million. BleepingComputer describes two large clusters. One, labelled "Bing-Search", has 37 extensions and about 2.2 million users and was often promoted through ads from a network called Bidbrain. The other, "SecuryBrowse", has 58 extensions and about 4.9 million users, and uses security-themed names such as Fire Shield, Securify and WatchTower. Most of the extensions had already been removed from the Chrome Web Store by the time of publication. New ones keep appearing. BleepingComputer asked Google for comment and had not received a reply when it published. How the hijack worked A single manifest setting Chrome lets an extension declare a replacement search provider through a manifest field called chrome_settings_overrides. The field exists for legitimate search tools. The campaign used it as the whole attack. Socket noted that one example had only a manifest and icons, with no background scripts, no content scripts and no requested permissions. An extension like that can look harmless in a review of what it is allowed to do. The detour Once the extension is installed, a search typed in the address bar goes first to a server controlled by the operator. That server passes the query on to Bing or Yahoo, tagged with a partner identifier that tells the search engine whom to pay. Tuckner ties the revenue to a syndication partner ID, which is how these referral programs normally track traffic. In one of his tests, an extension called Predator Search sent six identical searches to four different places: Yahoo with partner tags, a landing page on searchlio.net, a chain through searchtosearch.com to another domain, and a Cloudflare error page. The same search did not always lead to the same result. How people ended up installing them The extensions presented themselves as PDF converters, manual finders, safe-search tools and AI search tools. Most were unlisted in the Chrome Web Store, which means they did not appear in store search results and could only be installed through a direct link. Ads sent people to those links. Malwarebytes says the ads ran on networks that include Google Ads. What the risk actually is Malwarebytes quotes Socket on the main risk: the operators could see what users searched for. Queries were often tied to a unique identifier, which would let an operator link searches from the same browser over time. A person's searches can reveal medical concerns, finances and workplace issues. The second risk is the destination. Because the redirect sits on the operator's server, the page a user lands on can change without any extension update. Socket said it did not find evidence that the extensions had sent users to phishing or malware sites. It treats the behaviour as closer to a potentially unwanted program than to malware, but says the risk of malware remains. Claim What the reporting supports 13.4 million people were infected Not quite. It is the combined reported install count over about a decade, not the number of people newly affected this week. The extensions stole passwords No such finding has been reported. The extensions saw search queries Yes. Queries went through operator-controlled servers. Users were sent to malware pages Socket found no evidence of it, but the destination could be changed at any time. The problem is over No. Many of the listed extensions are gone, but new ones keep appearing. How to check your browser Malwarebytes recommends three checks. They take a few minutes and work the same way in other Chromium-based browsers, with a different address at the start. Review your extensions. Type chrome://extensions in the address bar. In Microsoft Edge the address is edge://extensions, and in Brave it is brave://extensions. Remove anything you do not recognise, no longer use or do not trust. If you are unsure about one, compare it with the list at the end of Socket's report. Check your search engine. Open the three-dot menu, choose Settings, then Search engine, and confirm the default is the one you picked. If the page says an extension controls this setting, open that extension and remove it. Run a security scan. Use an antivirus or anti-malware tool you already trust to look for other unwanted software. Do not treat a missing warning as proof of safety. Malwarebytes points out that the absence of a notice about an extension controlling a setting does not mean your extensions are clean. Signs that something changed Your default search engine changed and you did not change it. Results look unfamiliar, or a search leads to a site you did not expect. The extension list contains tools you do not remember installing. You installed a "PDF", "manual" or "safe search" tool after clicking an ad. Habits that reduce the risk Treat an ad for an extension as a warning sign. The campaign relied on advertising. A legitimate tool rarely needs it. Install only what you use. Each extension is code that runs inside your browser with access you granted once and may have forgotten. Look at the publisher, the install history and the reviews, and remember that a tool can sit in the official store for a long time before it is removed. Review your extension list and default search engine every few months. The two screens above take a minute. Keep work and personal browsing apart. A separate browser profile for work and money limits what a single bad extension can see. The reasons are covered in the profiles guide. Know who can see your searches. The same logic applies to proxies and VPN services. The proxy and VPN comparison explains what each one can and cannot hide. Where Rapid+ fits We build Rapid+ Browser, so the relevant fact is plain. Rapid+ for Android and Windows does not run browser extensions. This kind of hijack cannot arrive through an extension store because the feature does not exist. That is a limit as well as a protection, since you cannot add the tools that extensions provide. The search engine is set in Settings, and a change there is made by you. Rapid+ also has a built-in ad and tracker blocker, so there is less reason to install a separate blocking extension. None of this replaces the habits above on the computers and browsers where you do use extensions. Frequently asked questions How many Chrome extensions were involved? Socket researcher John Tuckner documented 319 extensions with about 13.4 million reported installs. That includes 57 extensions from his April 2025 report and 264 newly identified ones. What did the extensions do? They replaced the browser's default search engine and sent searches through servers controlled by the operator before passing them to Bing or Yahoo. The operators earned referral payments for the traffic. Were passwords or files stolen? No theft of passwords or files has been reported. Socket says it found no evidence that searches were redirected to phishing or malware pages, though the redirect could be changed at any time. Does this affect browsers other than Chrome? The extensions were found in the Chrome Web Store. Other Chromium-based browsers, such as Edge and Brave, can install Chrome extensions, so it is sensible to check the extension list there too. Reports in this campaign focus on Chrome. I removed the extension. Is my browser clean? Check that the default search engine is back to the one you chose and run a scan with a security tool you trust. Search results that still look unfamiliar are a reason to look further. Sources BleepingComputer: Chrome extensions with 13.4 million installs caught hijacking searches (29 Oct 2026) Malwarebytes: Fake PDF and search tools hijacked searches for 13.4 million Chrome users (Oct 2026) eSecurity Planet: Researchers uncover 319 Chrome extensions hijacking search traffic Gridinsoft: Searchjacked, hidden Chrome extensions put a proxy between you and search browsers.to: This week in browsers (1 Nov 2026) Socket's own report (the full extension list) is linked from the BleepingComputer and Malwarebytes articles above. Written by the Rapid+ Team. We build Rapid+ Browser for Android and Windows. Spotted a mistake or have a question? Email us at admin@rapidplusbrowser.online.

title: How Wars Cut the Internet: What Iran and Russia Show, and What Actually Helps
desc: Iran spent 88 days almost fully offline and Russia switches off mobile internet region by region. Here is what happened, what a VPN can and cannot do, and what you can prepare.
text: Written on 4 November 2026. Rules on the internet change often in countries at war. The newest reporting we could find on Iran is from mid-October, and on Russia from the spring. Treat the numbers below as a snapshot, and check the live trackers listed in the sources before you rely on them. When a war starts, the first thing many people try is to message their family. In Iran on 28 February 2026, that stopped working. On the day the strikes began, the monitoring group NetBlocks measured the country's connection to the outside internet at about 4 percent of normal. About a week later it was around 1 percent. The country stayed cut off for 88 days. Wartime internet cuts are not new, but 2026 has shown how complete they can get, and how different governments use them. Iran switched much of its population off. Russia switches off mobile internet region by region, saying it is a response to Ukrainian drones, and slowly squeezes the tools people use to get around blocks. This article explains what happened in both countries, what a VPN or proxy can and cannot do in each case, and what ordinary people can prepare in advance. The short version Iran's blackout that began with the strikes on 28 February lasted 88 days. NetBlocks called it the longest nationwide internet shutdown in modern history. Partial restoration began on 26 May, and social media stayed blocked. Iran's officials now say more restrictions are possible if the war escalates. They have also described a "tiered" system where some groups, such as traders, researchers and journalists, would keep international access. In Russia, authorities cut mobile internet in many regions, citing the threat of Ukrainian drones, and keep a growing list of approved websites that still work during cuts. A VPN or proxy cannot work if the whole connection is switched off. It can help when specific sites or apps are blocked, until the blockers learn to spot it. Using circumvention tools or satellite equipment can be illegal or dangerous in some countries. Know your local law before you decide. Three different things people call "an internet shutdown" News reports use one phrase for several different problems, and the fix for each is different. What it is What you see Does a VPN help? Full shutdown Almost nothing connects to the outside world. Domestic services may still work. No. A VPN needs a working connection to reach its server. Filtering The internet works, but certain sites and apps are blocked. Often, until the blocking system learns to recognise the VPN. Whitelisting or throttling Only approved services load, or everything is very slow. Only if the VPN's own traffic is on the approved list, which is rare. Most of the confusion comes from mixing these up. Advice that works against filtering, such as "install a VPN", does nothing in a full shutdown. Iran: from protests to war What happened, and when Iran's year of disruption began before the war. During nationwide protests in January, authorities cut access for about three weeks, according to Al Jazeera. When the war began, the internet went down again. When What happened 8 January Nationwide internet and phone blackout during protests. NetBlocks confirms the country is almost fully offline. Late January Access relaxes, but most users are limited to a list of approved sites. 28 February US and Israeli strikes on Iran begin. NetBlocks reports connectivity at about 4 percent of ordinary levels. 6 March Traffic is about 1 percent of normal. April A ceasefire takes effect on 8 April, but the shutdown continues. Around 21 April, authorities begin restoring access to "favoured groups". 25 to 26 May The president orders the blackout ended. NetBlocks confirms partial restoration on day 88, after about 2,093 hours. Late May onward Fixed broadband returns first and mobile networks in stages. Foreign social media stays blocked. The timeline above follows the Wikipedia summary of the blackout and the NetBlocks and Al Jazeera reporting it cites. The dates of the ceasefire are described differently in different sources, and Al Jazeera notes that fighting later eased but that there is still no permanent ceasefire. What it cost NetBlocks estimated the economic loss at up to $37 million a day, and about $1.8 billion in total by mid-April. Iran's communications minister gave a similar figure of $35.7 million a day. These are estimates, not audited numbers, but both the monitor and the government are in the same range. The human cost is harder to count. Families abroad could not reach relatives, including over the Nowruz holiday. Because Iran has no official public alert system, a crowdsourced app called Mahsa Alert was used to share missile warnings. Human rights groups including Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch have said the blackout hid violence during the crackdown on protesters. The government says it limits the internet to protect national systems from cyberattacks, and a spokesperson told reporters in October, "We don't deny this issue." Where it stands now The newest reporting is about satellite internet. Starlink is outlawed in Iran. According to Al Jazeera, using or owning a terminal carries a sentence of six months to two years, importing or distributing them up to five years, and the death penalty is possible if national security or espionage charges are added. Officials call Starlink a "tool of war" and say they have systems to cut off terminals. On 4 October, Iran summoned the Norwegian ambassador over the service. Officials also say more restrictions are possible if the war intensifies. The secretary of the Supreme National Cyberspace Council has backed tiered access, with protected international connections for selected groups. When a version of the idea was proposed in April, students and creators publicly called it discriminatory. A governance framework released in October says some platforms could be unblocked in future, but gives no timeline. Russia: switching off by region, and narrowing the exits Russia's approach looks different. There is no single national blackout. The reporting here comes mostly from Mediazona, an independent outlet, and much of it rests on residents' accounts rather than measurements. Regional mobile shutdowns. Authorities say they are a response to Ukrainian drones. Reports name regions including Omsk, Tyumen, Arkhangelsk, Rostov-on-Don, Bryansk and Krasnodar. Moscow's mobile internet was out for nearly three weeks in March, according to The Bell, which cited the FSB as the body that ordered base stations switched off. In February the State Duma passed a bill that lets the FSB demand shutdowns without the earlier condition of a security threat. A list of approved services. A "registry of socially significant services" was introduced in September 2025 with 57 websites. It includes state media, banks, government services and Russian apps such as VK, Yandex and the state-backed messenger Max. These keep working when ordinary internet is cut. Pressure on VPNs. Apple has removed VPN apps from its Russian App Store almost monthly. Mobile operators were told to charge for international mobile traffic above 15 GB a month from 1 May. Big Russian companies were told to block users who connect through a VPN or risk losing their place on the approved list. Messaging apps. Calls on Telegram and WhatsApp were restricted from August 2025, and tougher limits on Telegram were announced in February 2026. The day-to-day effects described to Mediazona are small and practical. Taxis could not be ordered, bus-tracking apps stopped, and in Bryansk many shops stopped accepting card payments. The article also says shutdowns do not appear to stop the drone strikes they are meant to prevent, and that the military has been frustrated by disrupted communications. That is the outlet's reading, not an official statement. What a VPN or proxy can and cannot do How blocking works Networks block in layers. They can remove a site's name from the directory that turns names into addresses (DNS). They can block the server addresses themselves. And they can inspect the traffic and block anything that looks like a known VPN, a method called deep packet inspection. Mediazona reports that the blocking of one VPN protocol in late 2025 was patchier than first claimed, and that most providers answered with new configurations. It is a game of catch-up, and it is why a tool that works one week may not work the next. When there is no connection at all In a full shutdown, the problem is not a blocked website. The link to the outside world is cut. A VPN, a proxy or a different browser cannot create a connection that is not there. Only a different physical route can, such as satellite, and in Iran that route carries serious legal risk. Three things to be careful about Fake VPN apps. When blocking increases, demand for VPNs jumps and so does the number of fake ones. Proton's censorship tracker, which is published by a VPN company and measures against an undefined baseline, reports surges of hundreds or thousands of percent in VPN use in countries during shutdowns and crackdowns, including Iran and Russia. Treat its figures as signs of demand, not exact measurements. Install any such tool only from its maker's own official page or a trusted app store. Free and unknown servers. A proxy or VPN operator can see the sites you visit and any unencrypted traffic. A server you do not know is a risk, not just a convenience. Legal risk. The law differs by country and changes quickly. This article is not advice to break any law. What ordinary people can prepare before a cut Most of what helps is not about software tricks. It is about what you have ready if the connection drops for days. Agree a plan with family. Decide in advance who contacts whom, at what time, and by which fallback, such as a regular phone call or SMS if those still work. Save the essentials offline. Download offline maps for your area, keep key phone numbers on paper, and save copies of important documents on your device. Know your local alert channels. Many countries send emergency alerts by SMS or cell broadcast, which can work when apps do not. Keep your apps and system updated, and install software only from official sources. Do this before a crisis, not during one. Keep sensitive accounts apart. A separate browser profile for banking and email keeps those logins away from everything else. The profiles guide explains how. If you are abroad and cannot reach someone, keep calls short and avoid pushing relatives to take risks to get online. Rely on verified news sources and not on forwarded messages. Where Rapid+ fits, and where it does not We build Rapid+ Browser, so here is the honest version. Rapid+ has a proxy and VPN mode that sends a profile's traffic through a SOCKS5 or HTTP proxy server that you provide. We do not run proxy servers or sell access. It cannot restore a connection that has been cut, and it does not make you anonymous. An HTTP proxy can read unencrypted traffic, and whoever runs the server can see where you go. It may help with filtering if you already have a proxy you trust and it is legal to use where you are. Rapid+ for Windows 1.3 also has a WebRTC setting that hides your real IP address from websites when you use a proxy, and a time zone setting. The matching options arrive on Android in the next update. None of this is a promise of safety in a country that actively hunts for circumvention tools. Frequently asked questions Can a VPN work during a total internet shutdown? No. A VPN needs an internet connection to reach its server. If the country's link to the outside world is cut, the VPN has nothing to connect through. It only helps when the connection works but certain sites or apps are blocked. What is the difference between a shutdown, filtering and a whitelist? A shutdown cuts most or all connections to the outside internet. Filtering lets the internet work but blocks specific sites and apps. A whitelist allows only approved services and leaves everything else unreachable. Why do governments cut the internet in wartime? Officials usually say they are protecting national systems from cyberattacks or preventing drone attacks. Human rights groups say the cuts also hide abuses and stop people sharing information. Both claims exist in the reporting above, and we cannot independently verify either. Is it legal to use a VPN? It depends on the country, and the rules change. In some places VPNs are legal but certain uses are not, and in Iran, for example, Starlink terminals are outlawed with heavy penalties. Check the law where you are before you decide. How can I check whether a country's internet is being cut? Public trackers publish live measurements. NetBlocks, Cloudflare Radar, OONI and the Access Now campaign against shutdowns are the common ones. They measure different things, so compare more than one. Sources Al Jazeera: Iran targets Starlink as "tool of war" with hints of more internet curbs (14 Oct 2026) Wikipedia: 2026 Internet blackout in Iran (timeline and cost estimates, with its own cited sources) NetBlocks on X: partial restoration of connectivity in Iran on day 88 (26 May 2026) Iran International: Iran restores internet after 88-day blackout, keeps social media blocked (25 May 2026) Mediazona: Russia's internet censorship in 2026: VPN crackdowns, mobile shutdowns, Telegram blocks and the state messenger Max (7 Apr 2026) Proton VPN: Internet censorship observatory 2026 (published by a VPN vendor; baseline not defined) NetBlocks · Cloudflare Radar · OONI · Access Now #KeepItOn (live trackers) Written by the Rapid+ Team. title: The Binance Hack: What Happened, What Was Lost, and What It Means for You
desc: Binance says about $6.3 billion was taken, the largest crypto theft on record. Here is what is confirmed, what is only reported, and what nobody knows yet.
text: Developing story. This was written on 1 November 2026 with the information available that day. Several figures are still preliminary and will change as analysts finish tracing the money. Binance has promised a detailed technical report, and this article is best read alongside it once it is published. On the evening of Thursday 29 October 2026, UTC, money started leaving Binance's wallets faster than anyone could react. Within hours the world's largest crypto exchange had paused withdrawals, its founder was telling people on X that the company had probably been hacked, and analysts were counting a loss that Binance itself put at about $6.3 billion. If that figure holds, it is the biggest theft in the history of cryptocurrency. Elliptic, a blockchain analysis firm, calls it "almost certainly the largest single theft of any kind in history." Two days on, the picture is clearer but far from complete. The FBI has named the group it believes is responsible. Binance says it has already replaced most of what was taken. Roughly half of the stolen value has been frozen. The question engineers care about most, how a company with that much security spending lost control of its wallets, has only a partial answer. This article keeps three layers apart: what Binance has confirmed, what outside analysts and officials have reported, and what nobody knows yet. The short version Binance estimates about $6.3 billion in assets was affected. Independent estimates range from about $5.9 billion to $6.43 billion. Around $3 billion has been frozen, mostly stablecoins. Elliptic independently verified about $2.85 billion. Binance's first explanation was a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer. It later said there were additional points of breach and has not described them. On 31 October the FBI said North Korea's TraderTraitor group was responsible. Binance says it will absorb the loss, reports replacing about 90 percent of the stolen amount, and planned to reopen withdrawals in stages on 1 November. No reporting so far says customer personal data was taken. What happened, and when Times are UTC. Most of the on-chain detail comes from Elliptic's reconstruction. The statements come from Binance and from news coverage. Binance has not yet published its own timeline. When What happened 28 to 29 Oct An attacker-controlled wallet receives three small withdrawals (0.1 ETH each) from Tornado Cash, a mixing service. The attacker's sweeper contract is rehearsed on another wallet about four hours before the attack. Thu 29 Oct, about 20:05 Five Binance wallets on the XRP Ledger send 233 million XRP to one attacker address. Hot wallets on the other chains follow over roughly the next half hour. 29 Oct, 20:20 to 20:24 On Ethereum, one transaction carries 50 authorizations tied to a Binance hot wallet that Elliptic calls "Binance 14". Minutes later the attacker's contract empties it of 167,464 ETH and 63 tokens, including about 1.6 billion USDT. 29 Oct, about 21:00 Tether freezes the attacker's main Ethereum wallet, locking about $1.18 billion in USDT. Circle freezes about $823 million in USDC. 29 Oct Binance tells reporters it is investigating a potential security issue and suspends withdrawals on multiple networks. Founder Changpeng Zhao posts that the company likely was hacked. 30 Oct Binance publishes a preliminary finding: a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, no evidence of a leaked wallet key, about $6.3 billion affected and about $3 billion frozen. TRM Labs and Chainalysis point to North Korea. The attacker sells stolen AVAX and bridges the proceeds to Ethereum. 30 Oct, later Co-CEO Richard Teng calls it a "complex attack" and says the attackers used malicious software built to delete evidence. Sat 31 Oct The FBI, with the Secret Service and IRS Criminal Investigation, names TraderTraitor and asks crypto businesses to block addresses the group uses. Binance says it has replaced 90 percent of the stolen amount and publishes a new proof of reserves snapshot. Sun 1 Nov Binance plans a staged reopening of withdrawals from 06:00 to 09:00 UTC across 15 networks, starting with Bitcoin, Ethereum, BNB Chain and Solana, according to reports. At the time of writing, we could not confirm it had happened. Speed is the first thing that stands out. Elliptic counts movements across 11 blockchains in about three hours, and the largest single sweep, the Ethereum hot wallet, took roughly three and a half minutes once the attacker's contract was in place. Tether's freeze landed about 40 minutes after that. By then most of the damage was done. How the attack appears to have worked What Binance has said Binance's own first explanation, posted on X, is that the incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which let an attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. It added that it had found no evidence of a leaked wallet private key. A DevOps engineer builds and runs the systems that other software runs on, so their laptop tends to hold credentials for servers and deployment tools. A service container is a packaged program running on one of those servers. The withdrawal service is the part of an exchange that takes a customer's request, builds the blockchain transaction and gets it signed from a hot wallet. A hot wallet is one connected to the internet so payouts can happen in seconds. If an attacker can reach a service that already has the authority to sign, they do not need to steal the keys. They ask the machine to sign for them. One reading that fits Binance's statement is exactly that. Elliptic's analysis points the same way: it describes abuse of Binance's own signing systems and sees a resemblance to the Bybit theft of February 2025. What the blockchain shows Elliptic's reading of the Ethereum data adds a detail. A feature called EIP-7702 lets an ordinary wallet hand control to a smart contract. The attacker used it: a single transaction carried 50 authorizations linked to a Binance hot wallet, after which a sweeper contract the attacker had written could drain the wallet in minutes. Elliptic quotes Teng saying the use of that feature "did not pass through our normal approval controls." The same report says a second Binance wallet, "Binance 16", sent about $174 million directly to the attacker, and that the attacker used a wallet's owner rights to pull 823 million USDC out of another one. What is still unknown The laptop was probably not the whole story. Binance has since said there were additional points of breach, and Teng said the attack "was not carried out by one person," according to Elliptic. Nobody outside Binance knows how the approval controls were bypassed, how long the attacker had access, or what the other points of breach were. The promised post-mortem is the document to wait for. How much was taken, and how much was frozen The amounts Elliptic's breakdown of what left Binance, at prices when it was taken: Network Taken Ethereum and Ethereum-based tokens about $3.80 billion across 186 tokens, including about 1.9 billion USDT and 823 million USDC Bitcoin 18,270 BTC, about $1.48 billion Tron 612.7 million USDT XRP Ledger 233 million XRP Total about $6.43 billion You will see several totals in the news, and they are not contradictions so much as different ways of counting: Binance: about $6.3 billion, its own estimate. Elliptic: $6.43 billion. It counts transfers from Binance to the attacker at the time of theft, and leaves out $169 million that left Binance after withdrawals were paused, which went to long-established addresses and looks like Binance moving its own funds. Chainalysis: roughly $5.9 billion at the time of the theft, as reported by CoinDesk. Early reports: "at least $2 billion" and then $5.7 to $5.8 billion. BleepingComputer's figure of up to $5.8 billion was a total of wallet holdings, not a confirmed loss. Dollar values also drift because the stolen assets are priced in a market that fell on the news. Treat every number here as preliminary. The frozen part Binance says about $3 billion has been frozen, including $2.3 billion in the stablecoins USDT and USDC. Elliptic verified $2.85 billion frozen or seized on-chain, 44 percent of the theft, and 94 percent of that was stablecoins on Ethereum and Tron. Tether's chief executive said it froze more than $1.57 billion, and Circle's said it froze more than $800 million. Optimism and Arbitrum secured all of the stolen funds on their networks through governance, and Aave froze the affected markets, according to Elliptic. Stablecoins freeze easily because a company stands behind each one. The issuer's contract can blacklist an address so that its tokens cannot move. Bitcoin and ether have no issuer. They can only be stopped if an exchange, bridge or other service in the path agrees to refuse the funds. That is why the unfrozen remainder, which Elliptic puts at about $3.21 billion and which includes 18,270 BTC and more than 519,000 ETH, is the part to worry about. Where the rest is going Elliptic's tracing shows an attacker in a hurry. About $786 million of stablecoins was swapped into ETH and TRX before freezes landed. One batch of 434 million USDT was converted to ETH at an implied loss of 12 to 26 percent, a haircut the attacker evidently accepted for speed. The bitcoin was split through a peel chain, a series of transfers that each peel a chunk off a large balance, into 19 addresses, mostly 1,000 BTC each. None had reached an exchange or other service at the time of Elliptic's report. The pace looks automated. The main Tron laundering wallet made 546 transfers from 30 October, with a median gap of 96 seconds. Chainalysis chief executive Jonathan Levin said the attackers had already used thousands of addresses and that the count could reach tens of thousands in the coming weeks as the money moves through bridges, instant exchanges and swappers. The FBI said the actors were mainly converting the haul into ether and expects them to keep laundering it in stages. Who is blamed, and how sure anyone is The attribution has two layers. The first is analyst judgment. TRM Labs assessed with high confidence that TraderTraitor, a North Korean state hacking unit linked to the Lazarus Group, was behind it, and Chainalysis and Elliptic reached the same view. Elliptic listed its evidence: the stolen funds are being laundered alongside proceeds of a September 2026 exploit of the exchange Bitget that it assessed as likely North Korean, the same services appear in three earlier TraderTraitor thefts, the preparation was long and appeared to target staff, and the abuse of signing systems resembles Bybit. It also argued that very few groups could coordinate across 11 chains in about three hours. The second layer is official. On 31 October the FBI said North Korea's TraderTraitor was responsible, the same group it blamed for the $1.5 billion Bybit theft. It urged crypto businesses to block transactions tied to the laundering and shared more than 600 Ethereum addresses, just under 20 Bitcoin addresses and one Solana address. What is still open: the FBI has not published the evidence behind its conclusion, and Binance has not described the attackers itself. The attribution is strong. The details of the intrusion are not yet public. What it means if you have money on Binance What Binance says Binance says customer funds are safe and that it will cover the loss. Its words: "Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users." It reports funding the replacement from its Secure Asset Fund for Users, known as SAFU, which holds about $1 billion in bitcoin, part of a futures insurance fund, and corporate money. SAFU alone could not cover $6.3 billion, so company money is doing most of the work. By Saturday Binance said it had replaced 90 percent of the stolen amount by buying new tokens, with the remainder mostly in less liquid assets it was still buying. Crypto Briefing reported that its ten most-held assets, including BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB and SOL, were fully covered. Later reports put overall replacement at about 95 percent, a figure that so far appears only in secondary coverage. What you can check Binance published a new proof of reserves snapshot at 00:00 UTC on 31 October, and outlets report a more detailed verification expected on 2 or 3 November. A proof of reserves compares the wallets an exchange controls against what it owes customers, and lets you confirm your own balance is counted. It is a useful signal, but it is not an audit and it says little about other debts. Treat it as one input. The market Bitcoin fell about 5 percent to below $77,000, ether about 5.7 percent, BNB about 8 percent and Aave about 11 percent, according to CoinDesk. DefiLlama put Binance's assets at roughly $144 billion before the theft, so the stolen amount is around 4 percent of that. Macquarie University's Sean Foley, quoted by Al Jazeera, said that "Any assets held at a centralised exchange are only as safe as the exchange itself." This article does not tell you whether to withdraw, hold or buy. It can tell you what is known, and a lot of it is still Binance's word. What about personal data? Nothing in the coverage so far says customer personal data, such as ID documents used for verification or email addresses, was accessed. Binance's statements are about wallets and funds. Read that as not reported, not as ruled out. If customer data was involved, the post-mortem is where it should show up. Binance has denied claims of leaked customer data in the past, including an alleged breach it said did not come from its systems, and those older claims are unrelated to this incident. The more immediate data risk is scams. Binance warned users to distrust unofficial links and messages asking for account details. News like this reliably triggers phishing: texts and emails claiming your withdrawal was cancelled, your account is locked, or you are owed compensation. In 2022 CoinDesk reported Binance's then chief executive warning about a text-message campaign built around a link to cancel a withdrawal, which led to a page that harvested logins. How it compares with earlier hacks Incident Amount Notes Binance (2026) about $6.3 billion (Binance), $6.43 billion (Elliptic) FBI blames TraderTraitor Bybit (2025) about $1.4 to $1.5 billion FBI and analysts blame TraderTraitor; a planned transfer was manipulated Ronin Network (2022) roughly $550 to $620 million, depending on prices Validator keys; US Treasury tied it to Lazarus BNB Chain bridge (2022) $570 million minted, about $100 million actually taken Chain was paused Poly Network (2021) about $611 million Nearly all returned within two weeks Coincheck (2018) about $530 million in NEM More than 260,000 users; about $400 million refunded Binance (2019) about 7,000 BTC, over $40 million One hot wallet; covered from SAFU Elliptic says the Binance theft is more than four times the size of Bybit and more than six times the roughly $1 billion taken from the Central Bank of Iraq in 2003. It also says the haul almost doubles what North Korea is believed to have stolen over the years, which it puts at more than $6.5 billion before this incident. TRM's 2026 report counted $2.87 billion stolen in nearly 150 hacks during all of 2025. Binance's own 2019 theft is a useful contrast. Then, hackers used phishing, viruses and stolen API keys and two-factor codes against a hot wallet holding about 2 percent of its funds, and SAFU covered the loss. This time the same fund is a fraction of what was needed. One laptop, six billion dollars Exchanges spend heavily on cold storage, approval workflows and hardware security. The reported way in was still a single employee's computer. That is the pattern in many large breaches: the strongest lock does not matter if someone can be handed the key, or a machine that already holds it can be made to act. Bybit's 2025 loss came from a manipulated transfer rather than a cracked wallet, and Ronin's from compromised validator keys. Your own setup is smaller, but the principle scales down. Your laptop or phone holds your email, your password manager, your exchange login and an open browser session. Malware that can read a page can use a logged-in account without ever learning the password, and two-factor codes do not help once a session has been hijacked. The device is the weak point more often than the algorithm. Protecting your own accounts None of this requires special skill. These are the habits that would have helped in the incidents above. Expect scams this week. Do not click links in texts or emails about the hack. Open the exchange's app or type the address yourself. Set an anti-phishing code in your account if the exchange offers one, so genuine emails carry it. Use passkeys or a hardware security key instead of SMS codes. SIM swapping and text interception are old and still effective. Turn on a withdrawal address whitelist and, where offered, a delay. An attacker who gets into your account then cannot send funds to a new address immediately. Revoke API keys you do not use and log out other sessions. Stolen API keys and two-factor codes were part of Binance's 2019 theft. Do not leave everything on an exchange. A balance there is a promise from a company. Holding your own keys has risks of its own, because losing a recovery phrase loses the funds, so decide with your eyes open. If you buy a hardware wallet, buy it from the maker. Never type a recovery phrase into a website or app, and ignore anyone who asks for it, including "support". Keep finance in its own browser profile with no extensions you do not need, a bookmarked exchange address, and an operating system and browser that are up to date. A separate profile keeps your shopping and social logins away from it. The reasons are covered in the profiles guide. Check the address bar every time. Look-alike domains and sponsored search ads are how many people reach fake exchange sites. Read proof of reserves reports with their limits in mind. They show one moment in time, and they are not a statement of everything an exchange owes. Frequently asked questions How much was stolen from Binance? Binance estimates about $6.3 billion in assets was affected. Elliptic puts the figure at about $6.43 billion and Chainalysis at roughly $5.9 billion at the time of the theft. The totals are preliminary and move with crypto prices. About $3 billion has been frozen. Is my money on Binance safe? Binance says user funds are safe and that it will absorb the loss. It reports replacing about 90 percent of the stolen assets and has published a new proof of reserves snapshot. Those are Binance's own statements, and a fuller independent check is still pending. This article is not financial advice. Who hacked Binance? The FBI said on 31 October 2026 that North Korea's TraderTraitor group, which is part of the wider Lazarus Group, was responsible. Private analysts at TRM Labs, Chainalysis and Elliptic had reached the same assessment earlier. Binance has not described the attackers itself. Was my personal data leaked? No reporting so far says customer personal data, such as ID documents or email addresses, was accessed in this incident. That means not reported, which is different from proven absent. Binance's technical post-mortem is where it should be settled. When can I withdraw again? Binance planned to reopen withdrawals in stages on 1 November 2026, starting with networks including Bitcoin, Ethereum, BNB Chain and Solana, and said exact timing could shift after security checks. Check Binance's official channels for the current status. Can the stolen money be recovered? Part of it has been frozen already, about $3 billion by Binance's count and $2.85 billion by Elliptic's verification, mostly stablecoins. The rest includes bitcoin and ether, which no company can freeze, and it is being moved through swaps and bridges. In the 2022 Ronin theft, which the US Treasury tied to Lazarus, only about $30 million was recovered, according to Decrypt. A note on Rapid+ Rapid+ Browser lets you keep a profile just for banking and crypto, with its own cookies and logins, on Android and Windows. It will not protect you from malware on your device, which is the lesson of this story: a browser is one layer, not the whole defense. Details are on the multiple profiles page. title: Browser Fingerprinting: How Websites Recognize You Without Cookies
desc: Nothing is stored on your device, so there is nothing to clear. Here is what fingerprinting measures, how well it works in practice, and what helps.
text: Clearing your cookies used to be the way to start fresh with a website. It still matters, but it is no longer the whole story. A fingerprinting script can recognize your browser by measuring it: the screen size, the fonts you have installed, your graphics hardware, your time zone and language, and small differences in how your machine draws text and processes sound. Nothing is saved on your device, so there is nothing to delete. This article explains what a fingerprint is made of, what the research says about how identifying it really is, how often it shows up on real websites, and which defenses make a difference. What a browser fingerprint is A fingerprint is a set of facts about your browser and device that, taken together, are rare enough to tell you apart from most other visitors. No single fact is special. Plenty of people use Chrome on Windows with an English interface and a 1920 by 1080 screen. The trick is in the combination. Once you add the time zone, the exact list of fonts, the graphics card and a few dozen other values, the group of browsers that match yours can shrink to one. The attributes fall into two groups. Passive signals These arrive with every request, whether or not a page runs any script. They include your IP address, the User-Agent header that names your browser and operating system, the Accept-Language header that lists your preferred languages, and the other headers your browser sends by default. Our article on the user agent string covers the first of those in detail. Active signals These require JavaScript on the page to go and collect them. Common ones include: Screen and window: resolution, available space, color depth and pixel density. Hardware hints: the number of processor cores and, in some browsers, an approximate amount of memory. Locale: the time zone reported by the system and the date and number formats it uses. Fonts: a script draws the same text in a long list of font names and measures the width of each result. A width that differs from the fallback font means that font is installed. Canvas: the script draws text and shapes into a hidden canvas element and reads the pixels back. Graphics drivers, font rendering and anti-aliasing all leave tiny differences, so the image hashes to a value that varies between machines. WebGL: the 3D graphics interface can report the graphics vendor and renderer, and rendered scenes vary between graphics stacks the same way canvas output does. Audio: the Web Audio API can generate a tone with an oscillator, run it through processing nodes, and hash the output. Differences in audio processing between systems change the result. None of these were designed for tracking. Each exists so that pages can lay themselves out, pick a language or draw graphics. Fingerprinting simply reads them all at once. How unique are browsers, really? Three large studies give a useful picture, and they do not all agree, which is itself informative. The 2010 EFF study Peter Eckersley at the Electronic Frontier Foundation ran the first large experiment through a test site called Panopticlick. Over two weeks it collected roughly 470,000 fingerprints from visitors who chose to take part. 83.6% of them were unique in the sample. Among browsers with Flash or Java installed, which exposed the full list of system fonts, 94.2% were unique. The paper is often credited as the first to use the term browser fingerprinting. The 2016 AmIUnique study Researchers Pierre Laperdrix, Walter Rudametkin and Benoit Baudry collected 118,934 fingerprints over a year through a site called AmIUnique, using 17 attributes including canvas and WebGL. Around 90% of desktop fingerprints were unique. Mobile fingerprints were somewhat less distinctive, but still around 81% unique. The 2018 large-scale study The same research group then partnered with one of the 15 most visited websites in France and analyzed 2,067,942 fingerprints from its ordinary visitors. Only 33.6% were unique. Among mobile visitors, fewer than one in five were. Why the drop? The earlier studies relied on people who went out of their way to visit a privacy test site, and those people tend to run unusual setups. Plugins such as Flash and Java, which leaked a lot, had also largely disappeared by 2018. Writing about the result for Princeton's Center for Information Technology Policy, Arvind Narayanan argued that the early numbers had overstated how well fingerprinting works, and that browsers could realistically reduce it further. The same paper made a less comforting point. Fingerprints that are not unique tend to be fragile. Change a few attributes, by installing a font or updating a driver, and a browser that was hiding in a crowd can become one of a kind. What this means in practice: a third of real visitors being identifiable from their browser alone is a lot less than headlines once suggested, but it is not small. Trackers also rarely rely on the fingerprint alone. They combine it with IP addresses, logins and whatever cookies survive. How common is it on real websites? In 2016, Steven Englehardt and Arvind Narayanan crawled the top one million websites with an instrumented browser. They found canvas fingerprinting on 14,371 sites, served by scripts from about 400 different domains, which works out to nearly 1.5% of the sites they measured. They also found a canvas based font fingerprinting technique on 3,250 sites, and documented audio fingerprinting through the AudioContext interface in the wild for the first time. Fingerprinting is not only used for advertising. Banks and online stores use it to notice when a login comes from an unfamiliar device. Bot detection services use it to tell scripted browsers from real ones. The difficulty for an ordinary visitor is that the same script can serve either purpose, and there is no way to tell from the outside which one it is doing. Why clearing cookies does not help A cookie is something a site stores and reads back. You can see it, delete it, or block it. A fingerprint is computed fresh on every visit from properties the browser already exposes. Deleting cookies, opening a private window or switching to a new browser profile on the same device leaves most of those properties unchanged: the screen, the graphics card, the fonts and the time zone are all still there. That does not make cookie controls pointless. They still stop the easiest and most reliable form of tracking. It just means they are one layer, not the whole defense. What actually reduces fingerprinting Browser makers have settled on two broad strategies, which pull in opposite directions. One makes everyone look the same. The other makes everyone look different every time. Blending in Tor Browser is the clearest example of the first approach. The Tor Project describes it as "specifically engineered to minimize the uniqueness of each user's fingerprint." Its users get the same set of values for as many attributes as possible. Even the window size is controlled: the browser starts with a content area rounded to a multiple of 200 by 100 pixels, and a feature called letterboxing adds margins when the window is resized so the reported size stays in a small number of buckets. The project also explains why it limits user choice, since "any option to choose would only make users more unique." Firefox takes a lighter version of the same path. It blocks scripts from Disconnect's list of known fingerprinters by default, and in private windows or with Enhanced Tracking Protection set to Strict it also limits the information exposed to suspected fingerprinters. Mozilla warns that these protections can occasionally break a site, and that turning protection off for that site fixes it. Randomizing Brave chose the opposite approach in 2020. It adds small amounts of random noise to the output of canvas, WebGL and audio APIs. The changes are invisible to people but change the hash. The important detail is that the noise differs between websites and between browsing sessions, so one site cannot use the value to link you to your activity on another, and a site cannot link today's visit to last week's. Brave's reasoning was that making every browser identical is unrealistic because the fingerprinting surface is so large. Shrinking what browsers reveal The third front is quieter. Browser makers have been reducing the detail they expose by default. Chrome's user agent string no longer carries the full version number or, on Android, the phone model. The W3C publishes guidance for authors of new web standards on how to avoid adding fresh fingerprinting surface in the first place. Blocking the scripts Finally, a tracker blocker that stops known fingerprinting domains from loading prevents the measurement from happening at all on pages that use those services. This does nothing against a site that runs its own fingerprinting code, but it covers the large third-party providers. Things that make you easier to fingerprint Unusual configurations. Rare fonts, a rare screen size or an uncommon language list all narrow the crowd you belong to. Many extensions. Some extensions change pages in ways a script can detect, and a particular combination of them can be distinctive. Inconsistent spoofing. Changing only your user agent can backfire. A browser that claims to be Safari on a Mac while reporting a Windows font list and an Android graphics driver is more unusual than one that tells the truth. Too many tweaks. The Tor Project's point applies everywhere: every setting you change away from the default is another thing that separates you from other people. How to check your own browser You can see what a fingerprinting script sees by visiting a test site. The EFF's Cover Your Tracks, the successor to the original Panopticlick, runs a set of common fingerprinting tests and compares the result with other recent visitors to the site. It reports how many bits of identifying information each attribute carries and whether your overall fingerprint looks unique. AmIUnique, run by the research group behind the 2016 study, does something similar and shows how each value compares with its own dataset. Read the results with the earlier caveat in mind. Visitors to these sites are self-selected and unusually privacy minded, so being unique among them is not the same as being unique among everyone. The useful part is the breakdown. If one attribute, such as a rare font list or an unusual screen size, carries far more information than the rest, that is the thing worth fixing. A practical checklist Keep your browser updated, since vendors keep reducing what they expose. Turn on the anti-tracking features your browser already has before reaching for extra tools. Keep extensions to the ones you actually use. Use separate browser profiles for separate identities. Profiles do not change your hardware fingerprint, but they keep logins and cookies apart, which removes the strongest link between them. If you need a different IP address for one profile, a proxy or VPN handles that part, though it does not change the fingerprint either. Test your setup on EFF's Cover Your Tracks site to see which attributes stand out. A note on Rapid+ Rapid+ Browser includes a built-in ad and tracker blocker that stops requests to known tracking domains, and it keeps each profile's cookies, logins and history separate. It does not claim to make you impossible to fingerprint, and no browser honestly can. You can read about these features on the features page. Sources Eckersley, How Unique Is Your Web Browser?
