title: Do Ad Blockers Make Pages Load Faster? What the Measurements Show
desc: Ads and trackers are a big share of what many pages download. What researchers measured, how blocking works, and what it costs.
text: The first thing many people notice after turning on an ad and tracker blocker is not the missing ads. It is that pages finish loading sooner and stop jumping around while they do. That impression is backed by measurements, though the size of the effect depends a great deal on the site you are looking at. This article looks at what a typical page actually loads, what researchers measured when they blocked ads and trackers, how blocking works, and what you give up in return. What a modern page actually loads When you open a news article, the article text is usually the smallest part of the job. The page also pulls in scripts, images and frames from other companies: ad networks, analytics services, consent banners, video players, chat widgets and social buttons. These are called third parties, because they come from domains other than the site you visited. The HTTP Archive measures this every year by crawling millions of pages. In its 2024 Web Almanac: 92% of pages loaded at least one third party. The median page among the top thousand websites used 66 different third parties. Across the top million it was 27. Scripts made up the largest share of third-party requests at 30.5%, followed by images at 26.0%. Nearly a third of third parties served advertising, analytics or consent management. Each of those third parties costs something. The browser has to look up a new domain name, open a new connection, download the file, and for scripts, parse and run the code. A script can then load more scripts of its own, so one ad slot can turn into a chain of requests to companies you have never heard of. What happens when one ad loads It helps to follow a single ad slot from start to finish, because the chain is longer than most people expect. The page loads the publisher's ad script, usually from an ad platform's domain. That script often runs an auction. It asks several ad exchanges at once what they will pay to show something to this visitor, sending along whatever it knows about the page and the browser. Each exchange may consult its own partners before answering, which means more requests to more domains. The winning bid returns an ad, which might be an image, a block of HTML or a video player. The ad itself frequently loads more scripts: one to confirm the ad was actually visible, one to count the impression for the advertiser, one or two tracking pixels for audience building. None of this is visible to you. You see one rectangle. Behind it, the browser may have contacted a dozen companies and run several scripts on your phone's processor. Multiply that by the number of ad slots on a long article and the numbers in the Web Almanac start to make sense. What the measurements found The Firefox Tracking Protection study The most cited controlled measurement comes from a 2015 paper by Georgios Kontaxis and Monica Chew, written while Firefox was preparing its Tracking Protection feature. They loaded the 200 most popular news sites, as ranked by Alexa at the time, with and without Tracking Protection, which blocks requests to domains on a list of known trackers. With protection on, they measured: a median 44% reduction in page load time, a median 39% reduction in data used, and a 67.5% reduction in the number of HTTP cookies set during the crawl. Those are medians across sites. Some pages barely changed. Others got dramatically faster. The New York Times mobile test Later that year The New York Times loaded the mobile home pages of 50 news sites with and without an ad blocker and compared the data used. Across the pages tested, more than half of all data came from ads and other content that ad blockers filter out. The results varied widely between sites, which is the same pattern the Firefox study found. Reading these numbers carefully Both studies are from 2015 and focus on news sites, which have always been among the heaviest users of advertising. The web has changed since then. Pages are larger overall, some publishers have trimmed their ad stacks, and browsers have added protections of their own. It would be wrong to promise you a 44% speedup on every site. A page built without heavy advertising, such as a documentation site or a small blog, has little to remove and will load about the same either way. What the research does show, consistently, is that on ad supported pages, third-party advertising and tracking code is a large share of the work, and removing it saves real time and data. Where the time goes Blocking helps in several different ways at once. Fewer network round trips. Every blocked domain is a lookup and a connection that never happens. Less JavaScript on the main thread. Scripts have to be parsed and run on the same thread that responds to your taps and scrolls. On a budget phone this is often a bigger cost than the download itself. Fewer layout jumps. Ads that load late push the text you are reading down the page. Without them, the layout settles sooner. Less data on metered plans. On a prepaid mobile plan, every megabyte of video ad you did not ask for comes out of your allowance. How blocking works Filter lists Most blockers rely on filter lists: large, community maintained collections of rules. Some rules match request addresses, so the browser never sends the request. Others are cosmetic rules that hide the empty boxes and leftover page elements an ad would have filled. Built into the browser Several browsers now block trackers without any extension. Firefox's Enhanced Tracking Protection blocks social media trackers, cross-site tracking cookies, fingerprinters and cryptominers by default. Built-in blocking runs inside the browser itself, so it does not depend on what the extension system allows. At the network level Some people block at the DNS level, with a home server or a filtering DNS service that refuses to resolve known ad domains. This covers every device on the network, including smart TVs and apps. The tradeoff is precision: it can only block whole domains, it cannot hide the empty space an ad leaves behind, and it cannot touch ads served from the same domain as the content. The Chrome extension change Extension based blocking in Chrome changed significantly with Manifest V3. The older extension platform let blockers inspect each request with the webRequest API and decide whether to cancel it. Manifest V3 moves that decision into the browser through a declarative rules system. Google's published timeline shows Manifest V2 extensions disabled for all Chrome users from Chrome 138 in July 2025, after a gradual rollout that began in late 2024. The most popular blocker, uBlock Origin, depended on the older API. Its author released a separate Manifest V3 version, uBlock Origin Lite, and its FAQ explains some of the limits: the declarative system cannot enforce rules according to the address shown in the address bar, so certain capabilities of the original cannot be carried over. The tradeoffs Some sites break Blocking a script a page depends on can break a login button, a video player or a checkout. Mozilla notes that its Strict tracking protection mode may cause breakage on some sites. Every good blocker lets you switch it off for a single site, and that is usually the fix. Publishers lose income Much of the free web is paid for by advertising. If you rely on a site, consider allowing it in your blocker or supporting it directly. Blocking trackers while allowing ordinary ads is a reasonable middle ground on sites you want to support. Blockers are only as good as their lists New ad and tracking domains appear all the time. A blocker with stale lists catches less, and a first-party tracker served from the site's own domain may slip through any list based approach. Why phones feel it most On a fast laptop with a wired connection, a page full of trackers might load in a second or two either way, and the difference is easy to miss. On a mid-range phone on a weak mobile signal, the same page has a slower processor running the scripts and a slower, less reliable network fetching them. Every extra connection costs more time, and every script takes longer to run while the page stays unresponsive. The same blocklist that saves a fraction of a second on a desktop can save several seconds on a phone, along with a noticeable share of a small data allowance. Choosing a blocker A few questions separate a good choice from a poor one: Who maintains the lists, and how often are they updated? A blocker is only as current as its rules. Can you turn it off for one site in a couple of taps? You will need this sooner or later. Does it block trackers as well as ads? For speed and privacy, the tracking scripts matter as much as the ads themselves. Does it depend on an extension platform that may change? The Chrome change above is a reminder that extension capabilities are decided by the browser maker. What does the blocker itself collect? Some extensions have been sold or changed hands over the years. Prefer ones with a clear owner and a clear privacy policy, or blocking built into a browser you already trust. How to measure it yourself You do not have to take anyone's word for it. In a desktop browser: Open the developer tools and switch to the Network panel. Tick the option to disable the cache, so every load starts from scratch. Load a page with your blocker switched off for that site and note the number of requests, the amount transferred and the finish time shown at the bottom of the panel. Turn the blocker back on, reload, and compare. Repeat a few times, since network conditions vary from one load to the next. Try a news site, a recipe site and a site with no ads at all. The differences between those three tell you more than any average. It blocks requests to known ad and tracking domains before they are sent, and Rapid+ itself collects no analytics from the app. You can read more on the features page. title: Proxy vs VPN: What Each One Actually Hides
desc: Both put another server between you and the web. They cover different traffic, protect it differently, and hide different things from different people.
text: A proxy and a VPN both put another computer between you and the websites you visit. That shared idea is why people use the two words as if they meant the same thing, and why some apps sell a plain proxy with a "VPN" label on it. They are not the same. The difference decides which of your traffic gets rerouted, whether anyone on your network can read it, and who ends up holding the list of sites you visit. This guide walks through how each one works at the network level, what each one hides and from whom, and when you would pick one over the other. The short version A proxy is something a single app is told to use. Your browser sends its requests to the proxy, the proxy talks to the website, and the website sees the proxy's IP address instead of yours. Apps that are not configured to use it keep connecting directly, as if the proxy did not exist. A VPN works one layer lower, inside the operating system. It creates a virtual network interface and routes traffic from every app on the device through an encrypted tunnel to the VPN server. Your browser, your mail client and the game updating in the background all leave through the same exit. Proxy (HTTP or SOCKS5) VPN What it covers Only apps set up to use it Traffic from the whole device, unless split tunneling is on Encryption to the server None of its own Yes, that is the purpose of the tunnel What the website sees The proxy's IP address The VPN server's IP address What your Wi-Fi or ISP sees The proxy's address, and usually the names of the sites you request through it One encrypted connection to the VPN server Where DNS lookups happen Depends on settings, often still on your own resolver Inside the tunnel, if the VPN is configured properly Typical setup A host, a port, and sometimes a username and password An app or a system profile from the provider How a proxy server works A proxy is a server that makes connections on a client's behalf. Your browser opens a connection to the proxy and asks it to reach a particular site. The proxy connects from its own address and passes data back and forth. MDN's guide to proxy servers separates the two directions you will see described: a forward proxy sits in front of clients, which is the kind you type into browser settings, while a reverse proxy sits in front of servers, the way a content delivery network does. The two forward proxy types you will meet most often are HTTP proxies and SOCKS5 proxies. They solve the same problem in different ways, and the differences matter. HTTP proxies and the CONNECT method An HTTP proxy speaks HTTP. When you load a plain http:// page through it, the browser hands the proxy the full request: the address, the headers, any cookies and any form data. The proxy reads all of it, fetches the page and returns the response. It can log that content, cache it, or change it before you see it. This is the main reason open proxies copied from public lists are a bad idea for anything that matters. You are giving a stranger a seat in the middle of your traffic. HTTPS works differently. For an https:// address the browser sends the proxy a short request such as CONNECT example.com:443. The HTTP specification defines this method in RFC 9110: the proxy opens a TCP connection to that host and from then on relays bytes in both directions without interpreting them. The browser then performs its TLS handshake with the real website through that tunnel. The result is that the proxy knows which host you asked for, when, and roughly how much data moved. It cannot read the pages, your passwords or your cookies, because those are encrypted between your browser and the website. An HTTP proxy is a reasonable tool for HTTPS browsing as long as you accept that its operator learns which sites you visit. SOCKS5 SOCKS is older and more general. Version 5 is defined in RFC 1928, published in 1996. A SOCKS server does not care which application protocol you speak. It relays TCP connections, and version 5 added a way to relay UDP as well through a command called UDP ASSOCIATE. The client tells the server which address and port it wants, the server connects, and after that it simply forwards data. Two details in the specifications matter in day to day use. First, SOCKS5 has no encryption of its own. The protocol negotiates how to authenticate and where to connect, nothing more. The most common login method, username and password, is defined in RFC 1929, and that document is blunt about it: the request "carries the password in cleartext," so the method is "not recommended for environments where 'sniffing' is possible and practical." If you use a password protected SOCKS5 proxy across the open internet, anyone on the path between you and that proxy can read the password. Second, a SOCKS5 request can name the destination either as an IP address or as a domain name. When the client sends the name, the proxy performs the DNS lookup. When the client resolves the name itself and sends only the IP address, the lookup happens on your own connection. That choice has real consequences. Where your DNS lookups happen Before a browser can connect anywhere it has to turn a name like example.com into an IP address. If that lookup goes to your usual resolver, which is often run by your internet provider, the provider still receives a list of every domain you visit, proxy or no proxy. Firefox exposes this as its own checkbox, "Proxy DNS when using SOCKS v5," backed by the network.proxy.socks_remote_dns preference. Mozilla's enterprise policy documentation lists the same switch as UseProxyForDNS. The command line tool curl makes the same distinction in its proxy schemes: socks5:// resolves names locally, while socks5h:// hands the name to the proxy. If the point of your SOCKS5 setup is to keep your browsing away from your provider, check that name lookups go through it too. How a VPN works A VPN, or virtual private network, adds a virtual network adapter to your device. The operating system routes traffic into that adapter, the VPN software encrypts it and sends it to the VPN server, and the server decrypts it and forwards it to the internet. Replies come back the same way. Common protocols include WireGuard, OpenVPN and IPsec. They differ in speed and design, but all of them encrypt the traffic between your device and the server. The Electronic Frontier Foundation's Surveillance Self-Defense guide puts it plainly: a VPN "routes all your web traffic through an 'encrypted tunnel' between your devices and the VPN server," and it "hides your outgoing traffic from your ISP and the local network owner." That second part is the main thing a VPN gives you that a basic proxy does not. The same guide is just as clear about the limits. Your browsing becomes visible to the VPN provider instead of your ISP, and "a VPN is not a tool for anonymity," because cookies, logins and fingerprinting can still identify you to the sites you visit. A VPN label is not a guarantee A VPN is only as trustworthy as the company that runs it and the app you install. In a 2016 study, researchers from CSIRO and partner institutions examined 283 Android apps that request the system VPN permission. 18% of them used tunneling protocols with no encryption at all, around 84% leaked IPv6 traffic outside the tunnel, and 66% leaked DNS traffic. Apps have improved since then, but the lesson still applies. The word on the label tells you nothing about how the app actually behaves. Who sees what The clearest way to compare the two is to go through each party that could be watching and ask what they learn. The website you visit With either one, the site sees the IP address of the proxy or VPN server instead of yours. That changes the location the site guesses for you and keeps your home connection out of its logs. It does not change anything else. If you are signed in, the site knows who you are. Cookies from earlier visits still identify you. Your browser's fingerprint is identical. Our guide to browser fingerprinting explains how much a site can learn with no cookies at all. Your Wi-Fi network and internet provider This is where the two really diverge. With an unencrypted proxy, whoever runs the café Wi-Fi, and your ISP, can see that you are connecting to the proxy. They can usually also see where you are asking it to go, because the destination travels in the clear, either in the CONNECT line of an HTTP proxy or inside the SOCKS request. For HTTPS sites they still cannot read the pages. For plain HTTP sites they can read everything. With a working VPN they see an encrypted stream to one server and nothing about what is inside it. There is a useful middle ground. OpenSSH's -D option makes ssh listen on a local port and "act as a SOCKS server," forwarding each connection over the encrypted SSH channel. Point your browser at that local port and the hop from your device to the SSH server is encrypted, so the local network sees only an SSH connection. You get proxy behavior for the apps you choose, with the network protection of a VPN. The proxy or VPN operator Both see the destinations of everything you send through them. A VPN operator sees this for every app on the device, not only the browser. Neither can read HTTPS content. Both can log timing, volume and destinations, and both can be compelled to hand those records over. The EFF guide notes that VPN providers receive law enforcement requests like anyone else, and that many keep as much information as ISPs do. Your other apps A proxy configured in the browser does nothing for other apps. Your mail client, messengers and system updates keep using your normal connection. Sometimes that is exactly what you want. Sometimes it is a leak you did not notice. When a proxy is the better choice You want routing per app or per profile. A proxy lets one browser profile appear to come from another country while everything else on the device, your banking app included, stays on your real connection. You need to see a site the way another region sees it. Developers, marketers and support staff do this constantly to check regional pricing, language redirects and geo restrictions. Your school or employer provides one. Many organizations require browser traffic to pass through an authenticated HTTP proxy. You already have a server. Any machine you can SSH into becomes a SOCKS5 proxy with a single command, and nothing extra needs to be installed on it. You care about overhead. A proxy adds no encryption layer of its own, so it asks less of the battery and processor on older phones. When a VPN is the better choice You are on a network you do not trust. Hotel and café Wi-Fi is the classic case. A VPN hides your traffic from whoever runs it. You want every app covered. Plenty of apps have no proxy setting at all. You want destinations hidden from your ISP. A plain proxy leaves them visible on the wire. You can also use both. A browser profile pointed at a proxy, on a device connected to a VPN, sends that profile's traffic into the VPN tunnel first and then out through the proxy. Mistakes worth avoiding Treating either one as anonymity Changing your IP address hides one signal out of many. A logged in account, a saved cookie or a distinctive browser fingerprint links your visits together regardless of the exit address. Using random free proxies An open proxy from a public list belongs to someone you know nothing about. For HTTP pages it can read and alter everything you send and receive. Even for HTTPS it learns every site you visit. If you would not hand a stranger your browsing history, do not route your browser through one. Forgetting DNS and IPv6 A SOCKS5 proxy without remote DNS still tells your resolver every domain you look up. On the VPN side, the leaks found in the Android study were mostly DNS and IPv6 traffic slipping around the tunnel. After changing anything, load a DNS leak test page and confirm the results match what you expect. Sending proxy passwords in the clear SOCKS5 username and password authentication is not encrypted. For a proxy you reach over the internet, wrap it in SSH or use a provider that offers an encrypted connection. A note on Rapid+ Rapid+ Browser has a proxy mode for HTTP and SOCKS5 that you set separately for each profile, with an optional username and password and a test button that checks the connection before you rely on it. It does not supply proxy servers. It connects to the one you choose. The details are on the proxy browser page. title: Separate Browser Profiles for Work, Personal and Shopping: Why They Work
desc: One browser, several separate lives. How profiles keep logins and cookies apart, what they do not protect, and how to set them up well.
text: Most people run their whole online life through one browser window. Work email sits next to personal email, the shopping site remembers last week's search, and every service you are signed into shares the same store of cookies. Browser profiles split that into separate spaces, each with its own logins, history and saved data. It is one of the simplest improvements you can make to both privacy and daily sanity, and every major browser already has it. What a profile actually separates A profile is a separate set of browser data kept in its own folder on your device. Google's help page for Chrome sums it up in one line: "With profiles, you can keep all your Chrome info separate, like bookmarks, history, passwords, and other settings." Apple's documentation for Safari, which added profiles in Safari 17, is more specific. Each profile has its own history, cookies, website data, extensions, Tab Groups and favorites. Extensions are installed once but switched on or off per profile, and new profiles start with them off. When you delete a profile, its history, cookies and website data go with it. The details vary between browsers, but the core is the same everywhere: cookies and site storage in one profile are invisible to the others. That one property is what makes profiles useful. Why cookies make this matter Cookies are small pieces of data a site asks your browser to store and send back with later requests. The cookie standard, RFC 6265, ties each cookie to the site that set it. That is how a site keeps you logged in: it hands your browser a session cookie, and every request after that carries the cookie back. Inside one profile, this means every tab that opens a given site shares the same login. If you are signed into one account, you are signed in everywhere in that profile. Want to use a second account on the same service at the same time? Most sites either do not allow it or make you juggle an account switcher. What browsers already do for third-party cookies For years, the bigger privacy problem was third-party cookies. An advertising network embedded on thousands of sites could set one cookie and read it back on every one of those sites, building a picture of your browsing. Browsers have since cut this down with storage partitioning. MDN explains that Firefox now "double-keys all client-side state by the origin of the resource being loaded and by the top-level site," so an embedded tracker gets a different storage area on each website it appears on. Mozilla turned this on for all desktop Firefox users in June 2022 under the name Total Cookie Protection, describing it as a separate "cookie jar" for every website you visit. Partitioning is a real improvement, but it solves a different problem. It stops one site's embedded tracker from following you to another site. It does nothing about the cookies of the sites you visit directly, which is exactly where your logins, carts and recommendations live. If you want your work account and your personal account kept apart, or your gift shopping kept off the family computer's main profile, partitioning will not do it. Separate profiles will. Profiles, private windows and containers Three features get confused with each other. They solve different problems. Private window Firefox container Profile Separate cookies and site data Yes, temporary Yes Yes Kept after you close it No Yes Yes Separate history Not saved at all No, shared Yes Separate extensions and settings No No, shared Yes Good for A one-off session you want forgotten Several accounts side by side in one window Long-term separate identities A private window is a throwaway profile. It is perfect for checking something without leaving a trace in your main history, but you cannot keep a login in it, because everything is discarded when you close it. Firefox's Multi-Account Containers extension gives each container its own storage, such as cookies and localStorage, so tabs in different containers can be signed into different accounts on the same site. All containers still live inside one Firefox profile, so bookmarks, extensions and the history list are shared. A profile is the most complete of the three. It keeps nearly everything apart, and it stays that way until you delete it. Where profiles earn their keep Work and personal accounts This is the classic case. Your work email, calendar and documents live in one profile. Your personal accounts live in another. You never send a work file from the wrong account, your personal bookmarks do not end up in front of a colleague during a screen share, and logging out of one does not log you out of the other. Shopping and research Shopping sites and their partners are among the heaviest users of tracking and personalization. Keeping that activity in its own profile means the recommendations and ads that follow your shopping stay in that profile, instead of appearing in the browser you use for everything else. Shared devices On a family tablet or laptop, a profile per person keeps each person's accounts, history and saved passwords out of the others' way. It is not a security wall against someone determined, but it prevents the everyday accidents. Clients and side projects Freelancers and agency staff often keep one profile per client, each signed into that client's accounts. Switching clients means switching profiles, not signing out of a dozen services. Testing and troubleshooting A clean profile with no extensions and no saved data is the quickest way to tell whether a broken site is broken for everyone or only for your setup. Pairing a profile with its own network settings Some browsers let a profile carry its own proxy or user agent. That turns a profile into a complete separate identity: its own logins, its own exit IP address and its own reported device, while your other profiles stay on your normal connection. A sample setup Here is a layout that works for a lot of people, to make the idea concrete. Profile Signed into Kept here Left out Work Work email, calendar, company tools Work bookmarks, the password manager your employer requires Personal social accounts, personal extensions Personal Personal email, banking, family photos Everyday bookmarks, your own password manager Shopping sites, random sign-ups Shopping and sign-ups Store accounts, newsletters, coupon sites Order tracking pages, wish lists Email and banking The rule of thumb is that each profile has one job. When you sign up for something new, ask which profile it belongs to before you create the account. That one habit does most of the work. Profiles and sync In browsers with a sync account, sync is usually tied to the profile, not to the whole browser. That is a feature. Your work profile can sync to a work account and your personal profile to a personal one, so bookmarks and passwords never cross between them, even on another computer. It also means a mistake carries over. If you sign your personal sync account into the work profile, your personal passwords and history arrive there on every device you use. Check which account each profile is synced to when you set it up, and again after reinstalling. What profiles do not do Profiles separate stored data. They do not change the device underneath, and that has consequences. Your fingerprint is the same. Every profile on a device shares the same screen, graphics hardware, fonts and time zone. A site that uses browser fingerprinting could recognize two profiles as the same machine. Your IP address is the same, unless you give a profile its own proxy or route it through a VPN. They are not a security boundary. Malware on the device, or anyone with access to your user account, can reach every profile's files. They do not lock by default. In most browsers anyone using the computer can open any profile. Some browsers add a lock, but check before you rely on it. Setting them up well Give each profile a clear name and color. The point is to always know which one you are in. A colored icon in the toolbar is enough. Start with two or three. Work, personal and one for shopping or experiments covers most people. Too many and you will stop using them consistently. Keep extensions minimal in each. An extension you need for work does not have to run while you shop. Lock the sensitive one. If your browser supports a lock per profile, use it for the profile that holds banking or work accounts. Decide where links open. Links from other apps usually open in the last used profile. Know which one that is. Mistakes that undo the benefit Signing in from the wrong profile The most common slip is clicking a link from an email or chat app, having it open in whichever profile was used last, and signing in there without noticing. The account is now in two profiles. Glance at the profile color before you type a password. Saving passwords everywhere When the browser offers to save a password, it saves it into the current profile. Saving the same password in several profiles spreads it around and defeats part of the separation. Save each login once, in the profile it belongs to. Making too many A profile per website is not organization, it is clutter. If you have to think about which profile to open, you will eventually stop opening the right one. What about phones? Profiles grew up as a desktop feature, and on phones the picture is patchier. Mobile browsers vary a lot here: some have no profiles at all, some offer only a separate private mode, and a few support several full profiles. Many people fall back on using two different browser apps, one for work and one for personal use, which gives the same separation at the cost of two sets of settings to maintain. If your phone is where most of your browsing happens, check what your mobile browser actually supports before building a habit around it. Cleaning up Deleting a profile is the cleanest reset a browser offers. Google's help page notes that when you delete a Chrome profile, "the profile's bookmarks, history, passwords, and other settings are erased from the computer." Apple says deleting a Safari profile removes its history, cookies and website data. That makes a throwaway profile useful for short projects: use it for a few weeks, export anything you need to keep, then delete it and everything it collected goes with it. A note on Rapid+ Profiles are at the center of Rapid+ Browser. Each profile has its own tabs, logins, cookies, history, bookmarks, saved passwords, proxy and settings, and you can switch between them in one tap. On Android a profile can be locked with your fingerprint or face, and on Windows with a PIN. The multiple profiles page has the details. Sources Google Chrome Help: Manage Chrome with multiple profiles Apple Support: Use profiles in Safari on Mac Mozilla Support: Multi-Account Containers RFC 6265: HTTP State Management Mechanism (cookies) MDN: State Partitioning Mozilla Blog: Firefox rolls out Total Cookie Protection by default to all users worldwide (June 2022) Written by the Rapid+ Team. title: What Is a User Agent String, and Why Do Websites Care?
desc: Your browser names five other browsers every time it loads a page. The reason is thirty years of browsers pretending to be each other.
text: Every request your browser makes carries a short line of text describing the software that sent it. In Chrome on Windows it reads something like this: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/143.0.0.0 Safari/537.36 That line mentions Mozilla, AppleWebKit, KHTML, Gecko, Chrome and Safari. You are using one browser. This is the user agent string, and the clutter inside it is the result of three decades of browsers pretending to be one another so that websites would treat them properly. Here is where it came from, what sites actually do with it, why browser makers have started freezing it, and when changing it is useful. What the user agent string is HTTP, the protocol every web page travels over, lets a client describe itself in a User-Agent request header. The current HTTP specification, RFC 9110, defines the header, and MDN describes it as "a characteristic string that lets servers and network peers identify the application, operating system, vendor, and/or version of the requesting user agent." The same value is available to scripts on the page through navigator.userAgent. So a site can read it both on its server, when the request arrives, and in the browser, after the page loads. For web browsers MDN gives the usual shape as: Mozilla/5.0 (<system-information>) <platform> (<platform-details>) <extensions> How it got so strange The best known telling of this history is a 2008 post by Aaron Andersen on the WebAIM blog. The short version goes like this. Early browsers named themselves honestly. NCSA Mosaic sent NCSA_Mosaic/2.0 (Windows 3.1). Then Netscape arrived. Its internal name was Mozilla, which the WebAIM post explains as short for "Mosaic Killer," and it identified itself as Mozilla/1.0. Netscape supported frames and Mosaic did not, so web developers started checking the user agent and sending framed pages only to browsers that said "Mozilla." When Internet Explorer arrived it also supported frames, but it was not Mozilla, so it got the plain version. Microsoft's answer was to make Internet Explorer say it was "Mozilla compatible," with strings like Mozilla/1.22 (compatible; MSIE 2.0; Windows 95). That pattern repeated for every new engine: The Mozilla project's Gecko engine, which later powered Firefox, used Mozilla/5.0 plus a Gecko/ token, and sites began checking for Gecko. Konqueror's KHTML engine was not Gecko, so it added (KHTML, like Gecko) to receive the same pages. Apple built Safari on KHTML, forked it into WebKit, and kept the "like Gecko" wording so sites written for KHTML kept working. Google's Chrome used WebKit and kept the Safari tokens too. Each browser inherited the previous browser's disguise and added its own name at the end. MDN's summary of the first token is dry but accurate: "For historical reasons, almost every browser today sends it." Reading a modern user agent Take the Chrome string from the top of this article apart, piece by piece: Token What it means Mozilla/5.0 Historical compatibility claim. Carries no real information. (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) Operating system and architecture. Windows 11 still reports itself as NT 10.0. AppleWebKit/537.36 Engine family. Chrome's Blink engine was forked from WebKit, and this version number has stayed fixed for years. (KHTML, like Gecko) Inherited compatibility claim from the KHTML days. Chrome/143.0.0.0 The actual browser and major version. The trailing zeros are deliberate. Safari/537.36 Another compatibility claim, so sites checking for Safari still serve WebKit friendly code. Firefox is shorter, and still carries its own fossil: a fixed Gecko/20100101 build date. Safari on a Mac reports a version token such as Version/26.0 next to a macOS version of 10_15_7, a number that no longer changes with the real operating system. Chrome on Android now reports something like (Linux; Android 10; K), where the Android version is fixed and the phone model has been replaced by a single letter. What websites do with it Sites read the user agent for a handful of reasons, some sensible and some not. Choosing a mobile or desktop page Many sites still decide between a phone layout and a desktop layout on the server. MDN's advice for this case is simple: look for the string Mobi anywhere in the user agent, and serve the desktop site when it is absent. Offering the right download Software sites read the operating system to put the right installer at the top of the page. It is a convenience, and it is why a download page sometimes guesses wrong when you have changed your user agent. Counting visitors Analytics tools group visits by browser and operating system so site owners know what to test against. Blocking or warning Some sites show an "unsupported browser" banner, or refuse to load at all, when they do not recognize the name in the string. Bot filters also look at it, since badly written scrapers often send an empty or obviously fake value. Guessing at features The worst use is deciding which features a browser supports from its name. MDN warns that parsing the user agent this way "is very hard to do reliably, and is often a cause of bugs," partly because browsers "routinely pretend to be another browser." Its example is a site that checks for the word "Chrome" before using a JavaScript feature. That check wrongly includes older Chrome versions and other Chromium based browsers, and wrongly excludes any other browser that adds the feature later. The recommended alternative is feature detection: test whether the feature exists, and use a fallback if it does not. Not just browsers Anything that speaks HTTP sends a user agent, and the ones outside browsers are often more honest. The command line tool curl, for instance, sends curl/ followed by its version number unless you tell it otherwise. Its manual notes that the header can be replaced with any value, or removed entirely by passing an empty one. Search engine crawlers identify themselves too. Google's crawler includes the word Googlebot in its user agent, and many sites treat it differently from ordinary visitors, since being crawled properly affects how they appear in search. That creates an obvious incentive to lie, and Google's own documentation addresses it. It describes "spammers or other troublemakers" accessing sites "while claiming to be from Google," and tells site owners to check the visitor's IP address instead: run a reverse DNS lookup, confirm the name ends in googlebot.com, google.com or googleusercontent.com, then run a forward lookup on that name and confirm it returns the original address. That advice sums up the user agent's place on the web. It is a useful hint that the client chooses to send. It is not proof of anything. Why browsers are freezing it A long, detailed user agent is useful for fingerprinting, since it adds identifying detail to every request without a single line of script. MDN notes that this "historically raised privacy concerns" and that supporting browsers now provide "a reduced set of information" in the header and in related JavaScript properties. Chrome made the biggest change. The Chromium project's User-Agent Reduction plan rolled out in stages: Chrome 101: the minor version became 0.0.0. Chrome 107: the reduced desktop string rolled out. Chrome 110: the reduced Android string rolled out, with the fixed Android 10 and the model replaced by K. Chrome 113: the last opt-out ended and every page load received the reduced string. The operating system tokens have been frozen too. Microsoft states that user agent strings "won't be updated to differentiate between Windows 11 and Windows 10," which is why both report Windows NT 10.0. User-Agent Client Hints The information did not disappear. It moved behind a request. Under the User-Agent Client Hints proposal, browsers that support it send only a few low detail values by default, in headers such as Sec-CH-UA and Sec-CH-UA-Platform. A server that needs more asks for it with an Accept-CH response header, and the browser includes the requested values on later requests. Scripts can do the same through navigator.userAgentData.getHighEntropyValues(). Microsoft's documentation shows how this works for the Windows question: a Sec-CH-UA-Platform-Version value of 13.0.0 or higher means Windows 11. It also lists which browsers support it at all. Edge, Chrome and Opera do. Firefox does not, so a site using Client Hints alone cannot tell which Windows version a Firefox user is on. How to see your own The quickest way is to open your browser's developer tools, switch to the Console, type navigator.userAgent and press Enter. The string your browser reports to scripts appears straight away. To see the header itself, open the Network panel, reload the page, click the first request and look under Request Headers. In browsers that support Client Hints you will see the Sec-CH-UA headers listed there as well, and you can compare how much each one reveals. Doing this once is worth it. It makes the freezing described above concrete: the version number ends in zeros, and on Windows 11 the operating system still reads as NT 10.0. When changing your user agent helps Most browsers can send a different user agent, either through a "desktop site" option, through developer tools, or through a dedicated switcher. There are good reasons to do it: Getting the full desktop site on a phone, when the mobile version hides a feature you need. Testing, to see how your own site responds to an iPhone or an older browser without owning one. Getting past lazy blocking, on sites that turn away browsers they do not recognize even though the browser would work fine. It also has limits that are easy to forget: It does not change your engine. Claiming to be Safari does not make your browser render like Safari. If a site sends code tailored to the browser it thinks you are, things can break. It does not hide you. The user agent is one attribute among dozens. A string that does not match your other signals, such as a desktop Mac claim from a touch screen device with an Android graphics driver, can make you stand out more. Our guide to browser fingerprinting explains why. Client Hints and scripts can still see the truth. If your browser sends Client Hints, or a page checks other properties, the disguise may only cover the header. A sensible habit is to change the user agent only where you need it, rather than everywhere. Keeping it per profile works well: one browser profile set to a desktop identity for a stubborn site, and your everyday profile left at the default.
